docs.title: Privacy Policy
docs.text:
Last updated: November 2, 2026

This page describes how ADC With Mounir Upload handles data. ADC With Mounir Upload is a private tool used only by Mounir Sahrani, the owner of the YouTube channel ADC with Mounir. It uploads the course videos and Shorts Mounir produces to his own channel, fills in their details (title, description, tags, thumbnail, playlist), tracks their publishing progress and publishes their translations.

docs.title: YouTube API Services
docs.text:
ADC With Mounir Upload uses the YouTube API Services. By using it, you agree to be bound by the YouTube Terms of Service. Google's handling of your data is described in the Google Privacy Policy.

The tool requests these Google OAuth scopes:

  • https://www.googleapis.com/auth/youtube.upload: upload videos and Shorts to the channel, with their title, description and thumbnail
  • https://www.googleapis.com/auth/youtube.force-ssl: list the channel's own videos (title, status, publication date) to track publishing progress, add them to playlists, download their caption tracks, and publish translated titles, descriptions and caption tracks

docs.title: What data is accessed and why
docs.text:
• The tool only acts on the YouTube channel of the account that authorized it (Mounir's own channel). It does not access any data about viewers or other YouTube users.
  • It reads the channel's own video list and caption tracks (with their timestamps) in order to: track publishing progress, translate videos, find segments that Mounir cuts from his original source files to create Shorts, and select excerpts of his own content that he posts on his X account.
  • It uploads videos, Shorts, translated titles and descriptions, and translated caption tracks to the channel.

docs.title: Storage and sharing
docs.text:
• The tool is operated through the Claude AI assistant (Anthropic). Caption tracks and video details are sent to Claude only to perform the tasks above, under Anthropic's Privacy Policy. They are not used to train AI models.
  • Excerpts of Mounir's own content may be published by him on his own X account.
  • No data is sold, used for advertising, or shared with anyone else.
  • The only stored credential is the authorization token of Mounir's own account, kept in a private environment and never published.
  • The use of information received from Google APIs adheres to the Google API Services User Data Policy, including the Limited Use requirements.

docs.title: Data retention and deletion
docs.text:
• Caption tracks and video details are kept only as long as needed to complete a task, then deleted.
  • To delete all stored data, revoke access (see below); the stored token is then deleted. Deletion requests can also be sent to adcwithmounir@gmail.com.

docs.title: Revoking access
docs.text: Access can be revoked at any time from the Google Account permissions page: https://myaccount.google.com/permissions (or https://security.google.com/settings/security/permissions). Once revoked, the tool can no longer access the channel.

docs.title: This website
docs.text: This website is a static site hosted on GitHub Pages. It has no account system and no contact form, and it does not collect personal data. GitHub may process technical data (such as IP addresses) to serve the pages, as described in the GitHub Privacy Statement.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: Questions about this policy: adcwithmounir@gmail.com

docs.title: Part 1 practice questions: Java fundamentals
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Part 1 · Java Fundamentals / Core Syntax

Optional page

Ten exam-style questions covering all of Part 1. Try each one before opening its answer. To review a topic, go back to the Part 1 recap.

1. Which are valid entry points for a program run from the command line? (Choose all that apply.)

A. public static void main(String[] args) B. public static final main(String[] args) C. public void main(String[] args) D. public static void main(String... args) E. static public void main(String[] args)

Answer

A, D and E. B has no return type at all, so it doesn't even compile. C misses static. Varargs and swapping public/static are both fine.

2. In which order must these lines appear for the file to compile?

X: class StreamingPlatform {}
Y: import java.util.*;
Z: package com.netflix;

A. X, Y, Z B. Y, Z, X C. Z, Y, X D. Z, X, Y

Answer

C. Package, then imports, then the class.

3. Which are legal identifiers? (Choose all that apply.)

A. _streamingService B. 4kResolution C. $contentId D. true E. MAX_EPISODES F. java.lang

Answer

A, C and E. B starts with a digit, true is a literal and can't be used as a name, and a dot isn't allowed in an identifier.

4. Which statements about this class are true? (Choose all that apply.)

public class Movie {
    private String title;
    public Movie() { title = "Unknown"; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
}

A. Movie is a class B. title is a class C. getTitle() is a constructor D. Movie() is a constructor

Answer

A and D. Movie() matches the class name and has no return type. title is a field, and getTitle() is a method: it returns a String.

5. Which lines compile? (Choose all that apply. Each line is a local variable.)

A. var title = "Stranger Things";
B. var episodes = 8;
C. var rating;
D. var content = null;
Answer

A and B (String and int). C has no value to infer from, and D gives null, which has no type.

6. What is the output?

public class Subscription {
    static int totalUsers = 0;
    int userId;
    { userId = ++totalUsers; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Subscription s1 = new Subscription();
        Subscription s2 = new Subscription();
        System.out.println(s1.userId + " " + s2.userId);
    }
}

A. 0 0 B. 1 1 C. 1 2 D. Compilation error

Answer

C. The instance initializer runs for each new object: totalUsers becomes 1 for s1, then 2 for s2.

7. Which statements about garbage collection are true? (Choose all that apply.)

A. System.gc() runs garbage collection immediately B. An object is eligible when no reference can reach it C. The collector frees unused heap memory automatically D. A final variable prevents its object from being collected

Answer

B and C. System.gc() is only a hint. final prevents reassignment, nothing more: the object can still become unreachable.

8. What happens?

public class Episode {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int season = 1;
        {
            int episode = 5;
            season++;
        }
        System.out.println(season);
        System.out.println(episode);   // line 9
    }
}

A. Prints 2, then 5 B. Prints 2, then throws an exception C. Compilation error on line 9 D. Compilation error on line 5

Answer

C. episode belongs to the inner block and is out of scope on line 9. It's a compile-time error, so nothing prints.

9. Which imports let this class compile? (Choose all that apply.)

package com.netflix;
// INSERT IMPORT HERE
public class ContentLibrary {
    public void load() {
        List<String> titles = new ArrayList<>();
    }
}

A. import java.util.*; B. import java.util.List; import java.util.ArrayList; C. import java.util.List.*; D. import java.util.concurrent.*;

Answer

A and B. C is a legal line, but it imports the types nested inside List, not List or ArrayList. D imports a sub-package that contains neither.

10. What is the output?

public class StreamingApp {
    static int count;
    { System.out.print(count + "-"); }
    static { count = 5; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StreamingApp a = new StreamingApp();
        StreamingApp b = new StreamingApp();
        System.out.print(count);
    }
}

A. 0-0-5 B. 5-5-5 C. 0-5-5 D. Compilation error

Answer

B. The static block runs once, when the class is set up, before main: count is 5 before any object exists. Each instance initializer then prints 5-.

docs.title: How Java Works Under the Hood
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

Before writing real Java code, it helps to know what Java actually does with it. Your code goes through a short journey — compile, then run — and a handful of tools make it happen.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 From source code to running program 3 min 2 Your JDK: what's inside and which version 3 min 3 Lab: your first Java file 3 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: none — this is where the course starts.

Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

docs.title: From source code to running program
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · How Java Works Under the Hood · 1/3

docs.title: Three steps, every time
docs.text:
Every Java program follows the same journey:

Step Tool Input → output 1. Write your editor Movie.java — source code, plain text 2. Compile javac Movie.java → Movie.class — bytecode 3. Run java (the JVM) executes Movie.class 
$ javac Movie.java     # compile: creates Movie.class
$ java Movie           # run: the JVM executes the bytecode

Bytecode is a middle language. It is no longer human-readable source code, but it is not machine code either. The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) turns it into instructions for the machine it runs on.

docs.title: Write once, run anywhere
docs.text: Bytecode doesn't depend on the operating system. The same Movie.class runs unchanged on Windows, macOS or Linux, as long as a JVM is installed. That's the promise Java made in 1995, and it still holds: you compile once, and the JVM of each machine does the rest.

docs.title: The tools in the JDK
docs.text:
The JDK (Java Development Kit) is the toolbox you install to write Java. Four of its tools come up early:

Tool Role Example javac compiler: .java → .class javac Movie.java java launcher: starts the JVM and runs a class java Movie jar packager: bundles .class files into one .jar archive jar cf app.jar *.class javadoc generates HTML documentation from code comments javadoc Movie.java

To start, you only need two: javac to compile, java to run. The other tools come in later, when a project grows.

docs.title: Two details that matter from day one
docs.text:
• javac takes a file name, with its extension: javac Movie.java.
  • java takes a class name, without any extension: java Movie, never java Movie.class.

Java is also case-sensitive everywhere: Movie, movie and MOVIE are three different names.

Now that the journey is clear, let's look at the JDK itself and which version to install.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

Next: your JDK →

docs.title: Your JDK: what's inside and which version
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · How Java Works Under the Hood · 2/3

You know the journey: write, compile with javac, run with java. Now let's set up the toolbox that makes it possible.

docs.title: Where did the JRE go?
docs.text:
Older tutorials mention the JRE (Java Runtime Environment). Here is what changed:

Up to Java 10 Since Java 11 JRE: JVM + core libraries, to run programs only No separate JRE anymore JDK: the JRE + developer tools (javac, jar…) JDK contains everything: JVM, libraries and tools

Today the rule is simple: install the JDK, and you have everything needed to write and run Java.

docs.title: Which version?
docs.text:
A new Java version comes out every six months, but most teams use the LTS versions (Long-Term Support), which stay supported for years:

  • Java 17 — LTS, released in September 2021. This course targets it.
  • Java 21 — the next LTS, released in September 2023. Almost everything in this course applies to it too.

Pick one version and stick with it while you learn.

docs.title: Which distribution?
docs.text:
Several builds of the same JDK exist. Any of these works for this course:

Distribution Where Notes Oracle JDK oracle.com/java official, free for development and personal use OpenJDK jdk.java.net fully open source, same code base Eclipse Temurin adoptium.net popular free build with long-term support

After installing, check both tools in a terminal:

$ java -version
$ javac -version

Both should report version 17.

docs.title: IDE or command line?
docs.text:
An IDE (IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, VS Code with the Java extensions) gives you autocomplete, error highlighting, a debugger and refactoring tools. Use one for real projects.

But when you click Run, the IDE simply calls javac and java for you. Knowing those two commands keeps you in control: you understand what the IDE does, and you can still build and run a program on a machine without one.

Time to put this into practice with the very first file of our streaming platform.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

← From source to running program · Next: the lab →

docs.title: Lab: your first Java file
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · How Java Works Under the Hood · 3/3

Goal: go through the full write → compile → run cycle with the first class of our Netflix-style streaming platform.

Setup: open an empty folder (for example netflix-platform) in your editor, open a terminal in it, and create a file named exactly Movie.java — capital M. No build tool needed.

docs.title: Step 1 — Declare the class
docs.text:
public class Movie {

}
  • public makes the class visible to everything, including the JVM.
  • class says you are defining a blueprint, and Movie is its name.
  • The public class name must match the file name exactly: Movie lives in Movie.java.

docs.title: Step 2 — Add two fields
docs.text:
Inside the braces:

    // Title of the movie on the platform
    String title;

    // Duration in minutes
    int durationMinutes;

String holds text, like "Inception". int holds a whole number, like 148. Lines starting with // are comments: notes for humans, ignored by the compiler.

docs.title: Step 3 — Add a main method
docs.text:
To run the class, it needs a main method. Add it after the fields:

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Welcome to the Netflix Platform!");
        System.out.println("Movie class loaded successfully.");
        System.out.println("Fields defined: title (String), durationMinutes (int)");
    }

main is static, so it can't use title directly yet: that needs an object, which comes a few sections later.

docs.title: Step 4 — Compile
docs.text:
$ javac Movie.java

No output means no errors. A new file, Movie.class, appears next to Movie.java: that's the bytecode.

docs.title: Step 5 — Run
docs.text:
$ java Movie
Welcome to the Netflix Platform!
Movie class loaded successfully.
Fields defined: title (String), durationMinutes (int)

The JVM loaded Movie.class, found main and ran its lines from top to bottom.

docs.title: Final code
docs.text:
public class Movie {

    // Title of the movie on the platform
    String title;

    // Duration in minutes
    int durationMinutes;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Welcome to the Netflix Platform!");
        System.out.println("Movie class loaded successfully.");
        System.out.println("Fields defined: title (String), durationMinutes (int)");
    }
}

docs.title: OCP exam prep: how Java works
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · How Java Works Under the Hood

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — javac compiles, java runs

javac Movie.java takes a file name with its extension and produces Movie.class. java Movie takes a class name, without .class. The exam shows command-line snippets, not IDE buttons.

Trap 2 — Public class name = file name

public class Movie must live in Movie.java. A mismatch, even only in letter case, is a compilation error.

Trap 3 — Case-sensitive everywhere

Movie, movie and MOVIE are three different identifiers: class names, variables and keywords alike.

Trap 4 — The JDK includes everything

Since Java 11 there is no separate JRE download: the JDK brings the JVM, the libraries and javac, java, jar and javadoc.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. A file named StreamingPlatform.java contains public class streamingPlatform { }. What happens when you run javac StreamingPlatform.java?

A. It compiles and produces streamingPlatform.class B. Compilation error C. It compiles and produces StreamingPlatform.class D. It compiles, but java StreamingPlatform fails at runtime

Answer

B. The public class must have exactly the file's name, letter case included. streamingPlatform ≠ StreamingPlatform, so the compiler refuses the file. Running never even starts.

2. Movie.class exists and has a valid main method. What happens with java Movie.class?

A. The program runs B. Compilation error C. Error: java expects a class name, without .class D. The JVM ignores the extension and runs the program

Answer

C. java looks for a class literally named Movie.class, which doesn't exist, so the launcher fails to find or load it. It isn't a compilation error: javac isn't involved. The right command is java Movie.

docs.title: Your First Java Class
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

The class is the building block of every Java program. Here you'll see what a class is made of — data, behavior and comments — how Java maps classes to files, and how the main method turns a class into a runnable program.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 Anatomy of a class: fields and methods 3 min 2 Comments, files and the main method 3 min 3 Lab: the StreamingPlatform class 3 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: How Java Works Under the Hood.

Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

docs.title: Anatomy of a class: fields and methods
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · Your First Java Class · 1/3

docs.title: A class is a blueprint
docs.text:
An architect's plan isn't a house, but it describes everything about the house. A class works the same way: it describes what an object looks like and what it can do.

public class Movie {

    String title;
    int releaseYear;

    public String getTitle() {
        return title;
    }
}
Part In the example Role class + name class Movie declares the blueprint; class names start with an uppercase letter Fields title, releaseYear the object's data (its state) Methods getTitle() the object's behavior: what it can do

docs.title: Fields: the data
docs.text:
A field is a variable that lives inside a class. It answers the question what do we need to know about a movie? Every field has a type and a name:

public class Movie {
    String title;          // text
    String genre;
    int releaseYear;       // whole number
    double rating;         // decimal number
    boolean isAvailable;   // true or false
}
Type Holds Example value String text "Inception", "Action" int whole numbers 2010 double decimal numbers 8.5 boolean true or false is the movie available to stream?

These four types cover most of the data you'll store at first. More types come later in the course.

docs.title: Methods: the behavior
docs.text:
A method is something the object can do. It has a return type, a name, optional parameters and a body:

public class Movie {
    String title;

    public String getTitle() {               // returns a String
        return title;
    }

    public int countWatchers(int month) {    // takes an int parameter
        return 10;
    }

    public void markUnavailable() {          // returns nothing
        // no value returned
    }
}
Part Example Meaning Return type String, int, void what the method gives back; void means nothing Name getTitle, markUnavailable a verb describing the action Parameters (int month) input values; empty () means none Body { ... } the code that runs when the method is called

public means the method can be called from anywhere. Access modifiers get their own section later.

A class with fields and methods is a good start, but it can't run on its own yet. Next: comments, how classes map to files, and the main method.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

Next: comments, files and the main method →

docs.title: Comments, files and the main method
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Your First Java Class · 2/3

You can now write a class with fields and methods. Three more things turn it into a real, runnable program.

docs.title: Comments: notes for humans
docs.text:
The compiler ignores comments completely. Java has three kinds:

// Single-line comment: everything after // on this line is ignored

/*
 * Multi-line comment: everything between the markers is ignored.
 */

/**
 * Javadoc comment: read by tools to generate HTML documentation.
 * @author Mounir
 */
public class StreamingPlatform {
    String name;   // store the platform name
}
Comment Starts / ends Use it for Single-line // to the end of the line short notes Multi-line /* … */ longer explanations Javadoc /** … */ documenting classes and methods

docs.title: One public class per file
docs.text:
Java ties classes to files with strict rules:

// File: Movie.java

public class Movie {      // the public class: same name as the file
    String title;
}

class Helper {            // allowed: a second class, but not public
}
  • A public class named Movie must live in Movie.java: same spelling, same letter case.
  • A file can hold several classes, but only one can be public.
  • Compiling Movie.java produces one .class file per class (Movie.class, Helper.class).

In practice, you'll put each class in its own file.

docs.title: The main method: where a program starts
docs.text:
The JVM starts every program in a method with this exact signature:

public class StreamingPlatform {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Welcome to ADC Flix!");
    }
}

$ javac StreamingPlatform.java
$ java StreamingPlatform
Welcome to ADC Flix!
Keyword Why it's there public the JVM must be able to call it from outside static it belongs to the class: the JVM calls it without creating an object void main returns nothing to the JVM String[] args the words typed after the class name on the command line

System.out.println(...) prints a line to the console.

docs.title: Command-line arguments
docs.text:
args is an array of String. Its first element is args[0]:

public class Greeting {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, " + args[0]);
    }
}

$ java Greeting Mounir
Hello, Mounir

Run it without any argument and args[0] doesn't exist: the program stops with an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

You now have every piece of a complete class. Let's assemble them in the lab.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

docs.title: Lab: the StreamingPlatform class
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Your First Java Class · 3/3

Goal: write a complete class with documentation, data, behavior and an entry point, then run it.

Setup: in your project folder, create StreamingPlatform.java. Compile and run it from the terminal.

docs.title: Step 1 — Document the class
docs.text:
Start with a Javadoc comment, then the class declaration:

/**
 * Entry point of the ADC Flix platform.
 * @author Mounir
 */
public class StreamingPlatform {

}

The double asterisk /** makes it Javadoc. @author is a standard Javadoc tag. Editors show this text when you hover over the class name.

docs.title: Step 2 — Add a field
docs.text:
// Platform name
    String name;

Every StreamingPlatform object will have a name. It gets its value later, once an object exists.

docs.title: Step 3 — Add a method
docs.text:
// Display a welcome message
    public void launch() {
        System.out.println("ADC Flix is live!");
    }

void: the method does something and returns nothing.

docs.title: Step 4 — Add the main method
docs.text:
public static void main(String[] args) {
        StreamingPlatform p = new StreamingPlatform();
        p.name = "ADC Flix";
        p.launch();
    }
  • new StreamingPlatform() creates an object in memory, and p refers to it.
  • p.name = "ADC Flix" sets the object's field: the dot reaches what belongs to an object.
  • p.launch() calls the method on that object.

docs.title: Step 5 — Compile and run
docs.text:
$ javac StreamingPlatform.java
$ java StreamingPlatform
ADC Flix is live!

docs.title: Final code
docs.text:
/**
 * Entry point of the ADC Flix platform.
 * @author Mounir
 */
public class StreamingPlatform {

    // Platform name
    String name;

    // Display a welcome message
    public void launch() {
        System.out.println("ADC Flix is live!");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StreamingPlatform p = new StreamingPlatform();
        p.name = "ADC Flix";
        p.launch();
    }
}

docs.title: OCP exam prep: class structure
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Your First Java Class

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Create classes, and define and use instance and static fields and methods.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — The main signature must be exact

public static void main(String[] args) (or String... args). Without static, with int instead of void, or with String instead of String[], the JVM can't use it as an entry point.

Trap 2 — File name = public class name

A public class Movie must be in Movie.java, letter case included. A mismatch is a compiler error, not a runtime error.

Trap 3 — Code hidden in comments

Questions often comment out lines that look like code. Before tracing anything, check what // and /* */ remove.

Trap 4 — args starts at index 0

args[0] is the first argument. Reading it when no argument was passed throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at runtime.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Which signature lets the JVM run the program?

A. public static void main(String[] args) B. public void main(String[] args) C. static void main(String args) D. public static int main(String[] args)

Answer

A. B misses static: the JVM doesn't create an object to call main. C takes a String, not a String[]. D returns int, but main must return void.

2. Which statement is true about this file?

// File: Content.java
public class Series {
    String title;
}
class Content { }

A. It compiles B. It fails: a file can hold only one class C. It fails: the file name doesn't match the public class D. It fails: Content is not public

Answer

C. The public class is Series, so the file must be Series.java. Two classes in one file are fine as long as only one is public, and non-public classes don't need public.

docs.title: Writing Your First main() Method
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

Every Java program starts in the same place: the main method. Here you'll learn what each word of its signature does, which variations Java accepts, which ones break your program, and how to pass data to a program when you launch it.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 The main signature, word by word 3 min 2 What breaks main, and command-line arguments 3 min 3 Lab: launching the streaming platform 3 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: Your First Java Class.

Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

docs.title: The main signature, word by word
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · Writing Your First main() Method · 1/3

docs.title: The front door of your program
docs.text:
When you run java StreamingApp, the JVM looks inside StreamingApp for one specific method and starts there: main.

public class StreamingApp {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // the program starts here
        System.out.println("Netflix is loading...");
    }
}

In Java, everything lives inside a class, including the entry point. If the JVM finds no valid main, the program doesn't start.

docs.title: Each word has a job
docs.text:
public static void main(String[] args) { ... }
Word Meaning Why the JVM needs it public visible from outside the class the JVM calls it from outside static belongs to the class, not to an object no object exists yet when the program starts void returns nothing when main ends, the program ends main the name the JVM looks for lowercase, exactly String[] args an array of String receives the words typed after the class name

Change any of these incorrectly and the JVM no longer recognizes the method as the entry point.

docs.title: Valid variations
docs.text:
Java is flexible on a few details. All of these work:

public static void main(String[] args) { }          // the classic form: use this one
public static void main(String[] arguments) { }     // the parameter name is free
public static void main(String... args) { }         // varargs: same as String[]
static public void main(String[] args) { }          // public and static in any order
public static final void main(String[] args) { }    // final is allowed

What must stay fixed:

  • the method is public and static,
  • it returns void,
  • it's named main, in lowercase,
  • it takes one String[] or String... parameter.

String... is varargs syntax: for the JVM it's the same as an array of String.

You know what a valid entry point looks like. Next: the mistakes that silently break it, and how to use args.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

Next: what breaks main →

docs.title: What breaks main, and command-line arguments
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Writing Your First main() Method · 2/3

A valid main is public static void main(String[] args), with a few allowed variations. Here's what goes wrong when it isn't.

docs.title: It compiles, but it doesn't run
docs.text:
Each of these methods compiles without any error. The class is fine: it just has no entry point the JVM can use.

public void main(String[] args) { }                   // ❌ missing static
public static int main(String[] args) { return 0; }   // ❌ must return void
public static void main(int[] args) { }               // ❌ must take String[] or String...
public static void Main(String[] args) { }            // ❌ Main is not main

The problem shows up only when you launch the class:

$ java StreamingApp
Error: Main method is not static in class StreamingApp, please define the main method as:
   public static void main(String[] args)

This difference between compiling and running matters: a class doesn't need a main to compile. Only the class you launch needs one.

docs.title: Passing data at launch
docs.text:
Every word typed after the class name becomes one element of args:

public class StreamingLauncher {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Args count: " + args.length);
        System.out.println("First arg: " + args[0]);
    }
}

$ java StreamingLauncher Netflix Premium
Args count: 2
First arg: Netflix
  • Spaces separate the values: args[0] is Netflix, args[1] is Premium.
  • Indexes start at 0.
  • args.length gives the number of arguments.

docs.title: Check before you read
docs.text:
Launch the same program without arguments and args is an empty array. Reading args[0] stops the program:

$ java StreamingLauncher
Args count: 0
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 0 out of bounds for length 0

The fix is to check args.length first, and stop with a helpful message when something is missing:

if (args.length < 1) {
    System.out.println("Usage: java StreamingLauncher <name>");
    return;   // leaves main: the program ends cleanly
}
System.out.println("First arg: " + args[0]);

This is defensive programming: guard first, then act. The lab uses exactly this pattern to launch our streaming platform.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

← The main signature · Next: the lab →

docs.title: Lab: launching the streaming platform
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Writing Your First main() Method · 3/3

Goal: boot our platform with a name and a region passed on the command line, without crashing when they're missing.

Setup: in src/, create the folders com/netflix/platform/ and the file StreamingPlatform.java inside. Open a terminal in src/.

docs.title: Step 1 — Package and class
docs.text:
package com.netflix.platform;

public class StreamingPlatform {
    private String platformName;
    private String region;
}

The two fields belong to each object. main is static, so it can't use them without an object: we'll come back to that in a later section.

docs.title: Step 2 — Guard the arguments
docs.text:
Add main inside the class:

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        if (args.length < 2) {
            System.out.println("Usage: <name> <region>");
            return;
        }
    }

If fewer than two arguments are given, the program explains how to run it and return leaves main right away.

docs.title: Step 3 — Read and print
docs.text:
After the if block:

        String name = args[0];   // "Netflix"
        String region = args[1]; // "France"
        System.out.println("Launching " + name + " in " + region);

+ joins the text and the values into one message.

docs.title: Step 4 — Compile and run
docs.text:
From src/, compile with the file path and run with the full class name (package included):

$ javac com/netflix/platform/StreamingPlatform.java
$ java com.netflix.platform.StreamingPlatform Netflix France
Launching Netflix in France

Now without arguments:

$ java com.netflix.platform.StreamingPlatform
Usage: <name> <region>

No crash: the guard caught the missing arguments before args[0] was read.

docs.title: Final code
docs.text:
package com.netflix.platform;

public class StreamingPlatform {
    private String platformName;
    private String region;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        if (args.length < 2) {
            System.out.println("Usage: <name> <region>");
            return;
        }
        String name = args[0];   // "Netflix"
        String region = args[1]; // "France"
        System.out.println("Launching " + name + " in " + region);
    }
}

docs.title: OCP exam prep: the main method
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Writing Your First main() Method

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — Compiles ≠ runs

A class with a wrong main (no static, int return type, wrong parameter) or no main at all compiles. The error only appears when the JVM tries to launch it.

Trap 2 — String[] and String... are both valid

public static void main(String... args) is a valid entry point. So is any parameter name.

Trap 3 — Modifier order doesn't matter

static public void main(String[] args) is as valid as public static void main(String[] args).

Trap 4 — args[0] without arguments

It compiles, then throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at runtime when no argument is passed. args is never null: it's an empty array.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Which are valid entry points? (Choose all that apply.)

A. public static void main(String[] args) { } B. public static void main(String... args) { } C. public static int main(String[] args) { return 0; } D. static public void main(String[] args) { }

Answer

A, B and D. Varargs is equivalent to String[], and public/static can be swapped. C returns int: it compiles, but the JVM won't use it as the entry point.

2. What happens with java NetflixLauncher (no arguments)?

public class NetflixLauncher {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Platform: " + args[0]);
    }
}

A. Compilation error B. Prints Platform: null C. ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at runtime D. Prints Platform:

Answer

C. args[0] is valid syntax, so it compiles. With no arguments, args is empty and index 0 doesn't exist.

docs.title: Organizing Your Code with Packages and Imports
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

Real projects have dozens of classes. Java groups them into packages, like folders, and lets one class use another through imports. Here you'll learn both, plus how to compile and run classes that live in packages.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 Packages: grouping your classes 3 min 2 Imports: using classes from other packages 3 min 3 Lab: compiling and running packaged classes 4 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: Writing Your First main() Method.

Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

docs.title: Packages: grouping your classes
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · Organizing Your Code with Packages and Imports · 1/3

docs.title: Why packages?
docs.text:
A streaming application quickly grows: content classes, user classes, platform classes. A package is a named group of related classes, like a folder:

com.netflix.content     Movie, Series, Episode
com.netflix.user        User, Subscription
com.netflix.platform    StreamingPlatform, ContentType

Packages bring two things:

  • Organization: related classes live together.
  • Unique names: a class's full name includes its package. com.netflix.content.Movie and com.thirdparty.catalog.Movie are two different classes, even though both are called Movie.

That full name is the fully qualified class name.

docs.title: Naming convention
docs.text: Package names are lowercase words separated by dots. Companies usually start with their domain name reversed: com.netflix.content, com.netflix.user.

docs.title: Declaring a package
docs.text:
The package statement says which package a class belongs to:

package com.netflix.content;

public class Movie {
    private String title;
    private int releaseYear;
}

Three rules apply:

Rule Detail First statement package comes before any other code; only comments and blank lines may precede it One per file a file belongs to exactly one package Matches the folders com.netflix.content means the file sits in com/netflix/content/

So Movie.java lives here:

project-root/
└── com/
    └── netflix/
        └── content/
            └── Movie.java

A class without a package statement belongs to the default package. That's fine for a first exercise, but real code always declares one.

Once classes live in different packages, they need a way to find each other. That's the job of import.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

Next: imports →

docs.title: Imports: using classes from other packages
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Organizing Your Code with Packages and Imports · 2/3

Your classes now live in packages. To use a class from another package, you import it.

docs.title: Single and wildcard imports
docs.text:
package com.netflix.platform;

import com.netflix.content.Movie;   // one class
import com.netflix.content.*;       // every class of the package

public class StreamingPlatform {
    Movie featured;
}
Import Brings in Notes import com.netflix.content.Movie; exactly Movie preferred: you see which classes are used import com.netflix.content.*; all classes directly in com.netflix.content not its sub-packages

Classes in the same package don't need an import.

docs.title: java.lang comes for free
docs.text: String, System, Math, Integer live in java.lang, which every Java file imports automatically. You never write import java.lang.String;. It's allowed, just useless.

docs.title: The order is fixed
docs.text:
A source file follows this order, always:

package com.netflix.content;     // 1. package (if any)

import java.util.List;           // 2. imports

public class Movie {             // 3. class
    List<String> genres;
}

An import before the package, or a class before the imports, is a compiler error.

docs.title: Two classes with the same name
docs.text:
Importing both Movie classes doesn't work: Java can't tell which one Movie means.

import com.netflix.content.Movie;
import com.thirdparty.catalog.Movie;   // ❌ compiler error: Movie is already imported

The fix: import one, and use the fully qualified name for the other.

import com.netflix.content.Movie;

public class Catalog {
    Movie mine = new Movie();
    com.thirdparty.catalog.Movie external = new com.thirdparty.catalog.Movie();
}

A fully qualified name works anywhere, even without any import.

You can now organize classes and connect them. The lab builds a small packaged project and runs it from the terminal.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

← Packages · Next: the lab →

docs.title: Lab: compiling and running packaged classes
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Organizing Your Code with Packages and Imports · 3/3

Goal: build a small project with two packages and run it from the terminal, without an IDE.

Setup: in an empty folder (the project root), create this tree:

project-root/
└── com/netflix/
    ├── content/
    │   ├── Movie.java
    │   └── Series.java
    └── platform/
        └── StreamingPlatform.java

Open a terminal in the project root and stay there for every command.

docs.title: Step 1 — The content classes
docs.text:
com/netflix/content/Movie.java:

package com.netflix.content;

public class Movie {
    private String title;
    private int releaseYear;

    public Movie(String title, int releaseYear) {
        this.title = title;
        this.releaseYear = releaseYear;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Movie: " + title + " (" + releaseYear + ")";
    }
}

com/netflix/content/Series.java:

package com.netflix.content;

public class Series {
    private String title;
    private int numberOfSeasons;

    public Series(String title, int numberOfSeasons) {
        this.title = title;
        this.numberOfSeasons = numberOfSeasons;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Series: " + title + " - " + numberOfSeasons + " season(s)";
    }
}

The package line matches the folder. The constructor and toString() are covered in later sections: here, toString() decides how an object prints.

docs.title: Step 2 — The platform class
docs.text:
com/netflix/platform/StreamingPlatform.java:

package com.netflix.platform;

import com.netflix.content.Movie;
import com.netflix.content.Series;

public class StreamingPlatform {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Movie movie = new Movie("Inception", 2010);
        Series series = new Series("Stranger Things", 4);

        System.out.println("=== Netflix Streaming Platform ===");
        System.out.println(movie);
        System.out.println(series);
        System.out.println("Platform is ready to stream!");
    }
}

Movie and Series are in another package, so they're imported.

docs.title: Step 3 — Compile from the project root
docs.text:
javac takes file paths, with slashes:

$ javac com/netflix/content/*.java
$ javac com/netflix/platform/StreamingPlatform.java

Each .class file appears next to its .java file: the compiled classes mirror the folder structure.

docs.title: Step 4 — Run with the fully qualified name
docs.text:
java takes the class name, with dots:

$ java com.netflix.platform.StreamingPlatform
=== Netflix Streaming Platform ===
Movie: Inception (2010)
Series: Stranger Things - 4 season(s)
Platform is ready to stream!

Java turns the dots into the folder path com/netflix/platform and loads the class from there.

docs.title: Step 5 — The classic mistake
docs.text:
Run the same command from inside com/:

$ cd com
$ java com.netflix.platform.StreamingPlatform
Error: Could not find or load main class com.netflix.platform.StreamingPlatform

Java now looks for com/com/netflix/..., which doesn't exist. Go back to the project root and it works again.

docs.title: OCP exam prep: packages and imports
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Organizing Your Code with Packages and Imports

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — A wildcard doesn't import sub-packages

import com.netflix.*; doesn't bring in com.netflix.content.Movie. Each sub-package needs its own import.

Trap 2 — Redundant imports are legal

Importing the same class twice, or a class from java.lang, compiles fine. It's useless, not wrong.

Trap 3 — package comes first

Only comments and blank lines may come before package. Then imports, then the class.

Trap 4 — Same simple name: use the full name

Two single-type imports of classes named Movie don't compile. Import one and write the other's fully qualified name.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Which statement is true?

1: import com.netflix.content.*;
2: package com.netflix.platform;
3: public class StreamingPlatform { }

A. It compiles B. Line 1 doesn't compile C. Line 2 doesn't compile D. Line 3 doesn't compile

Answer

C. The import on line 1 is valid on its own. The package statement on line 2 comes after it, which is no longer allowed: package must be first.

2. Which statements are true? (Choose all that apply.) Assume com.netflix.content exists.

package com.netflix.user;
import com.netflix.content.*;
import java.lang.String;
public class User { }

A. It doesn't compile B. The java.lang.String import is redundant C. The wildcard also covers com.netflix.content.extras D. Removing the String import changes the behavior

Answer

B only. The order is correct, so it compiles. java.lang is imported automatically, so that import is redundant and removing it changes nothing. A wildcard never covers sub-packages.

docs.title: Bringing Your Class to Life: Creating Objects
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

A class is only a blueprint. Here you'll see how new builds a real object in memory, what a constructor does at that moment, and how to read and write the data each object holds.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 new, references and constructors 3 min 2 Reading, writing and initializing fields 3 min 3 Lab: two independent streaming objects 3 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: Your First Java Class.

Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

docs.title: new, references and constructors
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · Bringing Your Class to Life: Creating Objects · 1/3

docs.title: From blueprint to object
docs.text:
public class Movie {
    String title;
    int releaseYear;
    boolean isAvailable;
}

This class describes every movie, but no movie exists yet. To create one, use new:

Movie m = new Movie();
  1. new Movie() reserves memory for one Movie object, in an area called the heap.
  2. Its fields start with default values (null, 0, false).
  3. new returns the object's address, stored in m.

m is a reference: it holds where the object lives, like a house address. m is not the object itself. This difference between references and objects comes back everywhere in Java.

docs.title: The constructor
docs.text:
Right after reserving memory, new runs the class's constructor: code that prepares the new object.

public class Movie {
    String title;

    public Movie() {                          // constructor
        System.out.println("A Movie was created!");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Movie m = new Movie();
    }
}

A Movie was created!

Three rules:

Rule Detail Same name as the class Movie() in class Movie No return type not even void — that's what makes it a constructor Called by new you never call it directly

A "constructor" with a return type, like public void Movie() { }, is just an ordinary method that happens to share the class name. new never runs it.

docs.title: The default constructor
docs.text:
A class with no constructor at all still works with new:

public class Series {
    String name;
    int totalEpisodes;
}

// elsewhere
Series s = new Series();   // ✅ compiles

The compiler silently adds a default constructor: no parameters, empty body.

But as soon as you write any constructor yourself, the compiler stops adding it:

public class Series {
    String name;

    public Series(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }
}

// elsewhere
Series s = new Series();   // ❌ compiler error: no constructor Series()

To support both new Series() and new Series("Dark"), write both constructors.

Now that objects exist, let's put data into them.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

Next: reading, writing and initializing fields →

docs.title: Reading, writing and initializing fields
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Bringing Your Class to Life: Creating Objects · 2/3

new gives you a reference to a fresh object. The dot lets you reach the object's fields through that reference.

docs.title: Dot notation
docs.text:
public class Movie {
    String title;
    int releaseYear;
    boolean isAvailable;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Movie m = new Movie();

        m.title = "Inception";          // write
        m.releaseYear = 2010;
        m.isAvailable = true;

        System.out.println(m.title);        // read
        System.out.println(m.releaseYear);
        System.out.println(m.isAvailable);
    }
}

Inception
2010
true
  • reference.field = value writes a field.
  • reference.field reads it.

docs.title: Each object owns its data
docs.text:
Every object gets its own copy of the fields:

Movie a = new Movie();
Movie b = new Movie();
a.title = "Inception";
b.title = "Dune";
System.out.println(a.title);   // Inception: b's change doesn't touch a

Two Movie objects are two independent blocks of memory. That's the point of objects: one class, as many instances as you need, each representing a different movie.

docs.title: Initializing a field on its declaration
docs.text:
You can give a field its starting value right where you declare it:

public class Episode {
    int episodeNumber = 1;
    String platform = "Netflix";

    public Episode() {
        System.out.println("Episode " + episodeNumber + " on " + platform);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Episode();
    }
}

Episode 1 on Netflix

The order is guaranteed:

  1. Fields get their inline values, top to bottom.
  2. Then the constructor body runs.

So the constructor already sees 1 and "Netflix". It can also assign new values: the last write wins.

A field with no inline value keeps its default (null, 0, false) until something assigns it. The lab shows both cases side by side.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

← new and constructors · Next: the lab →

docs.title: Lab: two independent streaming objects
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Bringing Your Class to Life: Creating Objects · 3/3

Goal: create two objects from the same class and prove they keep their own data, including inline defaults nobody changed.

Setup: create StreamingContent.java and NetflixDemo.java in the same folder.

docs.title: Step 1 — The class and its fields
docs.text:
StreamingContent.java:

public class StreamingContent {
    String title;
    int releaseYear = 2024;
    boolean isAvailable = true;
}

title has no sensible default, so it stays null until someone sets it. A new title is assumed to be from 2024 and available.

docs.title: Step 2 — A constructor
docs.text:
Inside the class:

    public StreamingContent() {
        System.out.println("Content ready: " + title);
    }

It runs automatically on every new.

docs.title: Step 3 — Create two objects
docs.text:
NetflixDemo.java:

public class NetflixDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StreamingContent movie1 = new StreamingContent();
        movie1.title = "Squid Game";
        movie1.releaseYear = 2021;

        StreamingContent movie2 = new StreamingContent();
        movie2.title = "Money Heist";
    }
}

movie1 overrides the year. movie2 deliberately leaves it alone.

docs.title: Step 4 — Print and run
docs.text:
At the end of main:

        System.out.println(movie1.title);
        System.out.println(movie2.title);
        System.out.println(movie2.releaseYear);

$ javac StreamingContent.java NetflixDemo.java
$ java NetflixDemo
Content ready: null
Content ready: null
Squid Game
Money Heist
2024
  • Content ready: null, twice: the constructor ran once per new, before any title was set.
  • Squid Game, Money Heist: each object has its own title.
  • 2024: movie2 kept the inline default. Changing movie1's year didn't affect it.

docs.title: Final code
docs.text:
// StreamingContent.java
public class StreamingContent {
    String title;
    int releaseYear = 2024;
    boolean isAvailable = true;

    public StreamingContent() {
        System.out.println("Content ready: " + title);
    }
}

// NetflixDemo.java
public class NetflixDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StreamingContent movie1 = new StreamingContent();
        movie1.title = "Squid Game";
        movie1.releaseYear = 2021;

        StreamingContent movie2 = new StreamingContent();
        movie2.title = "Money Heist";

        System.out.println(movie1.title);
        System.out.println(movie2.title);
        System.out.println(movie2.releaseYear);
    }
}

Setting fields one by one after new gets repetitive. Passing values to the constructor directly comes later in the course.

docs.title: OCP exam prep: creating objects
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Bringing Your Class to Life: Creating Objects

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Create classes and records, and define and use constructors and instance initializers.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — A return type means it's not a constructor

public void Movie() { } is a method named Movie. new Movie() uses the compiler's default constructor instead.

Trap 2 — Any constructor removes the default one

After public Movie(String t) { }, new Movie() doesn't compile unless you write a no-argument constructor too.

Trap 3 — Initialization order

Field initializers and instance initializer blocks run top to bottom, all before the constructor body.

Trap 4 — Locals have no default value

Fields get defaults (0, false, null). Local variables don't: reading one before assigning it is a compiler error.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. What is the output?

public class Series {
    int seasons = 3;
    public void Series() { seasons = 5; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Series s = new Series();
        System.out.println(s.seasons);
    }
}

A. 3 B. 5 C. Compilation error D. Runtime exception

Answer

A. void Series() has a return type, so it's a regular method, never called here. The default constructor runs and seasons keeps 3. A method may share the class name, so it compiles.

2. What happens when this code is compiled?

public class Subscription {
    String plan;
    public Subscription(String plan) { this.plan = plan; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Subscription s = new Subscription();
    }
}

A. Prints null B. Prints an empty string C. Compilation error D. NullPointerException

Answer

C. The class declares a constructor, so there is no default one: new Subscription() matches nothing. Fix: pass an argument, or add a no-argument constructor.

docs.title: Two Kinds of Data: Primitives and References
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

Java stores data in two very different ways. Primitives hold a raw value; references hold the address of an object. Knowing which is which explains how variables behave, what can be null, and why == sometimes surprises you.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 The eight primitive types and their literals 3 min 2 Reference types, and how they differ 3 min 3 Lab: choosing the right types for Movie 3 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: Creating Objects.

Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

docs.title: The eight primitive types and their literals
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · Two Kinds of Data: Primitives and References · 1/3

docs.title: Eight raw values
docs.text:
A primitive is a single value stored directly in the variable: no methods, never null. Java has exactly eight:

Type Holds Size Default (fields) boolean true / false — false byte whole number 8 bits 0 short whole number 16 bits 0 int whole number 32 bits 0 long whole number 64 bits 0L float decimal number 32 bits 0.0f double decimal number 64 bits 0.0 char one Unicode character 16 bits '\u0000'

Two families to remember:

  • Whole numbers: byte → short → int → long. Use int by default.
  • Decimals: float → double. Use double by default.

int goes up to about 2.1 billion. Beyond that, you need long.

docs.title: Writing number literals
docs.text:
A literal is a value written directly in the code, like 14000 or 8.5. Java gives each literal a type:

int totalMovies = 14_000;             // whole number literal: int
long totalStreams = 3_500_000_000L;   // L suffix: long
double averageRating = 8.5;           // decimal literal: double
float storageGB = 4.2f;               // f suffix: float
Rule Example A whole number literal is an int; add L for a long 3_500_000_000L A decimal literal is a double; add f for a float 4.2f Underscores are allowed between digits only 1_000_000 ✅ · _100, 100_, 10_.0 ❌

Prefer an uppercase L: a lowercase l looks like the digit 1.

These lines don't compile:

long bad1 = 3_500_000_000;   // ❌ too big for an int literal: add L
float bad2 = 4.2;            // ❌ 4.2 is a double: add f
double bad3 = _1000.0;       // ❌ an underscore can't start a number

docs.title: Other number bases
docs.text:
Whole numbers can be written in other bases with a prefix:

int hexColor = 0xFF5733;   // hexadecimal: 0x, digits 0-9 and A-F
int binary   = 0b1101;     // binary: 0b, digits 0-1   (13)
int octal    = 017;        // octal: leading 0, digits 0-7   (15)

A leading 0 changes the meaning: 017 is fifteen, not seventeen.

Primitives cover single values. Everything else — text, movies, lists — is an object, reached through a reference.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

Next: reference types →

docs.title: Reference types, and how they differ
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Two Kinds of Data: Primitives and References · 2/3

A primitive holds its value. Every other type — String, Movie, Integer, lists — is a reference type.

docs.title: A reference holds an address
docs.text:
Movie inception = new Movie("Inception");

The Movie object lives on the heap. inception holds its address, like a remote control pointing at a TV.

A reference can also point to nothing:

Movie upcoming = null;      // no object
upcoming.getTitle();        // ❌ NullPointerException at runtime

Calling a method through a null reference stops the program with a NullPointerException.

docs.title: Two references, one object
docs.text:
Assigning a reference copies the address, not the object:

Movie ref1 = new Movie("Inception");
Movie ref2 = ref1;                       // same object, two remotes

ref1.setTitle("Inception Remastered");
System.out.println(ref2.getTitle());     // Inception Remastered

There is still only one Movie. A change made through ref1 is visible through ref2.

docs.title: Wrapper classes
docs.text:
Each primitive has a matching class: Integer for int, Double for double, Boolean for boolean, and so on. Java converts between them automatically:

Integer views = 1_500_000;   // autoboxing: int → Integer
int count = views;           // unboxing: Integer → int

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text: Primitive Reference Stores the value itself the address of an object Can be null never yes Has methods no yes (length(), equals()…) Default (fields) 0, false, '\u0000' null == compares values addresses

docs.title: == compares addresses for objects
docs.text:
String a = new String("Dune");
String b = new String("Dune");

System.out.println(a == b);        // false: two different objects
System.out.println(a.equals(b));   // true: same content

To compare the content of two objects, use equals(). == only tells you whether two references point to the same object.

Choosing between a primitive and a reference type is a design decision. The lab makes those choices for each field of our Movie class.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

← Primitive types · Next: the lab →

docs.title: Lab: choosing the right types for Movie
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Two Kinds of Data: Primitives and References · 3/3

Goal: design the fields of our Movie class, choosing a type for each piece of data and explaining why.

Setup: create com/netflix/model/Movie.java under your source folder.

docs.title: Step 1 — Reference fields
docs.text:
package com.netflix.model;

public class Movie {
    // Reference types (default: null)
    private String title;
    private String genre;
}

Text is an object in Java, so String is a reference type. A movie whose genre isn't set yet simply has genre == null.

docs.title: Step 2 — Primitive fields
docs.text:
// Primitive types (default: 0 / false)
    private int releaseYear;
    private double rating;
    private float storageSizeGB;
    private long totalViews;
    private boolean isAvailable;
Field Type Why releaseYear int a whole number, far below 2 billion rating double needs decimals (9.3) storageSizeGB float decimals, but little precision needed totalViews long a hit show passes 2 billion views: an int would overflow isAvailable boolean available or not, nothing in between

docs.title: Step 3 — A summary method
docs.text:
public void printSummary() {
        var label = title + " (" + releaseYear + ")";
        var stars = rating >= 8.0 ? "Top Rated" : "Standard";
        System.out.println(label + " — " + stars);
        System.out.println("Views: " + totalViews);
    }

var lets the compiler infer a local variable's type from its value: both label and stars are String. (condition ? a : b picks a if the condition is true, b otherwise.) Next section covers var in detail.

docs.title: Step 4 — Run it
docs.text:
public static void main(String[] args) {
        Movie movie = new Movie();
        movie.title = "Stranger Things";
        movie.genre = "Sci-Fi";
        movie.releaseYear = 2016;
        movie.rating = 9.3;
        movie.storageSizeGB = 4.2f;
        movie.totalViews = 1_500_000_000L;
        movie.isAvailable = true;
        movie.printSummary();
    }

Remove the f from 4.2f and it no longer compiles: 4.2 is a double.

$ javac com/netflix/model/Movie.java
$ java com.netflix.model.Movie
Stranger Things (2016) — Top Rated
Views: 1500000000

docs.text:

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Use primitives and wrapper classes; use local variable type inference.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — Big whole numbers need L

long streams = 3_500_000_000; doesn't compile: the literal is an int, and it's too big. 3_500_000_000L works.

Trap 2 — Decimals are double

float rate = 4.5; doesn't compile. Write 4.5f.

Trap 3 — Underscore placement

Only between digits: 1_0.0 ✅, _10.0 ❌, 10_.0 ❌, 10._0 ❌, 100_ ❌.

Trap 4 — var needs a type to infer

var x = null; doesn't compile. var x = (String) null; does: the cast gives the type.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Which lines do NOT compile? (Choose all that apply. Each line is independent.)

A. long totalViews = 5_000_000_000;
B. float rating = 8.5f;
C. var genre = null;
D. double price = 9_99.99;
Answer

A and C. A: five billion doesn't fit in an int literal, it needs L. C: null gives var no type to infer. B is a valid float literal, and D has its underscore between digits.

2. What is the output?

Movie a = new Movie("Squid Game");
Movie b = a;
b.setTitle("Squid Game Season 2");
System.out.println(a.getTitle());

A. Squid Game B. Squid Game Season 2 C. null D. Compilation error

Answer

B. b = a copies the reference, not the object. Both variables point to the same Movie, so the change made through b shows through a.

docs.title: Declaring Variables
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

Every program stores data in variables. Here you'll learn how to declare them, which names Java accepts, the conventions professionals follow, and how final and var change a declaration.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 Declaring and naming variables 3 min 2 Local variables, final and var 3 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: Two Kinds of Data: Primitives and References.

Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

docs.title: Declaring and naming variables
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · Declaring Variables · 1/2

docs.title: Declaration and initialization
docs.text:
A variable is a named slot in memory. Declaring it means giving its type and its name; initializing it means giving it a first value:

String title;                        // declaration
title = "Stranger Things";           // initialization

int releaseYear = 2016;              // both on one line
double rating = 9.5;

The pattern is always: type, name, optionally = and a value, then ;.

docs.title: Declaring several variables at once
docs.text:
Variables of the same type can share one declaration, separated by commas. Each one may or may not get a value:

int season, episode, duration;
int season = 1, episode, duration = 45;   // only season and duration initialized

You can't mix types in one declaration:

int season, String title;    // ❌ doesn't compile
int season; String title;    // ✅ two separate declarations on one line (legal, but hard to read)

docs.title: Which names are legal?
docs.text:
Java checks every name, or identifier, against four rules:

Rule ✅ ❌ Starts with a letter, $ or _ movieTitle, _year2024, $price 3dMovie Then letters, digits, $, _ only season2 my-rating (that's a minus) Not a reserved word isActive class, int, for Not a single underscore _count _

Names are case-sensitive: rating, Rating and RATING are three different variables.

docs.title: Naming conventions
docs.text:
The compiler only enforces the rules above. Professional Java code also follows these conventions:

String streamingPlatformName = "Netflix";     // camelCase: variables and methods
class StreamingPlatform { }                   // PascalCase: classes
final int MAX_EPISODE_DURATION = 3600;        // SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE: constants
Convention Used for Shape camelCase variables, methods first word lowercase, next words capitalized PascalCase classes every word capitalized SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE constants (final) all uppercase, words joined by _

Stick to them: anyone reading your code knows at a glance what each name is.

Next, the variables you declare inside methods follow stricter rules, and two keywords change how a declaration works: final and var.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

Next: local variables, final and var →

docs.title: Local variables, final and var
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Declaring Variables · 2/2

You know how to declare and name a variable. Inside a method, a few more rules apply.

docs.title: Local variables have no default value
docs.text:
A local variable is declared inside a method or a block, and exists only there. Unlike fields, it gets no default value:

public void playEpisode() {
    int currentSecond;
    System.out.println(currentSecond);   // ❌ doesn't compile: not initialized

    currentSecond = 0;
    System.out.println(currentSecond);   // ✅ prints 0
}

Declaring first and assigning later is fine. Reading before assigning is a compiler error.

docs.title: final: one assignment only
docs.text:
final means the variable can be assigned once:

public void playEpisode() {
    final int MAX_RETRIES = 3;
    MAX_RETRIES = 5;                     // ❌ doesn't compile
}

final locks the variable, not what it points to. A final reference can't point elsewhere, but the object can still change:

final String[] titles = new String[3];
titles[0] = "Dune";                      // ✅ the array's content changes
titles = new String[5];                  // ❌ the reference can't change

Copying a final variable into another one is fine; only the final one stays locked:

final int MAX_STREAMS = 5;
int current = MAX_STREAMS;
current = 3;
System.out.println(current + " / " + MAX_STREAMS);   // 3 / 5

docs.title: var: let Java infer the type
docs.text:
Since Java 10, var lets the compiler infer a local variable's type from its value:

public void showDetails() {
    var movieTitle = "Inception";   // String
    var rating = 9.2;               // double
    var episodeCount = 10;          // int
}

The type is decided once, at compile time, and never changes: movieTitle = 42; doesn't compile. var saves typing, not type safety.

var has limits:

❌ Doesn't compile Why var genre; no value to infer a type from var x = null; null has no type var a = 1, b = 2; one variable per var declaration private var title; not for fields void play(var x) { } not for parameters or return types

Use var when the type is obvious from the right-hand side, and write the type when it helps the reader.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

docs.title: OCP exam prep: declaring variables
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Declaring Variables

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Understand variable scopes, use local variable type inference, and make objects immutable.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — var is not a reserved word

var is a reserved type name, not a keyword. var var = 5; compiles, and so does a method named var. But a class, interface or other type can't be named var.

Trap 2 — No compound var declarations

var a = 1, b = 2; doesn't compile. One variable per var statement.

Trap 3 — Uninitialized locals

int x; System.out.println(x); doesn't compile. Fields get defaults; local variables don't.

Trap 4 — final locks the reference, not the object

final String[] titles = new String[3]; titles[0] = "Dune"; compiles. Only titles = … is forbidden.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Inside a method, which line compiles?

A. var genre; B. var title = "Oppenheimer"; C. var season = 1, episode = 3; D. var rating = null;

Answer

B. A has no value to infer from, C declares two variables with one var, and D gives null, which has no type. Only B lets the compiler infer String.

2. What is the output?

public class StreamingApp {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        final int MAX_STREAMS = 5;
        int current = MAX_STREAMS;
        current = 3;
        System.out.println(current + " / " + MAX_STREAMS);
    }
}

A. 5 / 5 B. 3 / 5 C. Compilation error D. 3 / 3

Answer

B. current starts with a copy of 5, then is reassigned to 3. That's allowed: current isn't final. MAX_STREAMS is never reassigned and stays 5.

← Back to the series · All 1Z0-829 pages

docs.title: Giving Variables Their First Value
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

Java doesn't treat every variable the same way when it comes to its first value. Fields get defaults; local variables get nothing; final fields get strict rules. Here's the full picture.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 Three kinds of variables, three rules 3 min 2 final fields and "might not have been initialized" 3 min 3 Lab: watching the defaults 3 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: Declaring Variables.

Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

docs.title: Three kinds of variables, three rules
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · Giving Variables Their First Value · 1/3

docs.title: Initializing means giving a first value
docs.text:
String title;            // declared: no value yet
title = "Inception";     // initialized

String genre = "Sci-Fi"; // both at once

Whether Java fills in a value for you depends on where the variable is declared.

docs.title: Where a variable lives decides the rule
The default values
docs.text:
Fields (instance and static) start with these values:

Type Default byte, short, int, long 0 float, double 0.0 boolean false char '\u0000' (the null character) any object type (String, Movie…) null

In a Movie class, that gives sensible starting points: no views yet (0), no rating yet (0.0), not available yet (false), no title yet (null).

null means "points to no object". Printing a null field shows the word null; calling a method on it throws a NullPointerException.

docs.title: Fields versus locals, side by side
docs.text:
public class Movie {
    String title;        // → null
    double rating;       // → 0.0

    public void displayInfo() {
        String label = "Now Showing";   // local: assigned by you
        System.out.println(label + ": " + title);
    }
}

Class-level fields are initialized for you; method-level variables need your attention. One exception breaks the field rule: final fields.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

Next: final fields and definite assignment →

docs.title: final fields and "might not have been initialized"
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Giving Variables Their First Value · 2/3

Fields get default values, locals don't. final adds one more rule on top.

docs.title: final locals
docs.text:
A final local variable follows the local rule (assign before use), and can be assigned only once:

public void launch() {
    final String platformName = "NetStream";
    platformName = "Other";        // ❌ doesn't compile
    System.out.println(platformName);
}

docs.title: final fields get no default
docs.text:
A final field is not auto-initialized. You must assign it exactly once, in one of three places:

  1. on its declaration,
  2. in an instance initializer block,
  3. in every constructor.
public class StreamingPlatform {
    final int maxStreams;

    public StreamingPlatform(int max) {
        this.maxStreams = max;     // ✅ assigned in the constructor
    }
}

Forget all three and the class doesn't compile. The compiler reports it on the field itself:

public class Subscription {
    final int maxScreens;          // ❌ not initialized in the default constructor
}

Once assigned, the field can never change: a reliable value for the object's whole life.

docs.title: Every path must assign it
docs.text:
The compiler checks that a local variable is assigned on every possible path before it's read. This is called definite assignment:

public void show(boolean premium) {
    int views;
    if (premium) {
        views = 5;
    }
    System.out.println(views);     // ❌ might not have been initialized
}

When premium is false, views has no value. Assign it on every branch, or give it a starting value:

int views;
if (premium) {
    views = 5;
} else {
    views = 0;
}
System.out.println(views);         // ✅ assigned on both paths

The compiler doesn't run your code: it only looks at the possible paths. If one path could skip the assignment, it refuses.

Time to see the defaults with your own eyes.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

← Three kinds of variables · Next: the lab →

docs.title: Lab: watching the defaults
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Giving Variables Their First Value · 3/3

Goal: print the default values Java gives to fields, and see why a local variable needs a value from you.

Setup: create com/netflix/model/Movie.java under your source folder.

docs.title: Step 1 — Four fields, no values
docs.text:
package com.netflix.model;

public class Movie {
    String title;        // → null
    double rating;       // → 0.0
    int views;           // → 0
    boolean available;   // → false
}

No = anywhere: Java fills them in when an object is created.

docs.title: Step 2 — A method with a local variable
docs.text:
public void displayInfo() {
        String label = "Now Showing";
        System.out.println(label + ": " + title);
    }

Try writing String label; without a value: the next line no longer compiles, with variable label might not have been initialized. Put the value back.

docs.title: Step 3 — A main to print everything
docs.text:
public static void main(String[] args) {
        Movie movie = new Movie();
        System.out.println("--- Default Instance Variable Values ---");
        System.out.println("Title    : " + movie.title);
        System.out.println("Rating   : " + movie.rating);
        System.out.println("Views    : " + movie.views);
        System.out.println("Available: " + movie.available);
        System.out.println("--- Calling displayInfo ---");
        movie.displayInfo();
    }

docs.title: Step 4 — Run
docs.text:
$ javac com/netflix/model/Movie.java
$ java com.netflix.model.Movie
--- Default Instance Variable Values ---
Title    : null
Rating   : 0.0
Views    : 0
Available: false
--- Calling displayInfo ---
Now Showing: null

Every field shows its default. displayInfo() prints its local label, which you initialized, and the still-null title.

docs.title: OCP exam prep: initializing variables
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Giving Variables Their First Value

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

docs.title: Three traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — Reading a local before assigning it

int score; System.out.println(score); doesn't compile. The compiler never picks a default for a local.

Trap 2 — An unassigned final field

final int maxStreams; with no assignment in a field initializer, an initializer block or every constructor: compiler error, reported on the field declaration.

Trap 3 — Assigned on only some paths

int views; if (c) views = 5; System.out.println(views); doesn't compile: might not have been initialized. Every path must assign it.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. What is the output?

public class Movie {
    int views;
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Movie m = new Movie();
        System.out.println(m.views);
    }
}

A. Compilation error B. Runtime exception C. 0 D. null

Answer

C. views is an int field, so it defaults to 0. null is the default for object types only.

2. Where does this class fail to compile? (Choose all that apply.)

public class Subscription {
    final int maxScreens;                 // Line 1
    String plan;
    public void checkPlan() {
        String msg;
        System.out.println(msg);          // Line A
        System.out.println(plan);         // Line B
        System.out.println(maxScreens);   // Line C
    }
}

A. Line 1 B. Line A C. Line B D. Line C

Answer

A and B. Line A reads a local that was never assigned. maxScreens is final and never assigned, and javac reports that on its declaration (Line 1), not where it's read. Line B is fine: plan defaults to null. Line C has no error of its own.
