docs.title: Managing Variable Scope
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

Every variable has a scope: the region of code where it exists. Step outside it and the variable is gone. Here you'll see how braces define scope, how loops create and discard variables, and how to trace scope like the compiler does.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 Blocks define scope 3 min 2 Scope in loops, traced like a compiler 3 min 3 Lab: three levels of scope 3 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: Giving Variables Their First Value.

Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

docs.title: Blocks define scope
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · Managing Variable Scope · 1/3

docs.title: Three levels in one class
docs.text:
public class StreamingPlatform {
    String name = "Netflix";          // field

    public void launch() {
        int users = 1000;             // local variable
        if (users > 500) {
            int bonus = 50;           // block variable
        }
        // bonus doesn't exist here
        System.out.println(users);
    }
}
Variable Scope name (field) the whole class: every method can use it users (local) from its declaration to the end of launch() bonus (block) only inside the if braces

docs.title: A block is a pair of braces
docs.text:
Every { opens a new scope region; the matching } closes it. A variable declared inside belongs to that region only:

public void stream(boolean hungry) {
    if (hungry) {
        int snacks = 3;
        snacks++;
    }
    System.out.println(snacks);    // ❌ doesn't compile: snacks is out of scope
    System.out.println(hungry);    // ✅ a parameter lives for the whole method
}

Like nesting dolls:

  • an inner block can read the variables of the blocks around it,
  • an outer block can't see what's declared inside an inner block.

Once a block closes, its variables are gone for the compiler too: using them is a compile error, not a runtime one.

Method parameters behave like local variables declared at the very top of the method: in scope for the whole body, and nowhere else.

docs.title: No redeclaring a name in a nested block
docs.text:
Java forbids declaring a variable in an inner block with the same name as one still in scope:

public void playMovie(boolean vip) {
    int maxStreams = 3;
    if (vip) {
        int maxStreams = 5;        // ❌ already defined in this method
    }
}

Some languages allow this "shadowing" of locals; Java doesn't. Once the outer variable's scope ends, though, the name is free again:

if (vip) {
    int bonus = 5;
}
int bonus = 0;                     // ✅ the first bonus is already out of scope

Loops add one more twist: their variables come and go on every iteration.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

Next: scope in loops →

docs.title: Scope in loops, traced like a compiler
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Managing Variable Scope · 2/3

Braces define scope. Loops follow the same rule, with a detail that catches many people: the loop counter.

docs.title: The loop variable belongs to the loop
docs.text:
public void loadEpisodes(int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        String title = "Ep-" + i;
        System.out.println(title);
    }
    System.out.println(i);         // ❌ i is out of scope
    System.out.println(title);     // ❌ title too
}
  • i is declared in the for header, so its scope is the loop, not the method.
  • title is declared in the loop body: a fresh title is created on each iteration, and none survives the loop.

while loops work the same way for variables declared in their body. And var changes nothing: a var declared in a block dies with that block.

If you need a value after the loop, declare the variable before the loop.

docs.title: Tracing scope line by line
docs.text:
The safest way to reason about scope is to note where each variable is born and where it dies:

1  public void recommend(boolean premium) {
2      int suggestions = 5;
3      while (suggestions > 0) {
4          int watched = 1;
5          if (premium) {
6              var bonus = 2;
7              watched += bonus;
8          }
9          suggestions -= watched;
10     }
11     System.out.println(suggestions);
12 }
Variable Lives from → until premium line 1 → end of the method suggestions line 2 → end of the method watched line 4 → line 10, recreated on each iteration bonus line 6 → line 8, recreated each time the if runs

At line 11, only premium and suggestions exist. Using watched or bonus there would not compile.

docs.title: Declared but unused is fine
docs.text:
int episodes = 10;
for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
    int bonus = i * 3;
}
System.out.println(episodes);      // ✅ prints 10

bonus goes out of scope after the loop, but nothing tries to use it there, so the code compiles. Scope errors happen only when a variable is used outside its region.

The lab puts all three levels — field, method and loop — in one runnable class.

docs.title: Lab: three levels of scope
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Managing Variable Scope · 3/3

Goal: build a watch session that uses field scope, method scope and loop scope in one class, and see what each variable can reach.

Setup: create com/netflix/model/User.java under your source folder.

docs.title: Step 1 — A field
docs.text:
package com.netflix.model;

class User {
    String username;
}

Declared in the class body, username is reachable from every method of User.

docs.title: Step 2 — A method-level variable
docs.text:
public void watchContent(boolean premium) {
        int streamsLeft = premium ? 4 : 1;
    }

streamsLeft is declared at the top of the method, outside any block: it lives until the method ends. (premium ? 4 : 1 gives 4 if premium is true, 1 otherwise.)

docs.title: Step 3 — Loop-scoped variables
docs.text:
Inside watchContent, after streamsLeft:

        for (int i = 0; i < streamsLeft; i++) {
            var content = fetchNext();
            play(content);
        } // content and i are gone here

        // streamsLeft is still alive
        logSession(username, streamsLeft);

i and content disappear when the loop ends. streamsLeft and the field username are still in scope for logSession. Declare streamsLeft inside the loop instead, and the last line no longer compiles.

docs.title: Step 4 — Helper methods and main
docs.text:
String fetchNext() {
        return "Stranger Things S01E01";
    }

    void play(String content) {
        System.out.println("  Playing: " + content);
    }

    void logSession(String user, int streams) {
        System.out.println("Session logged for: " + user + " | Streams allowed: " + streams);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        User user = new User();
        user.username = "mounir_netflix";
        System.out.println("--- Starting watch session ---");
        user.watchContent(true);
        System.out.println("--- Session complete ---");
    }

docs.title: Step 5 — Run
docs.text:
$ javac com/netflix/model/User.java
$ java com.netflix.model.User
--- Starting watch session ---
  Playing: Stranger Things S01E01
  Playing: Stranger Things S01E01
  Playing: Stranger Things S01E01
  Playing: Stranger Things S01E01
Session logged for: mounir_netflix | Streams allowed: 4
--- Session complete ---

A premium user gets 4 streams, so the loop runs 4 times. After it, the method still reaches streamsLeft and the field username.

docs.title: OCP exam prep: variable scope
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Managing Variable Scope

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Understand variable scopes.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — The loop counter dies with the loop

A question uses i after for (int i = 0; …) { } and asks if it compiles. It doesn't.

Trap 2 — No redeclaring a name still in scope

Declaring a local in an inner block with the name of an enclosing local doesn't compile, even though the inner one would have a smaller scope.

Trap 3 — Parameters are locals

Method parameters are in scope for the whole method body, and nowhere else.

Trap 4 — var follows the same rules

A var declared in a block goes out of scope when the block ends, like any typed variable.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. What is the output?

public class Platform {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int episodes = 10;
        for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
            int bonus = i * 3;
        }
        System.out.println(episodes);
    }
}

A. 0 B. 10 C. Compilation error: bonus is out of scope D. Compilation error: episodes is out of scope

Answer

B. episodes is in method scope, so it's available after the loop. bonus is never used outside the loop, so its limited scope causes no error.

2. Which lines, if any, cause a compiler error? (Choose all that apply.)

1: public void playMovie(boolean vip) {
2:     int maxStreams = 3;
3:     if (vip) {
4:         int maxStreams = 5;
5:         System.out.println(maxStreams);
6:     }
7:     System.out.println(maxStreams);
8: }

A. Line 4 B. Line 5 C. Line 7 D. None

Answer

A. maxStreams from line 2 is still in scope inside the if, so line 4 can't declare another one. Lines 5 and 7 are fine on their own.

docs.title: Destroying Objects and Memory Management
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

In Java you never free memory yourself: the garbage collector does it. Here you'll see when an object becomes eligible for collection, what the collector does and doesn't guarantee, and how to trace eligibility line by line.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 When an object becomes unreachable 3 min 2 The garbage collector, and tracing eligibility 3 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: Managing Variable Scope.

Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

docs.title: When an object becomes unreachable
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · Destroying Objects and Memory Management · 1/2

docs.title: Objects on the heap, references in variables
docs.text:
Every object created with new lives on the heap, a memory area managed by the JVM. A variable only holds a reference to it:

Movie movie1 = new Movie("Inception");
Movie movie2 = new Movie("Interstellar");

Two objects on the heap, two references pointing at them.

In C or C++, you would free each object yourself. In Java, the JVM frees an object once nothing can reach it anymore. Such an object is eligible for garbage collection.

docs.title: Way 1 — The reference changes
docs.text:
Reassigning a reference, or setting it to null, can leave an object with no reference at all:

Movie m = new Movie("Dune");
m = new Movie("Avatar");   // "Dune" has no reference left → eligible
m = null;                  // "Avatar" has no reference left → eligible

Note the first case: m was never set to null, yet "Dune" became unreachable. Pointing a reference at another object is enough.

docs.title: Way 2 — The reference goes out of scope
docs.text:
A local variable disappears at the end of its block. If it was the only reference to an object, that object becomes unreachable:

void loadContent() {
    Episode ep = new Episode("S01E01");
    // ep is in scope: the Episode is reachable
} // ep goes out of scope

// after the method returns, the Episode has no reference → eligible

When a method ends, all its local variables go out of scope at once.

docs.title: Several references keep an object alive
docs.text:
An object stays reachable as long as at least one reference points to it:

Series s1 = new Series("Stranger Things");
Series s2 = s1;
s1 = null;                 // s2 still points to it → NOT eligible

What counts isn't one variable, but whether any part of the program can still reach the object. That includes references stored inside other objects: an object kept in a field of a reachable object is still reachable.

Becoming eligible doesn't mean being deleted right away. That's the collector's call.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_1_Fundamentals_Core_Syntax on GitHub

Next: the garbage collector →

docs.title: The garbage collector, and tracing eligibility
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Destroying Objects and Memory Management · 2/2

An object with no reachable reference is eligible for collection. Here's what happens next, and how to spot that moment in code.

docs.title: What the collector does
docs.text:
1. Your code creates objects with new.
  2. They live on the heap.
  3. At some point, nothing references some of them anymore.
  4. The garbage collector finds those unreachable objects and reclaims their memory.

Four facts to keep in mind:

Fact Meaning Automatic no delete, no free(): Java cleans up for you Unpredictable timing the JVM decides when to collect, based on memory needs System.gc() is only a hint it suggests a collection; the JVM may ignore it No guarantee at all a program can end without the collector ever running

So "eligible for garbage collection" and "deleted" are two different things. Code can only control the first.

docs.title: Tracing eligibility, line by line
docs.text:
To find when an object becomes eligible, count its references after each line:

1:  public class StreamingPlatform {
2:      public static void main(String[] args) {
3:          String one, two;
4:          one = new String("Netflix");
5:          two = new String("Disney+");
6:          one = two;
7:          String three = one;
8:          one = null;
9:      }
10: }
After line "Netflix" referenced by "Disney+" referenced by 5 one two 6 nobody → eligible one, two 7 — one, two, three 8 — two, three 9 — nobody (method ended) → eligible
  • Line 6: one now points to "Disney+", so "Netflix" loses its only reference.
  • Line 8: setting one to null removes only one of three references. "Disney+" is still reachable.
  • Line 9: the method ends, two and three go out of scope, and "Disney+" becomes eligible.

The method: draw each object, draw an arrow for each reference, and update the arrows line by line. An object with no arrow left is eligible.

docs.title: OCP exam prep: garbage collection
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Destroying Objects and Memory Management

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — System.gc() guarantees nothing

It's a hint the JVM may ignore. After the call, assume nothing about what was collected.

Trap 2 — Multiple references keep an object alive

Series s2 = s1; s1 = null; — s2 still reaches the object, so it's not eligible.

Trap 3 — Reassignment is enough

m = new Movie("Avatar"); makes the previous object unreachable, even though m was never set to null.

Trap 4 — Locals die at the closing brace

When a method ends, all its local variables go out of scope at once, and the objects only they referenced become eligible.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. At which line does the "Inception" object first become eligible for garbage collection?

1: Movie a = new Movie("Inception");
2: Movie b = new Movie("Parasite");
3: Movie c = a;
4: a = b;
5: c = null;
6: b = null;

A. Line 3 B. Line 4 C. Line 5 D. Line 6

Answer

C. After line 3, a and c both reach "Inception". Line 4 moves a to "Parasite", but c still holds "Inception". Line 5 removes that last reference.

2. Which statements are correct? (Choose all that apply.)

public static void main(String[] args) {
    User user = new User("alice@netflix.com");
    Subscription sub = new Subscription(user);
    user = null;   // Line X
}

A. The User object is eligible for GC at Line X B. System.gc() guarantees the User object is collected immediately C. The User object may not be eligible at Line X if sub keeps a reference to it D. Garbage collection is guaranteed to run before the program ends

Answer

C only. If the Subscription constructor stores the user in a field, sub still reaches it, so A can't be asserted. System.gc() guarantees nothing, and the collector may never run at all.

docs.title: Part 1 recap: Java fundamentals
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

Everything from Part 1 on one page. Each block links back to its section if you want the details.

docs.title: How Java runs your code
docs.text: .java source → javac → .class bytecode → the JVM runs it on any machine. Install the JDK: it contains the JVM, the libraries and the tools (javac, java, jar, javadoc). javac takes a file name (javac Movie.java); java takes a class name (java com.netflix.Main). → How Java Works

docs.title: Classes and the main method
docs.text: A class is a blueprint: fields hold data, methods define behavior. A public class lives in a file with exactly its name, and a file holds at most one public class. A program starts in public static void main(String[] args); String... and swapping public/static are also valid. → Your First Java Class · The main Method

docs.title: Packages and imports
docs.text: package first, then imports, then the class. A package matches its folder (com.netflix.content → com/netflix/content/). A wildcard import never covers sub-packages, java.lang is imported automatically, and a name clash is solved with a fully qualified name. → Packages and Imports

docs.title: Objects and constructors
docs.text: new creates an object on the heap and runs a constructor: same name as the class, no return type. With no constructor written, the compiler adds an empty no-argument one; write any constructor and it disappears. Inline field values are set before the constructor body runs. → Creating Objects

docs.title: Primitives and references
docs.text:
Primitives References What 8 types: boolean, byte, short, int, long, float, double, char everything else: String, Movie… Holds the value an object's address null never possible == compares values compares addresses (use equals() for content)

Literals: L for long, f for float, underscores only between digits. → Primitives and References

docs.title: Variables
docs.text: Identifiers start with a letter, $ or _, contain no hyphen and aren't keywords or a lone _. Conventions: camelCase, PascalCase, SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE. var infers a local variable's type; it needs a non-null value and one variable per declaration. final allows a single assignment. → Declaring Variables

docs.title: Initialization and scope
docs.text: Fields get defaults (0, false, null); local variables don't and must be assigned on every path before use; final fields must be assigned once, in an initializer or every constructor. A variable lives from its declaration to the end of its block; loop counters die with the loop; a name can't be redeclared while still in scope. → Initializing Variables · Variable Scope

docs.title: Garbage collection
docs.text: An object becomes eligible for collection when no reference can reach it: references reassigned, set to null, or out of scope. The JVM decides when to collect; System.gc() is only a hint, and collection may never happen at all. → Destroying Objects

docs.title: Part 6 practice questions: object-oriented basics
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Part 6 · Object-Oriented Basics

Optional page

Four exam traps and five exam-style questions covering all of Part 6. Try each question before opening its answer. To review a topic, go back to the Part 6 recap.

Exam objectives: Create classes and records, and define and use instance and static fields and methods, constructors, and instance and static initializers. Understand variable scopes, use local variable type inference, apply encapsulation, and make objects immutable.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — The missing super(...)

When the parent only has constructors that take parameters, a child constructor that doesn't call super(...) with arguments fails to compile, including the default constructor the compiler would add.

Trap 2 — static versus instance

A static method can't override an instance method, and an instance method can't hide a static one. Both are compilation errors.

Trap 3 — private is never overridden

A method with the same signature as a private parent method is a brand new method: there is no polymorphism.

Trap 4 — Forbidden pairs

abstract never combines with final, and an abstract method can't be private or static.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. What does this program print?

class Content {
    static { System.out.print("A"); }  { System.out.print("B"); }
    Content() { System.out.print("C"); } }
class Movie extends Content {
    static { System.out.print("D"); }  { System.out.print("E"); }
    Movie() { System.out.print("F"); } }
// main: new Movie(); new Movie();

A. ADBCEFBCEF B. ABCDEFBCEF C. ADBCEFADBCEF D. ABCDEFABCDEF

Answer

A. Static initializers run once, parent then child: A, D. Each object then runs B, C for Content and E, F for Movie. The second object repeats BCEF but never A or D.

2. Which statement is true?

1: class Content {
2:     Content(String title) { }
3: }
4: class Series extends Content {
5:     Series() { }
6:     Series(int seasons) { this(); }
7: }

A. The code compiles B. Line 5 does not compile C. Line 6 does not compile D. Content gets a default constructor

Answer

B. Line 5 gets an implicit super(), but Content has no no-argument constructor. Line 6 is fine: it starts with this(). Content gets no default constructor because it already declares one.

3. Which method, inserted in TvPlayer, overrides play()? Each option has a valid body.

class Player {
    protected Number play(String id) throws IOException {
        return 1;
    }
}
class TvPlayer extends Player { /* INSERT HERE */ }

A. Integer play(String id) B. public Integer play(String id) C. protected Object play(String id) D. public Number play(String id) throws Exception

Answer

B. public is wider than protected, Integer is a subtype of Number, and declaring no exception is allowed. A uses package access, narrower than protected. C returns Object, not a subtype of Number. D declares Exception, broader than IOException.

4. What is printed?

class Content {
    static String kind() { return "content"; }
    String name() { return "content"; } }
class Episode extends Content {
    static String kind() { return "episode"; }
    String name() { return "episode"; } }
// main:
Content c = new Episode();
System.out.println(c.kind() + " " + c.name());

A. content content B. content episode C. episode episode D. episode content

Answer

B. kind() is static, so it is hidden: the reference type Content decides. name() is overridden: the Episode object decides. Calling a static method through a variable compiles, but avoid it in real code.

5. Which two statements are true?

abstract class Content {
    abstract void play();
    void stop() { } }
abstract class Show extends Content { }
class Episode extends Show {
    void play() { } }

A. Show must implement play() B. Episode compiles C. new Show() compiles D. Content c = new Episode(); compiles

Answer

B and D. Episode, the first concrete class, implements play(), the only abstract method it inherits, and a Content variable can hold it. Show is abstract, so it doesn't have to implement play() and can't be created with new.

docs.title: Building Classes on Top of Other Classes
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

Movies and series share a title, a duration and a play button. Instead of writing that twice, Java lets one class build on another: inheritance. Here you'll see how extends works, what a child class really receives, and the rules that shape every class hierarchy.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 extends, and what a child inherits 3 min 2 Family rules: final, one parent, Object 3 min 3 Lab: a streaming catalog built on inheritance 4 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: classes, fields, methods and access modifiers (Part 1).

Code: Java17_Part_6_Object_Oriented_Basics on GitHub

docs.title: extends, and what a child inherits
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · Building Classes on Top of Other Classes · 1/3

docs.title: Why inheritance?
docs.text:
Movies and series both have a title, a duration and can be played. Copying those members into both classes means fixing every bug twice, until the copies drift apart.

Inheritance solves it: a new class automatically receives the members of an existing one.

Term Meaning Example Parent (superclass) the class inherited from Content Child (subclass) the class that inherits Movie

docs.title: extends
docs.text:
public class Content {
    String title;
    int durationMin;

    void play() {
        System.out.println(title);
    }
}

public class Movie extends Content {
    String director;
}

extends Content right after the class name makes Movie a child of Content. Movie now has title, durationMin and play() without rewriting them, plus its own director. The parent needs no special code: it just must not be final.

docs.title: Several levels
docs.text:
Inheritance is transitive:

public class Content { }
public class Movie extends Content { }        // child of Content
public class Documentary extends Movie { }    // child of Movie

Documentary's direct parent is Movie only. Content is an indirect ancestor, but its members still reach Documentary through Movie.

docs.title: What a child can really use
docs.text:
Access modifiers decide which inherited members the child can touch:

public class Content {
    private int views;
    protected String title;
    public int getViews() { return views; }
}

public class Movie extends Content {
    void describe() {
        title = "Inception";   // ✅ protected
        getViews();            // ✅ public
        views = 10;            // ❌ private: not accessible
    }
}
Modifier Usable in a child class? public always protected always, in any package none (package access) only if child and parent are in the same package private never directly: go through a method like getViews()

A Movie object still contains the views data. The child simply can't name it: it uses the parent's public methods instead.

Inheritance also comes with a few strict family rules.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_6_Object_Oriented_Basics on GitHub

Next: final, one parent, Object →

docs.title: Family rules: final, one parent, Object
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Building Classes on Top of Other Classes · 2/3

You can now build a child class and know what it inherits. Three rules shape every hierarchy.

docs.title: final: no children
docs.text:
A final class can never be extended:

public class Subscription { }

public final class PremiumPlan extends Subscription { }   // ✅ final, with a parent

public class FamilyPlan extends PremiumPlan { }           // ❌ PremiumPlan is final

final stops a class from having children, not from having a parent. PremiumPlan extends Subscription just fine; it simply ends its branch of the tree.

Other class modifiers (abstract, sealed, non-sealed) come in later sections.

docs.title: One direct parent
docs.text:
Every class has exactly one direct parent:

class Movie extends Content { }         // ✅ one parent
class Documentary extends Movie { }     // ✅ several levels
class Trailer extends Movie, Clip { }   // ❌ two parents

This is single inheritance: one class name after extends, never two. A parent can have many children (Movie and Series both extend Content), and the tree can be as deep as you need.

A class can, however, implement several interfaces: that's how Java offers multiple types without multiple parents. Interfaces come in a later chapter.

docs.title: Object: the ancestor of every class
docs.text:
A class without extends still has a parent:

// what you write
public class User { }

// what the compiler sees
public class User extends java.lang.Object { }

The compiler adds extends java.lang.Object automatically. That's why this works, even though User declares no method:

User user = new User();
String text = user.toString();   // inherited from Object

Object is the only class with no parent: every hierarchy ends there. Primitives like int and boolean aren't classes, so they're outside this tree; their wrappers (Integer, Boolean) are inside it.

A full hierarchy for our platform looks like this:

Object
 └─ Content
     ├─ Movie
     │   └─ Documentary
     └─ Series

The lab builds exactly this tree.

docs.title: Lab: a streaming catalog built on inheritance
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Building Classes on Top of Other Classes · 3/3

Goal: build a four-level hierarchy, from Object down to Documentary, and see one object use members from every level.

Setup: in an empty folder, create one file per class: Content.java, Series.java, Movie.java, Documentary.java, and StreamingCatalog.java for main. No package.

docs.title: Step 1 — The parent
docs.text:
public class Content {
    String title;

    void play() {
        System.out.println("Now playing: " + title);
    }
}

title and play() live here, and only here.

docs.title: Step 2 — A first child
docs.text:
public class Series extends Content {
    int seasons;
}

Series inherits title and play() and adds only seasons.

docs.title: Step 3 — Use it
docs.text:
public class StreamingCatalog {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Series dark = new Series();
        dark.title = "Dark";       // from Content
        dark.seasons = 3;          // from Series
        dark.play();               // from Content
        System.out.println(dark.title + " has " + dark.seasons + " seasons");
        System.out.println(dark.toString());   // from Object
    }
}

$ javac *.java
$ java StreamingCatalog
Now playing: Dark
Dark has 3 seasons
Series@4e50df2e

The last line is Object's default toString(): the class name, @, and a hash code that will differ on your machine.

docs.title: Step 4 — Grow the tree
docs.text:
public class Movie extends Content {
    int durationMinutes;
}

public class Documentary extends Movie {
    String topic;
}

Add to main:

        Movie inception = new Movie();
        inception.title = "Inception";
        inception.durationMinutes = 148;
        inception.play();

        Documentary ourPlanet = new Documentary();
        ourPlanet.title = "Our Planet";        // Content
        ourPlanet.durationMinutes = 50;        // Movie
        ourPlanet.topic = "Nature";            // Documentary
        ourPlanet.play();                      // Content
        System.out.println(ourPlanet.title + " is about " + ourPlanet.topic
                + " and lasts " + ourPlanet.durationMinutes + " minutes");

...
Now playing: Inception
Now playing: Our Planet
Our Planet is about Nature and lasts 50 minutes

One Documentary object holds data from Content, Movie and Documentary.

docs.title: Step 5 — One place to fix
docs.text:
In Content.java, change the message:

        System.out.println("Now streaming: " + title);

Recompile and run: Dark, Inception and Our Planet all say Now streaming. One line changed, in one file, and every kind of content picks it up.

docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Building Classes on Top of Other Classes

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Utilizing Java Object-Oriented Approach — implement inheritance, including visibility modifiers.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — final blocks children only

A final class can extend another class. Any class extending a final class doesn't compile.

Trap 2 — One name after extends

class X extends A, B never compiles. Only interfaces can be listed several at a time.

Trap 3 — private is not accessible

A child can't touch a parent's private field directly, even though the object still holds the data.

Trap 4 — Check the package lines

Members with no modifier reach a child only if both classes are in the same package. Read the first line of each file.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Each class is in its own file, same package. Which line does NOT compile?

1: public class Content { }
2: public final class Movie extends Content { }
3: public class Series extends Content { }
4: public class Trailer extends Movie { }
5: public final class Episode extends Series { }

A. Line 2 B. Line 3 C. Line 4 D. Line 5

Answer

C. Movie is final, so Trailer can't extend it. Lines 2 and 5 are fine: a final class may still have a parent.

2. Movie is in a different package. Which fields can it access directly?

package core;
public class Content {
    private int views;
    protected String title;
    String genre;
}

package app;
public class Movie extends core.Content { }

A. title only B. title and genre C. views and title D. All three

Answer

A. protected reaches subclasses in any package. genre has package access and the packages differ. views is private.

3. public class User { String email; } has no extends. Which TWO statements are true?

A. User implicitly extends Object B. User has no parent class C. user.toString() compiles D. User can extend two classes

Answer

A and C. The compiler adds extends java.lang.Object, so User inherits toString(). Only Object has no parent, and no class has two direct parents.

docs.title: Building Child Classes with this and super
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

A child class uses its parent's members, but not all of them, and sometimes two members share one name. Here you'll see how to reach private data properly, which modifiers a class itself can have, and how this and super point at exactly the field you mean.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: Building Classes on Top of Other Classes.

Code: Java17_Part_6_Object_Oriented_Basics on GitHub

docs.title: Child classes and class visibility
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · Building Child Classes with this and super · 1/3

docs.title: What flows down, what stays home
docs.text:
// Content.java
public class Content {
    private int rating;
    protected String title;

    public void setRating(int r) {
        rating = r;
    }
}

// Movie.java (same package)
class Movie extends Content {
    void setup(int r, String t) {
        setRating(r);    // ✅ public: inherited
        title = t;       // ✅ protected: inherited
    }
}

Movie uses setRating() and title as if it had written them. Every Movie object still holds a rating too, but only Content's own code can touch it.

docs.title: Reaching a private field
docs.text:
Naming a parent's private field from the child doesn't compile:

class Movie extends Content {
    void show() {
        System.out.print(rating);         // ❌ rating is private in Content
    }
}

From Movie's point of view, rating doesn't exist. The fix is a door the parent opens on purpose, a getter:

// in Content
public int getRating() {
    return rating;
}

// in Movie
void show() {
    System.out.print(getRating());        // ✅
}

Remember the rule for members with no modifier: a child inherits them only when both classes share a package.

docs.title: Which modifiers can a class have?
docs.text:
A top-level class is one not written inside another class. It has only two options:

// StreamingPlatform.java
public class StreamingPlatform { }   // ✅ public: matches the file name
class Catalog { }                    // ✅ package access
class Recommender { }                // ✅ as many as you like
protected class Billing { }          // ❌ doesn't compile
private class Logs { }               // ❌ doesn't compile
Top-level class Allowed? public ✅ at most one per file, named like the file no modifier (package access) ✅ any number, any name protected / private ❌

Classes declared inside other classes (nested classes) follow other rules, covered later.

Access decides what a child can reach. When a child and its parent, or a parameter and a field, use the same name, this and super decide which one you get.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_6_Object_Oriented_Basics on GitHub

Next: this and super →

docs.title: this and super
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Building Child Classes with this and super · 2/3

Two names can collide: a parameter and a field, or a child's field and its parent's. Two keywords resolve it.

docs.title: A parameter can hide a field
docs.text:
public class Series {
    private String name;

    void setName(String name) {
        name = name;        // ⚠️ compiles, but the field stays null
    }
}

Inside the method, Java always picks the closest name: the parameter. name = name copies the parameter into itself, and the field never changes. No error, no warning: a silent bug.

this means the current object, so this.name skips the parameter and reaches the field:

void setName(String name) {
    this.name = name;   // ✅ field = parameter
}

docs.title: The rules of this
docs.text:
public class Episode {
    private int number;
    private int duration;
    private String status;

    void set(int number, int mins) {
        number = this.number;    // ⚠️ backwards: copies the field INTO the parameter
        duration = mins;         // ✅ no name clash: this isn't needed
        this.status = "ready";   // ✅ allowed, even without a clash
    }

    static void reset() {
        this.status = null;      // ❌ no object in static code
    }
}
  • Watch the direction: the value on the right goes into the variable on the left.
  • Without a name clash, this is optional.
  • this needs an object, so it never compiles in static code.

docs.title: super reaches the parent's version
docs.text:
A child can declare a field with the same name as an inherited one. The object then holds two fields:

public class Content {
    protected int quality = 1080;
}

public class Movie extends Content {
    protected int quality = 2160;

    int mine()   { return quality; }         // 2160: Movie's own field
    int parent() { return super.quality; }   // 1080: the inherited one
}

The child's field hides the parent's. super.quality skips the current class and reads only what was inherited.

docs.title: How Java finds a name
docs.text:
Written as Where Java looks quality local variables and parameters first, then the current class, then the parents this.quality the current class, then the parents super.quality the parents only, never the current class

So super.x doesn't compile if x exists only in the child, while this.x sees both. Neither works in static code.

The lab puts both keywords to work on a premium subscription.

docs.title: Lab: premium plans with this and super
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Building Child Classes with this and super · 3/3

Goal: build a premium subscription, hit the classic shadowing bug, fix it with this, then use super to read the base price.

Setup: in an empty folder, create Subscription.java, PremiumSub.java and StreamingPlatform.java.

docs.title: Step 1 — The base plan
docs.text:
public class Subscription {
    protected int price = 10;
}

protected: the child will be able to read it.

docs.title: Step 2 — The premium plan, with a bug
docs.text:
public class PremiumSub extends Subscription {
    protected int price = 18;
    private int screens;

    PremiumSub(int screens) { screens = screens; }

    void printPlan() {
        System.out.println("Premium plan with " + this.screens + " screens");
    }
}

A PremiumSub now holds two price fields: the parent's 10 and its own 18.

docs.title: Step 3 — Run it
docs.text:
public class StreamingPlatform {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PremiumSub familyPlan = new PremiumSub(4);
        familyPlan.printPlan();
    }
}

$ javac *.java
$ java StreamingPlatform
Premium plan with 0 screens

Zero screens: the parameter screens hides the field, so screens = screens assigns the parameter to itself. The field keeps its default, 0.

docs.title: Step 4 — Fix it with this
docs.text:
PremiumSub(int screens) { this.screens = screens; }

Premium plan with 4 screens

docs.title: Step 5 — Read the base price with super
docs.text:
Add to PremiumSub:

    int upgradeCost() { return price - super.price; }

And two lines at the end of printPlan():

        System.out.println("Premium price: $" + this.price);
        System.out.println("Base price: $" + super.price);

In main, after printPlan():

        System.out.println("Upgrade cost: $" + familyPlan.upgradeCost());

Premium plan with 4 screens
Premium price: $18
Base price: $10
Upgrade cost: $8

price alone means the child's 18; super.price reaches the parent's 10.

docs.title: Final code
docs.text:
public class PremiumSub extends Subscription {
    protected int price = 18;
    private int screens;

    PremiumSub(int screens) { this.screens = screens; }

    void printPlan() {
        System.out.println("Premium plan with " + this.screens + " screens");
        System.out.println("Premium price: $" + this.price);
        System.out.println("Base price: $" + super.price);
    }

    int upgradeCost() { return price - super.price; }
}

docs.title: OCP exam prep: this and super
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Building Child Classes with this and super

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — private is never accessible to the child

A child naming a parent's private field doesn't compile, even deep inside a long method. Read every line.

Trap 2 — Top level: public or nothing

private or protected on a top-level class fails. Several package-access classes in one file are fine.

Trap 3 — The backwards assignment

x = this.x; compiles but changes nothing in the field. Expect 0, null or the initial value.

Trap 4 — super sees only the parent

super.x fails if x exists only in the child; this.x sees both. Neither works in static code.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Which statement is true?

class Content { protected String genre = "Drama"; }

public class Movie extends Content {
    int year = 2024;
    void showGenre() { System.out.print(this.genre + super.genre); }
    void showYear()  { System.out.print(this.year + super.year); }
}

A. It compiles B. Only showGenre() fails C. Only showYear() fails D. Both fail

Answer

C. year exists only in Movie, and super never looks in the current class. genre is inherited, so both this.genre and super.genre work.

2. What is the output?

public class User {
    private String name = "guest";
    void rename(String name) { name = this.name; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var u = new User();
        u.rename("Mounir");
        System.out.print(u.name);
    }
}

A. Mounir B. guest C. null D. It doesn't compile

Answer

B. name = this.name copies the field into the parameter: the field still holds guest. It compiles: main reads u.name through an object, inside User, so private is fine.

3. Each option alone is the top-level class of Episode.java. Which compile? (Choose two.)

A. public class Episode { } B. protected class Episode { } C. class Season { } D. private class Trailer { }

Answer

A and C. A is public and named like the file. C has package access, so its name doesn't have to match. protected and private aren't allowed on a top-level class.

docs.title: Building Objects the Right Way with Constructors
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

Every object starts its life in a constructor. Here you'll learn to write constructors, offer several ways to build the same object, reuse one constructor from another with this(), and build the parent part first with super() — including the call the compiler adds behind your back.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Code: Java17_Part_6_Object_Oriented_Basics on GitHub

docs.title: Writing and overloading constructors
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · Building Objects the Right Way with Constructors · 1/3

docs.title: Anatomy of a constructor
docs.text:
public class Movie {
    private String title;

    public Movie(String t) {
        title = t;
    }
}

// somewhere else
Movie m = new Movie("Dune");
  • Its name is exactly the class name, capital letter included.
  • It has no return type, not even void.
  • new reserves memory, then calls the constructor whose parameters match the arguments.
  • Parameters can be of any type, except var.

docs.title: Lookalikes that aren't constructors
docs.text:
public class Movie {
    public movie() { }          // ❌ wrong case: a method with no return type → doesn't compile
    public void Movie() { }     // ⚠️ a valid method, never called by new
    public Movie(var t) { }     // ❌ var isn't allowed for parameters
}

A return type, even void, turns a "constructor" into an ordinary method.

docs.title: Several ways to build a movie
docs.text:
A class can declare several constructors, each with a different list of parameter types. This is constructor overloading:

public Movie() { title = "Untitled"; }
public Movie(String title) { this.title = title; }
public Movie(String title, int minutes) { /* … */ }
public Movie(String title, String... genres) { /* … */ }

new Movie();              // runs the first one
new Movie("Dune", 155);   // runs the third one

As with methods, each signature must be unique: two constructors can't have the same list of parameter types. The arguments of new decide which one runs.

docs.title: The constructor Java writes for you
docs.text:
When a class declares no constructor at all, the compiler adds a default constructor: no parameters, empty body.

public class Clip { }                               // gets a default constructor
public class Teaser { public Teaser() { } }         // declares its own: no default added
public class Poster { public Poster(boolean hd) { } }
public class Banner { private Banner() { } }
Class new X() from another class Clip ✅ the default constructor Teaser ✅ its own no-argument constructor Poster ❌ it has a constructor, so no default one Banner ❌ its only constructor is private

A private constructor prevents other classes from creating instances at all.

With several constructors, the same assignments tend to repeat. The next page shows how one constructor reuses another, and how a child builds its parent first.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_6_Object_Oriented_Basics on GitHub

Next: chaining with this() and super() →

docs.title: Chaining with this() and super()
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Building Objects the Right Way with Constructors · 2/3

Overloaded constructors often repeat the same code. Two calls let a constructor delegate the work.

docs.title: Reusing a constructor with this()
docs.text:
public Movie(String t) {
    Movie(t, 90);        // ❌ a constructor can't be called by name
    new Movie(t, 90);    // ⚠️ compiles, but builds a second, wasted object
}

public Movie(String t) {
    this(t, 90);         // ✅ runs Movie(String, int) on THIS object
}

Don't confuse this (the current object) with this() (a call to another constructor of the same class).

docs.title: The rules of this()
docs.text:
1: public class Episode {
2:     Episode(int n, String t) { }
3:     Episode(int n) {
4:         System.out.println("new episode");
5:         this(n, "Untitled");             // ❌ not the first statement
6:     }
7:     Episode() { this("Pilot"); }
8:     Episode(String t) { this(); }        // ❌ 7 and 8 call each other forever
9: }
  1. First statement: nothing may run before it (a comment is fine).
  2. Only once: being first, it can't appear twice.
  3. No cycles: constructors can't end up calling each other in a loop.

docs.title: Building the parent first with super()
docs.text:
Every constructor starts by calling either this(…) or a parent constructor with super(…):

public class Content {
    String title;
    public Content(String t) { title = t; }
}

public class Movie extends Content {
    public Movie(String t) { super(t); }   // the Content part is built first
}

new Movie("Dune") → Movie(String) → Content(String) → Object(). The parent part of the object is always built before the child's.

super() follows the same rules as this(): first statement, once, and a constructor can't call both.

docs.title: The hidden super()
docs.text:
A constructor that doesn't start with this(…) or super(…) gets super(); added by the compiler. These three classes are identical:

public class Clip { }
public class Clip { public Clip() { } }
public class Clip { public Clip() { super(); } }

docs.title: When the parent needs arguments
docs.text:
The hidden super() can fail:

class Content {
    Content(String t) { }
}

class Movie extends Content { }               // ❌ default constructor calls super(): no match
class Series extends Content { Series() { } } // ❌ same hidden super()

class Trailer extends Content {
    Trailer() { super("Untitled"); }          // ✅ passes what the parent needs
}

If the parent has no no-argument constructor, every child constructor must call super(…) with arguments, or this(…). And super(…) always targets the direct parent only.

The lab chains this() and super() and prints each step, so you can watch the order.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_6_Object_Oriented_Basics on GitHub

docs.title: Lab: building movies for the catalog
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Building Objects the Right Way with Constructors · 3/3

Goal: chain constructors with this() and super(), and watch the order in which their bodies run.

Setup: in an empty folder, create Content.java, Movie.java and StreamingPlatform.java.

docs.title: Step 1 — The parent
docs.text:
public class Content {
    String title;

    Content(String t) {
        title = t;
        System.out.println("Content constructor: title set to " + title);
    }
}

The print shows exactly when this constructor runs.

docs.title: Step 2 — The full constructor
docs.text:
public class Movie extends Content {
    private int minutes;

    public Movie(String t, int min) {
        super(t);
        minutes = min;
        System.out.println("Movie(String, int): runtime set to " + minutes + " minutes");
    }
}

super(t) hands the title to Content first.

docs.title: Step 3 — A shortcut constructor
docs.text:
public Movie(String t) {
        this(t, 120);
        System.out.println("Movie(String): default runtime applied");
    }

    public void play() {
        System.out.println("Now playing: " + title + " (" + minutes + " min)");
    }

this(t, 120) reuses the full constructor with a default runtime, so the logic lives in one place.

docs.title: Step 4 — Build Dune
docs.text:
public class StreamingPlatform {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Movie dune = new Movie("Dune");
        dune.play();
    }
}

Predict the order, then run:

$ javac *.java
$ java StreamingPlatform
Content constructor: title set to Dune
Movie(String, int): runtime set to 120 minutes
Movie(String): default runtime applied
Now playing: Dune (120 min)

You called the one-argument constructor, yet Content prints first: Movie(String) → this(…) → Movie(String, int) → super(…) → Content(String). The bodies then finish from the top of the chain down.

docs.title: Step 5 — Build Oppenheimer directly
docs.text:
Add to main:

        System.out.println("---");
        Movie oppenheimer = new Movie("Oppenheimer", 180);
        oppenheimer.play();

---
Content constructor: title set to Oppenheimer
Movie(String, int): runtime set to 180 minutes
Now playing: Oppenheimer (180 min)

Only two messages: the default-runtime step never ran. But the parent still came first. Whatever constructor you start from, super runs before the child's own code.

docs.title: OCP exam prep: constructors
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Building Objects the Right Way with Constructors

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Create classes and records, and define and use constructors.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — A return type means it's a method

A "constructor" with any return type, even void, is a regular method.

Trap 2 — Default only if none

Declaring any constructor removes the default no-argument one.

Trap 3 — First, once, not both

this(…) or super(…) must be the first statement, appear once, never both. No cycles, no var parameters.

Trap 4 — A parent that needs arguments

If the parent has no no-argument constructor, each child constructor must call super(…) or this(…); the hidden super() matches nothing.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Which child classes compile?

class Content { Content(String t) { } }
class Movie extends Content { }
class Series extends Content { Series() { } }
class Episode extends Content { Episode() { super("E1"); } }

A. Movie and Series B. Episode only C. Series and Episode D. All three

Answer

B. Movie and Series both get a hidden super(), and Content has no no-argument constructor. Episode calls super(String).

2. Which line fails to compile?

1: class Trailer {
2:     Trailer() { this(30); }
3:     Trailer(int s) { System.out.print("init");
4:         this(s, true); }
5:     Trailer(int s, boolean hd) { seconds = s; }
6:     int seconds; }

A. Line 2 B. Line 4 C. Lines 2 and 4 D. It compiles

Answer

B. this(s, true) comes after a print statement. Line 2's this(30) is first, and matches Trailer(int).

3. What is printed by new Movie();?

class Content { Content() { System.out.print("C"); } }
class Movie extends Content {
    Movie() { this("M"); System.out.print("1"); }
    Movie(String s) { System.out.print(s); }
}

A. M1 B. CM1 C. 1MC D. MC1

Answer

B. Movie() calls Movie(String), whose hidden super() prints C first. Then M, then back in Movie(), 1.

docs.title: The Order Java Builds Your Objects In
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

When you write new Movie("Dune"), Java does much more than call a constructor. It sets up the class, fills in fields, runs initializer blocks and climbs up to the parent classes — always in the same order.

Once you know that order, you can read any class and predict exactly what it prints.

docs.title: Class setup: static code runs first
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · The Order Java Builds Your Objects In · 1/4

docs.title: Two moments, then the constructor
docs.text:
Every object goes through two setup moments before its constructor finishes:

Moment What runs How often 1. Class setup parent class first, then static fields and static blocks once per class 2. Object setup parent part first, then instance fields and instance blocks on every new 3. Constructor bodies run from the parent down to the child on every new

Three rules cover almost everything:

  • Static code belongs to the class and runs once.
  • Instance code belongs to each object and runs on every new.
  • Inside a class, Java runs fields and blocks from top to bottom.

docs.title: The three steps of class setup
docs.text:
class Content { }

class Movie extends Content {
    static int views = 0;          // 2. static fields, top to bottom
    static { views += 10; }        // 3. static blocks, top to bottom
}
  1. Parent class first. Movie extends Content, so Content is set up before Movie.
  2. Static fields, in the order they appear: views gets 0.
  3. Static blocks, in the order they appear. A static block is static followed by braces. Here it adds 10, so views ends at 10.

A class is set up at most once, just before its first use. Create one object or a thousand: its static code runs a single time.

docs.title: When exactly is a class set up?
docs.text:
public class StreamingApp {
    static { System.out.print("A"); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.print("C");
        new StreamingApp();
        new StreamingApp();
    }

    static { System.out.print("B"); }
}

Output:

ABC
  • main lives in StreamingApp, so Java must set up this class before main starts. That is why A and B come before C.
  • The two new StreamingApp() calls print nothing: the class is already set up.
  • The static blocks run in file order. The B block sits below main, but it still runs before main: what counts is its position in the file, not its position relative to main.

Once the class is ready, Java can start building the object itself.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_6_Object_Oriented_Basics on GitHub

Next: building an object →

docs.title: Building an object, step by step
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · The Order Java Builds Your Objects In · 2/4

The class is set up. Now new builds the object, and this part runs again for every object you create.

docs.title: From new to a ready object
docs.text:
class Movie extends Content {
    static int plays = 0;            // static field
    private String quality = "HD";   // instance field
    { plays++; }                     // instance block
    private final String title;

    Movie(String t) { title = t; }   // constructor body
}

When you write new Movie("Dune"):

  1. Class set up? If Movie isn't set up yet, Java does the class setup first (page 1).
  2. Parent part first. The first line of every constructor is this(...) or super(...). If you write neither, the compiler adds super();.
  3. Instance fields and blocks, top to bottom. An instance block is a pair of braces with no keyword.
  4. Constructor body. When constructors call each other with this(...), the last one called finishes first.

docs.title: Tracing one class
docs.text:
public class Player {
    private String quality = "HD";
    { System.out.print(quality + "-"); }

    private static int viewers = 0;
    static { System.out.print(viewers + "-"); }
    static { viewers += 5; System.out.print(viewers + "-"); }

    public Player() { System.out.print("play-"); }

    public static void main(String... args) { new Player(); }
}

Output:

0-5-HD-play-
Step Code Prints Class setup viewers = 0, then both static blocks in file order 0- 5- Object setup quality = "HD", then the instance block HD- Constructor Player() body play-

The static code is written below the instance code, yet it runs first: class setup always comes before object setup.

So far there was no parent class to worry about. Next: what happens when classes inherit from each other.

docs.title: Parents first, and final fields
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · The Order Java Builds Your Objects In · 3/4

Objects are built in layers: the parent part first, then the child part. Here is how constructors make that happen.

docs.title: Parents are built before children
docs.text:
class Content {
    Content() { System.out.print("Content-"); }
}

class Movie extends Content {
    Movie()      { System.out.print("Movie1-"); }
    Movie(int y) { System.out.print("Movie2-"); }
}

class Trailer extends Movie {
    Trailer() {
        super(2026);
        System.out.print("Trailer-");
    }
}

// new Trailer();

Output:

Content-Movie2-Trailer-

Always start from the new call:

  • Trailer() calls super(2026), so Movie(int) runs.
  • Movie(int) has no explicit first line: the compiler adds super();, so Content() runs.
  • The bodies then finish top-down: Content, then Movie2, then Trailer.

Constructors are called bottom-up, but their bodies run top-down. Only constructors on the real path run: Movie() is never called, so Movie1- never prints.

Since every constructor on the path runs, each one has a responsibility toward final fields.

docs.title: Final fields: set once, never twice
docs.text:
A final instance field must be assigned exactly once — never zero times, never twice.

This version does not compile:

class Episode {
    private final String title;
    private final int season = 1;

    Episode() { season = 2; }   // ❌ season assigned twice, title never
}
  • season already gets 1 on its declaration, so season = 2 is a second assignment.
  • This constructor never assigns title.

This version compiles:

class Episode {
    private final String title;
    private final int season = 1;

    Episode(String t) { title = t; }
    Episode() { this(null); }    // ✅ delegates to the first constructor
}

A final field can be assigned in three places: on its declaration, in an instance block, or in a constructor. The compiler checks each constructor separately: every path must leave every final field assigned once. null is a valid value, as long as you assign it.

You now have the whole picture. Time to see it run.

docs.title: Lab: booting the streaming catalog
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · The Order Java Builds Your Objects In · 4/4

Goal: make every piece of setup code print a numbered message, so the program shows its own initialization order.

Setup: create StreamingCatalog.java (no package). All classes go in this one file. Compile and run it with javac StreamingCatalog.java then java StreamingCatalog.

docs.title: Step 1 — The parent class alone
docs.text:
class Content {
    static void log(String message) { System.out.println(message); }
    static { log("1. Content class loaded"); }
    { log("3. Content fields ready"); }
    Content() { log("4. Content built"); }
}

public class StreamingCatalog {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Opening the catalog");
        new Content();
    }
}

log is a small static helper so every step prints the same way. Number 2 is skipped on purpose: it belongs to Movie.

Opening the catalog
1. Content class loaded
3. Content fields ready
4. Content built

Opening the catalog comes before the class is loaded: a class is set up the first time it's needed, here at new Content().

docs.title: Step 2 — Add the child class
docs.text:
Add Movie between Content and StreamingCatalog:

class Movie extends Content {
    static { log("2. Movie class loaded"); }
    private final String title;
    { log("5. Movie fields ready"); }
    Movie(String t) { title = t; log("6. Movie built: " + t); }
}

In main, replace new Content(); with:

Movie dune = new Movie("Dune");

Opening the catalog
1. Content class loaded
2. Movie class loaded
3. Content fields ready
4. Content built
5. Movie fields ready
6. Movie built: Dune
  • 1–2: class setup, parent before child.
  • 3–6: object setup, the Content part then the Movie part. The compiler's hidden super() in Movie(String) is what builds the Content part first.
  • The final title is assigned exactly once, in the constructor.

docs.title: Step 3 — Create a second movie
docs.text:
Add at the end of main:

System.out.println("--- second movie ---");
Movie arrival = new Movie("Arrival");

...
6. Movie built: Dune
--- second movie ---
3. Content fields ready
4. Content built
5. Movie fields ready
6. Movie built: Arrival

Messages 1 and 2 don't come back: both classes are already set up. Messages 3 to 6 run again, because instance blocks and constructors run on every new.

docs.title: Final code
docs.text:
class Content {
    static void log(String message) { System.out.println(message); }
    static { log("1. Content class loaded"); }
    { log("3. Content fields ready"); }
    Content() { log("4. Content built"); }
}

class Movie extends Content {
    static { log("2. Movie class loaded"); }
    private final String title;
    { log("5. Movie fields ready"); }
    Movie(String t) { title = t; log("6. Movie built: " + t); }
}

public class StreamingCatalog {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Opening the catalog");
        Movie dune = new Movie("Dune");
        System.out.println("--- second movie ---");
        Movie arrival = new Movie("Arrival");
    }
}

docs.title: OCP exam prep: initialization order
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · The Order Java Builds Your Objects In

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Create classes and records, and define and use instance and static fields and methods, constructors, and instance and static initializers.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — Static runs once

Static blocks run once per class, however many objects are created. Count the new calls, but print static output only once.

Trap 2 — Top to bottom

Fields and initializer blocks run in file order, all before the constructor body. Static code written below instance code still runs first.

Trap 3 — Final: exactly once

Every constructor must leave each final field assigned once: on the declaration, in an instance block, or in the constructor. Never twice, never zero times.

Trap 4 — Follow the real path

Only constructors actually called run. Start from the new call and trace every this() and super() before writing any output.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
print stands for System.out.print.

1. What does this program print?

class Content { static { print("A"); } { print("B"); } Content() { print("C"); } }
class Series extends Content { static { print("D"); } { print("E"); } Series() { print("F"); } }
// main: new Series(); new Series();

A. ABCDEFBCEF B. ADBCEFBCEF C. ADBCEFADBCEF D. ADEFBCEFBC

Answer

B. Classes first, parent first, once: A D. Each object: Content part B C, then Series part E F. The second object skips the static blocks: B C E F.

2. Which line or lines fail to compile?

1: public class Subscription {
2:     private final String plan;
3:     private final int screens = 2;
4:     public Subscription(String p) { plan = p; }
5:     public Subscription() { screens = 4; } }

A. Line 4 only B. Line 5 only C. Lines 3 and 5 D. It compiles

Answer

B. Line 5 assigns screens a second time and never assigns plan. Lines 3 and 4 each assign a final field once.

3. What is the output?

public class Catalog {
    static { System.out.print("load-"); }
    Catalog() { System.out.print("new-"); }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.print("start-"); new Catalog(); new Catalog();
    }
}

A. start-load-new-new- B. load-start-new-new- C. load-start-new-load-new- D. start-new-new-load-

Answer

B. main is in Catalog, so the class is set up before main runs: load- comes first. Static code runs once, the constructor twice.

docs.title: Rewriting What Your Parent Class Does
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

A child class inherits its parent's methods, but sometimes it needs to do things differently. Here you'll learn how to override a method safely, the four checks the compiler runs, how static methods and fields are hidden instead, and how final locks a method.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 Overriding a method: the four checks 4 min 2 @Override, hiding and final 4 min 3 Lab: subscription plans that override 4 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: The Order Java Builds Your Objects In.

Code: Java17_Part_6_Object_Oriented_Basics on GitHub

docs.title: Overriding a method: the four checks
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · Rewriting What Your Parent Class Does · 1/3

docs.title: Three choices for an inherited method
docs.text:
Choice How Result Keep it write nothing the child uses the parent's version Replace it declare the same method in the child overriding: the child's version runs Lock it the parent marks it final no child can replace it

Shared code is written once in the parent; each child rewrites only what differs.

docs.title: Replacing a parent method
docs.text:
class Subscription {
    public int getPrice() {
        return 10;
    }
}

class PremiumPlan extends Subscription {
    public int getPrice() {
        return super.getPrice() + 8;
    }
}

new Subscription().getPrice() returns 10; new PremiumPlan().getPrice() returns 18.

super.getPrice() calls the parent's version. Forget super and write getPrice() + 8: the method calls itself forever, and the program crashes with a StackOverflowError.

The real object decides which version runs, even through a parent-typed variable: Subscription s = new PremiumPlan(); s.getPrice() returns 18.

docs.title: The four checks
docs.text:
Every override must pass four compiler checks:

# Check Example 1 Same signature: name + parameter types play() vs play(int speed) is an overload, not an override 2 Same access or more open protected → protected or public, never package or private 3 No new or broader checked exception throws FileNotFoundException → the same, a narrower one, or none 4 Same return type, or a subtype CharSequence getTitle() → String getTitle() is fine

The logic: code that uses the parent type must be able to trust the parent's promises. A child may give more, never less.

docs.title: Access and exceptions in practice
docs.text:
class Content {
    public void play() { }
    void load() throws FileNotFoundException { }
}

class Movie extends Content {
    protected void play() { }               // ❌ narrower than public
    void load() throws IOException { }      // ❌ broader checked exception
}

The fixed version keeps public and drops the exception:

class Movie extends Content {
    public void play() { }                  // ✅
    void load() { }                         // ✅ throwing nothing is allowed
}

An override may always add unchecked exceptions (like IllegalStateException): check 3 only concerns checked ones.

docs.title: Return types can get more specific
docs.text:
class Content {
    public CharSequence getTitle() { return "Dune"; }
    public Number getYear() { return 2021; }
}

class Movie extends Content {
    public String getTitle() { return "Dune"; }   // ✅ String is a CharSequence
    public Integer getYear() { return 2021; }     // ✅ Integer is a Number
}

This is a covariant return type. The reverse fails: if the parent returns String, the child can't return CharSequence. Quick test: does the child's value fit the parent's return type without a cast? And void only matches void.

These checks apply to instance methods. Static methods, fields and private methods follow different rules.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_6_Object_Oriented_Basics on GitHub

Next: @Override, hiding and final →

docs.title: @Override, hiding and final
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Rewriting What Your Parent Class Does · 2/3

Instance methods are overridden. Private methods, static methods and fields behave differently.

docs.title: @Override checks your intent
docs.text:
class Content {
    public void play() { }
}

class Movie extends Content {
    @Override
    public void play(int speed) { }   // ❌ compiler error: nothing to override
}

Without the annotation, play(int) would silently become a new overloaded method. @Override tells the compiler this is meant to override something, and it refuses the code when no matching parent method exists. Put it on every override.

docs.title: Private methods aren't inherited
docs.text:
class Content {
    private String code() { return "C"; }
}

class Movie extends Content {
    private int code() { return 7; }   // ✅ a new, unrelated method
}

The child doesn't inherit code(), so redeclaring it creates a separate method: none of the override checks apply, even the return type can differ.

docs.title: Static methods are hidden, not overridden
docs.text:
When parent and child both declare a static method with the same signature, the child's version hides the parent's:

class Content {
    static String brand() { return "ADC"; }
}

class Movie extends Content {
    static String brand() { return "ADC Movies"; }   // ✅ hiding
}

Mixing static and instance never compiles:

class Content {
    static void stop() { }
    void pause() { }
}

class Movie extends Content {
    void stop() { }          // ❌ instance method vs static parent
    static void pause() { }  // ❌ static method vs instance parent
}

Access, exceptions and return types are checked when hiding too.

docs.title: Fields: two copies
docs.text:
Fields are never overridden, only hidden. One object can hold two fields with the same name:

class Content {
    String label = "content";
    String describe() { return "a title"; }
}

class Movie extends Content {
    String label = "movie";
    String describe() { return "a movie"; }
}

Movie m = new Movie();
Content c = m;

m.label         // movie
c.label         // content   ← the variable type decides
c.describe()    // a movie   ← the real object decides
Member Who decides which version? fields and static methods (hidden) the variable's type instance methods (overridden) the real object

docs.title: final locks a method
docs.text:
class Content {
    public final String id() { return "42"; }
    public final static void stop() { }
}

class Movie extends Content {
    public String id() { return "7"; }   // ❌ can't override a final method
    public static void stop() { }        // ❌ can't hide a final static method
}

A private final method isn't inherited, so a child may reuse its name freely.

The lab combines overriding, super, @Override and a final method in three subscription plans.

docs.title: Lab: subscription plans that override
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Rewriting What Your Parent Class Does · 3/3

Goal: build three subscription plans where each one overrides only what differs, while a final method keeps one format for all.

Setup: create SubscriptionPlans.java (no package). All classes go in this file. Compile with javac SubscriptionPlans.java, run with java SubscriptionPlans.

docs.title: Step 1 — The basic plan
docs.text:
class Subscription {
    String name() { return "Basic"; }
    int price() { return 10; }

    final String describe() {
        return name() + ": $" + price();
    }
}

public class SubscriptionPlans {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Subscription basic = new Subscription();
        System.out.println(basic.describe());
    }
}

describe() is final: every plan will describe itself in the same format.

Basic: $10

docs.title: Step 2 — The premium plan
docs.text:
Add between Subscription and SubscriptionPlans:

class PremiumPlan extends Subscription {
    @Override String name() { return "Premium"; }
    @Override int price() { return super.price() + 8; }
}
  • @Override makes the compiler check that each method really overrides one.
  • super.price() reuses the parent's 10. Without super, price() would call itself until a StackOverflowError.
  • PremiumPlan doesn't touch describe(): it can't (it's final) and doesn't need to.

In main, note the variable's type, Subscription:

        Subscription premium = new PremiumPlan();
        System.out.println(premium.describe());

Basic: $10
Premium: $18

describe() lives in Subscription, but when it calls name() and price(), the real object's versions run.

docs.title: Step 3 — The family plan
docs.text:
class FamilyPlan extends PremiumPlan {
    @Override String name() { return "Family"; }
    @Override int price() { return super.price() + 5; }
}

Here super.price() is PremiumPlan's, the direct parent. In main:

        Subscription family = new FamilyPlan();
        System.out.println(family.describe());

Basic: $10
Premium: $18
Family: $23

FamilyPlan.price() → PremiumPlan.price() → Subscription.price() = 10; then 10 + 8 = 18; then 18 + 5 = 23.

docs.title: Final code
docs.text:
class Subscription {
    String name() { return "Basic"; }
    int price() { return 10; }
    final String describe() {
        return name() + ": $" + price();
    }
}

class PremiumPlan extends Subscription {
    @Override String name() { return "Premium"; }
    @Override int price() { return super.price() + 8; }
}

class FamilyPlan extends PremiumPlan {
    @Override String name() { return "Family"; }
    @Override int price() { return super.price() + 5; }
}

public class SubscriptionPlans {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Subscription basic = new Subscription();
        System.out.println(basic.describe());
        Subscription premium = new PremiumPlan();
        System.out.println(premium.describe());
        Subscription family = new FamilyPlan();
        System.out.println(family.describe());
    }
}

docs.title: OCP exam prep: overriding and hiding
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Rewriting What Your Parent Class Does

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Implement polymorphism and differentiate object type versus reference type.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — Overload ≠ override

Same name, different parameters: an overload. None of the override rules apply.

Trap 2 — Static mismatch

One method static, the other not: doesn't compile. Both static: hiding. Neither: overriding.

Trap 3 — Who decides?

Fields and static methods: the variable's type. Overridden instance methods: the real object.

Trap 4 — private versus final

Private methods can be redeclared freely. Final methods can't be overridden or hidden.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Which lines fail to compile? (java.io.* is imported.)

1: class Content { public void play() { }
2:     protected Object info() { return "c"; }
3:     void load() throws IOException { } }
4: class Movie extends Content { void play() { }
5:     public String info() { return "m"; }
6:     void load() throws Exception { } }

A. Line 4 only B. Lines 4 and 6 C. Lines 5 and 6 D. Lines 4, 5 and 6

Answer

B. Line 4 narrows public to package access. Line 6 declares a broader checked exception. Line 5 is fine: wider access and a covariant return type.

2. With Content x = new Movie();, what does x.label + x.kind() + x.type() give?

class Content { String label = "content";
    static String kind() { return "C"; }
    String type() { return "c"; } }
class Movie extends Content { String label = "movie";
    static String kind() { return "M"; }
    String type() { return "m"; } }

A. contentCm B. movieMm C. contentMm D. movieCm

Answer

A. The field and the static method are hidden, so the variable's type (Content) decides: content, C. type() is overridden, so the real object (Movie) decides: m.

3. Which methods of Episode compile?

class Media { public final void play() { }
    public static void stop() { }
    private final void rate() { } }
class Episode extends Media { public void play() { }
    public void stop() { }
    private void rate() { } }

A. play() only B. rate() only C. stop() and rate() D. All three

Answer

B. play() is final. stop() mixes static and instance. rate() is private in Media, so not inherited: Episode declares a new method.
