docs.title: Blueprints You Can't Instantiate
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

Nobody watches "a piece of content" in general: they watch a movie or a series. An abstract class describes what every child shares, but can never be created on its own. Here you'll learn to declare abstract classes and methods, which class has to fill in the missing pieces, how constructors still run, and which declarations the compiler refuses.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 Abstract classes and abstract methods 4 min 2 Filling the gaps: concrete classes and the rules 4 min 3 Lab: a catalog on an abstract blueprint 4 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: Rewriting What Your Parent Class Does.

Code: Java17_Part_6_Object_Oriented_Basics on GitHub

docs.title: Abstract classes and abstract methods
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Blueprints You Can't Instantiate · 1/3

You know how a child class extends a parent and overrides its methods. Now the parent itself becomes a blueprint that nobody can create.

docs.title: A parent nobody can create
docs.text:
On a streaming platform, every piece of content has a title, a format and a running time, and every piece can be played. But a plain Content object makes no sense: what people watch is a Movie or a Series.

So you mark Content as abstract:

Class Kind new allowed? Content abstract: the shared blueprint ❌ Movie extends Content, fills in the details ✅ Series extends Content, its own running time ✅

You still write the shared code once, in the parent. Each child is forced to provide the pieces only it knows. And the rest of the program can work with the Content type while the real object decides what happens.

docs.title: Your first abstract class
docs.text:
abstract class Content {
    abstract String format();

    void play() {
        System.out.println("Playing " + format());
    }
}

class Movie extends Content {
    String format() { return "HD movie"; }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Movie().play();
        // new Content();   // ❌ Content is abstract; cannot be instantiated
    }
}

Playing HD movie
  • abstract class Content: the class can't be created with new.
  • abstract String format(); is an abstract method: a return type, a name, parentheses, then a semicolon. No body at all.
  • play() is a normal method. It can already call format(), even though Content doesn't know how format() works.
  • Movie keeps the promise by writing the body. Calling play() on a movie runs Content's play(), which calls Movie's format().

docs.title: Where abstract is allowed
docs.text:
The keyword can't go just anywhere:

class Podcast {
    abstract void play();      // ❌ abstract method in a normal class
}

abstract class Content {
    abstract String title;     // ❌ fields can't be abstract
    abstract Content();        // ❌ constructors can't be abstract
}
  • An abstract method can only live in an abstract class.
  • Only methods can be abstract: never fields, never constructors.

An abstract class can contain everything a normal class contains, and it doesn't even need an abstract method:

abstract class Content {
    abstract int length();
    String title;
    void share() { }
}

abstract class Short {        // ✅ no abstract method, still abstract
    void play() { }
}

new Short() doesn't compile either: an abstract class is never created directly, whatever it contains.

The modifier order is flexible with access modifiers: abstract public class and public abstract class both work. But abstract never comes after the word class, or after a method's return type.

docs.title: Filling the gaps: concrete classes and the rules
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Blueprints You Can't Instantiate · 2/3

An abstract class leaves gaps. This page shows who fills them, how its constructor still runs, and which declarations never compile.

docs.title: The first concrete class fills the gaps
docs.text:
A concrete class is a class that is not abstract. The first concrete class in a family must implement every abstract method that is still left.

abstract class Content {
    abstract String format();
    abstract int minutes();
}

abstract class Series extends Content {
    int minutes() { return 45; }          // fills one gap, skips format()
}

class Anime extends Series {
    String format() { return "SUB"; }     // fills what is left
}
Class Abstract? Must implement Content yes nothing: declares format() and minutes() Series yes nothing: implements minutes(), may skip format() Anime no format(), still abstract; minutes() is already done

If Anime skips format(), it no longer compiles: Anime is not abstract and does not override abstract method format().

docs.title: Abstract classes still have constructors
docs.text:
You can't create an abstract class, but it can declare constructors. They run every time a child object is built:

abstract class Content {
    Content() {
        System.out.println("Content ready: " + format());
    }
    abstract String format();
}

class Movie extends Content {
    String format() { return "4K"; }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Movie();
    }
}

Content ready: 4K

new Movie() calls the Movie constructor, which first calls super(): the Content constructor runs, and format() resolves to Movie's version. With no constructor written, the compiler adds the default one, as in any class.

docs.title: Broken abstract methods
docs.text:
abstract class Trailer {
    abstract long length()       // ❌ no semicolon
    abstract void play() { }     // ❌ has a body
    abstract void pause;         // ❌ no parentheses
    void stop();                 // ❌ not abstract, no body
}
  • An abstract method ends with a semicolon.
  • It never has braces, not even empty ones: { } is a body.
  • A method without abstract always needs a body.

docs.title: Three forbidden partners
docs.text:
abstract final class Show { }           // ❌
abstract class Clip {
    private abstract void cut();        // ❌
    static abstract void trim();        // ❌
    final abstract void crop();         // ❌
}
Pair Why it can't work abstract + final must be extended vs can't be extended abstract + private not inherited, so no child could implement it abstract + static static methods can't be overridden, so no body ever

The fixed version keeps each intent without the contradiction:

abstract class Clip {
    protected abstract void cut();
    abstract void trim();
    final void crop() { }
}

docs.title: Lab: a catalog on an abstract blueprint
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Blueprints You Can't Instantiate · 3/3

Goal: build a small streaming catalog on two abstract classes, where each concrete class fills in only what is left.

Setup: create AbstractCatalog.java (no package). All classes go in this file. Compile with javac AbstractCatalog.java, run with java AbstractCatalog.

docs.title: Step 1 — The blueprint and a movie
docs.text:
abstract class Content {
    abstract String title();
    abstract int minutes();

    String summary() {
        return title() + ": " + minutes() + " min";
    }
}

class Movie extends Content {
    String title() { return "Inception"; }
    int minutes() { return 148; }
}

public class AbstractCatalog {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Content movie = new Movie();
        System.out.println(movie.summary());
    }
}
  • title() and minutes() are abstract: Content has no idea what they return.
  • summary() is a normal method that relies on them anyway: the real object will provide the values.
  • Movie is concrete, so it must implement both abstract methods. It inherits summary().
  • new Content() would never compile, but a Content variable can hold any concrete child.
Inception: 148 min

docs.title: Step 2 — A second family: series
docs.text:
Add below Movie:

abstract class Series extends Content {
    abstract int episodes();
    int minutes() { return episodes() * 45; }
}

class MiniSeries extends Series {
    String title() { return "Chernobyl"; }
    int episodes() { return 5; }
}
  • Series is abstract too. It adds an abstract episodes() and implements minutes() from it.
  • Series doesn't implement title(): an abstract class may leave methods for its children.
  • MiniSeries is the first concrete class of this branch, so it implements everything still abstract: title() and episodes(). It doesn't rewrite minutes().

In main, add:

        Content show = new MiniSeries();
        System.out.println(show.summary());

Inception: 148 min
Chernobyl: 225 min

Follow the second line: summary() in Content calls title() (from MiniSeries) and minutes() (from Series), which calls episodes() (from MiniSeries): 5 × 45 = 225.

docs.title: Final code
docs.text:
abstract class Content {
    abstract String title();
    abstract int minutes();

    String summary() {
        return title() + ": " + minutes() + " min";
    }
}

class Movie extends Content {
    String title() { return "Inception"; }
    int minutes() { return 148; }
}

abstract class Series extends Content {
    abstract int episodes();
    int minutes() { return episodes() * 45; }
}

class MiniSeries extends Series {
    String title() { return "Chernobyl"; }
    int episodes() { return 5; }
}

public class AbstractCatalog {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Content movie = new Movie();
        System.out.println(movie.summary());
        Content show = new MiniSeries();
        System.out.println(show.summary());
    }
}

docs.title: OCP exam prep: abstract classes
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Blueprints You Can't Instantiate

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Create classes, and implement polymorphism by differentiating object type versus reference type.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — Modifier order

abstract public and public abstract are both fine. abstract after the word class, or after a method's return type, is an error.

Trap 2 — Braces mean a body

An abstract method never has { }, not even empty. A method without abstract always needs a body.

Trap 3 — Forbidden partners

abstract never goes with final, private or static.

Trap 4 — Zero abstract methods

An abstract class doesn't need any abstract method, and it still can't be created with new. When a question uses abstract, check the whole family before answering.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Which lines fail to compile?

1: abstract class Trailer {
2:     abstract int length();
3:     abstract void play() { }
4:     public abstract String name();
5:     void stop();
6:     abstract static void reset();
7: }

A. Lines 3 and 5 B. Lines 3, 5 and 6 C. Lines 2, 4 and 6 D. Line 5 only

Answer

B. Line 3 is abstract but has a body. Line 5 has no body but isn't abstract. Line 6 combines abstract and static. Lines 2 and 4 are valid: public before abstract is legal.

2. Which classes fail to compile?

abstract class Content { abstract String format();
    abstract int minutes(); }
abstract class Series extends Content {
    int minutes() { return 45; } }
class Anime extends Series { }
class Documentary extends Content {
    String format() { return "4K"; } }

A. Anime only B. Documentary only C. Anime and Documentary D. Series, Anime and Documentary

Answer

C. Anime is the first concrete class of its family and forgets format(). Documentary extends Content directly and forgets minutes() (it was Series that implemented it). Series is abstract, so it may leave methods unimplemented.

3. What does System.out.print(new Movie().format()) print?

abstract class Content {
    Content() { System.out.print("A"); }
    abstract String format(); }
class Movie extends Content {
    Movie() { System.out.print("B"); }
    String format() { return "C"; } }

A. BC B. ABC C. AC D. Does not compile

Answer

B. new Movie() runs the Content constructor first through the implicit super() (A), then the Movie constructor body (B). format() returns C, which main prints.

docs.title: Objects That Never Change
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

Imagine a movie in the catalog whose title any piece of code could quietly change. An immutable object removes that risk: once its constructor finishes, it never changes again. Here you'll learn the five rules of an immutable class, why a final field is not enough when it points to a list, and how copies protect your data on the way in and on the way out.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

docs.title: Immutable classes and the first four rules
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Objects That Never Change · 1/3

You know how to build objects with constructors and protect fields with access modifiers. This page goes one step further: objects that can't change at all.

docs.title: Mutable versus immutable
docs.text:
A mutable object can change at any moment: any code holding a reference can call a setter. An immutable object fixes its state in the constructor, and that state never changes again.

That brings three benefits:

  • Safe to share: hand the same object to ten parts of the program, and none of them can surprise the others.
  • Easy to trust: a value you read once stays true.
  • Thread friendly: several threads can share it without extra protection.

Java uses this idea everywhere. String is the best-known example: "Dune" stays "Dune".

docs.title: Your first immutable class
docs.text:
public final class Movie {
    private final String title;
    private final int year;

    public Movie(String t, int y) {
        title = t;
        year = y;
    }

    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public int getYear() { return year; }
}

This class follows three rules:

Rule In Movie 1. The class is final (or all its constructors are private) no subclass can add changing state 2. Every field is private and final assigned once, in the constructor 3. No setters callers can read, never write

With only strings and numbers inside, that is enough: both are immutable themselves.

docs.title: A final field isn't frozen content
docs.text:
A final field always points to the same object. It says nothing about the content of that object. Here is a playlist that follows the first three rules and still leaks:

import java.util.*;

final class Playlist {
    private final List<String> titles;

    Playlist() {
        titles = new ArrayList<>();
        titles.add("Dune");
    }

    List<String> getTitles() {
        return titles;           // hands out the list itself
    }
}

Any caller that gets the list can clear it or add to it. The field never changed, but the playlist did.

The safe version offers no getter for the list. It exposes delegate methods instead: small methods that answer a question about the list without handing it out.

import java.util.*;

final class Playlist {
    private final List<String> titles;

    Playlist() {
        titles = new ArrayList<>();
        titles.add("Dune");
    }

    int count() { return titles.size(); }
    String get(int i) { return titles.get(i); }
}
  • count() and get(i) read the data.
  • No method returns the list, so no caller can reach inside it.

That is rule 4: never let a caller modify a mutable object you hold.

The next page attacks the leaking version, then closes the last two doors with copies.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_6_Object_Oriented_Basics on GitHub

← Back to the series · Next: copies on the way in and out →

docs.title: Copies on the way in and on the way out
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Objects That Never Change · 2/3

A final field holding a list can still change. This page shows the attack, then the two copies that stop it, and ends with the five rules together.

docs.title: The attack through a getter
docs.text:
Take the leaking playlist from the previous page and use its getter:

import java.util.*;

final class Playlist {
    private final List<String> titles = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Dune"));
    List<String> getTitles() { return titles; }
}

public class Attack {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Playlist p = new Playlist();
        p.getTitles().clear();
        p.getTitles().add("Barbie");
        System.out.println(p.getTitles());
    }
}

[Barbie]

The caller rewrote an object that looked immutable, using nothing but a getter.

docs.title: Copy on read
docs.text:
When a caller really needs the whole list, return a new one:

List<String> getTitles() {
    return new ArrayList<>(titles);
}

The caller gets its own copy. Whatever it does with it, the playlist's list stays the same. Copying has a cost, so use it only when the caller needs the whole list; otherwise, delegate methods are lighter.

docs.title: A defensive copy in the constructor
docs.text:
There is a second door: the constructor. If it stores the list the caller passed in, the caller still holds a reference to that same list and can change it later.

The constructor must set every field, and it can also check the data. A rule that holds for every object of a class is an invariant: here, a playlist always has at least one title.

import java.util.*;

final class Playlist {
    private final List<String> titles;

    Playlist(List<String> titles) {
        if (titles == null || titles.isEmpty())
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("titles required");
        this.titles = new ArrayList<>(titles);
    }

    int count() { return titles.size(); }
}

public class Defensive {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> mine = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Dune"));
        Playlist p = new Playlist(mine);
        mine.add("Barbie");
        System.out.println(p.count());
    }
}

1

new ArrayList<>(titles) is a defensive copy: the playlist keeps its own list, so adding "Barbie" to mine changes nothing inside it. Without the copy, the program would print 2.

docs.title: The five rules together
docs.text:
# Rule Protects against 1 The class is final, or all constructors are private a subclass adding changing state 2 Fields are private and final reassignment 3 No setters writes from outside 4 No direct access to mutable parts: delegate methods or copy on read changes through the way out 5 The constructor sets every field and copies mutable inputs changes through the way in

Follow all five, and the object is truly immutable. Skip one, and some code, someday, will change it behind your back.

The lab builds a watchlist, breaks it through the constructor, and fixes it with one line.

docs.title: Lab: a watchlist nobody can tamper with
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Objects That Never Change · 3/3

Goal: build a watchlist for the streaming platform, break it from the outside, then make it truly immutable with one line.

Setup: create ImmutableWatchlist.java (no package). All classes go in this file. The first class has no main, so compile with javac ImmutableWatchlist.java, then run with java ImmutableWatchlist.

docs.title: Step 1 — The Watchlist class
docs.text:
import java.util.*;

final class Watchlist {
    private final String owner;
    private final List<String> titles;

    Watchlist(String owner, List<String> titles) {
        this.owner = owner;
        this.titles = titles;
    }

    int count() { return titles.size(); }
    String title(int index) { return titles.get(index); }
    String owner() { return owner; }
}
  • The class is final: no subclass can add changing state.
  • Both fields are private and final, and there are no setters.
  • No getter returns the list. count(), title() and owner() are delegate methods.
  • For now, the constructor stores the list it receives as is.

docs.title: Step 2 — Use it
docs.text:
Add the main class at the bottom of the file:

public class ImmutableWatchlist {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> picks = new ArrayList<>();
        picks.add("Dune");
        picks.add("Arrival");
        Watchlist sam = new Watchlist("Sam", picks);
        System.out.println(sam.owner() + ": " + sam.count() + " titles, first = " + sam.title(0));
    }
}

Sam: 2 titles, first = Dune

docs.title: Step 3 — Try to break it
docs.text:
The watchlist has no setters, but main still holds picks. At the end of main, clear that list, add another title, and print the summary again:

        picks.clear();
        picks.add("Barbie");
        System.out.println(sam.owner() + ": " + sam.count() + " titles, first = " + sam.title(0));

Sam: 2 titles, first = Dune
Sam: 1 titles, first = Barbie

The watchlist changed without anyone touching it. The constructor kept the caller's list, so main and the watchlist share it. final only guarantees that the field keeps pointing to that list, and the list itself changed.

docs.title: Step 4 — The defensive copy
docs.text:
In the constructor, replace the titles line:

        this.titles = new ArrayList<>(titles);

Sam: 2 titles, first = Dune
Sam: 2 titles, first = Dune

The watchlist now owns its copy, so clearing picks has no effect on it:

  • the copy in the constructor protects the data on the way in;
  • the delegate methods protect it on the way out;
  • the final class keeps subclasses from breaking the rules.

docs.title: Final code
docs.text:
import java.util.*;

final class Watchlist {
    private final String owner;
    private final List<String> titles;

    Watchlist(String owner, List<String> titles) {
        this.owner = owner;
        this.titles = new ArrayList<>(titles);
    }

    int count() { return titles.size(); }
    String title(int index) { return titles.get(index); }
    String owner() { return owner; }
}

public class ImmutableWatchlist {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> picks = new ArrayList<>();
        picks.add("Dune");
        picks.add("Arrival");
        Watchlist sam = new Watchlist("Sam", picks);
        System.out.println(sam.owner() + ": " + sam.count() + " titles, first = " + sam.title(0));
        picks.clear();
        picks.add("Barbie");
        System.out.println(sam.owner() + ": " + sam.count() + " titles, first = " + sam.title(0));
    }
}

docs.title: OCP exam prep: immutable objects
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Objects That Never Change

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Understand variable scopes, use local variable type inference, apply encapsulation, and make objects immutable.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — final is not immutable

A final field holding a list always points to the same list, but the list itself can still change.

Trap 2 — The leaking getter

A getter that returns a mutable field breaks immutability, even when the field is private and final.

Trap 3 — No copy in the constructor

A constructor that stores the caller's list without copying it lets the caller change the object later.

Trap 4 — The open class

A class that is not final and has public constructors can be extended by a mutable subclass.

When a question asks whether a class is immutable, check all five rules.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Which change makes this class immutable?

public final class Movie {
    private final List<String> cast;
    public Movie(List<String> c) { cast = c; }
    public List<String> getCast() { return cast; }
}

A. Make the class abstract B. Copy the list in the constructor only C. Copy the list in the constructor and in the getter D. Nothing: it is already immutable

Answer

C. The copy in the constructor stops the caller from changing the cast through its own reference; returning a copy from getCast() stops changes through the getter. Copying in only one place leaves the other door open (B). Making the class abstract doesn't help (A), and the class is not immutable yet (D).

2. What does this code print?

final class Show {
    private final List<String> tags;
    Show(List<String> t) { tags = t; }
    int size() { return tags.size(); }
}
// in main:
List<String> t = new ArrayList<>(List.of("drama"));
Show s = new Show(t);
t.add("crime");
System.out.println(s.size());

A. 1 B. 2 C. 0 D. Does not compile

Answer

B. The constructor stored the caller's list without copying it, so the show and the caller share it. Adding "crime" changes the show too. final doesn't help: the field still points to the same list, and that list changed. A defensive copy would have kept the size at 1.

3. Is Series immutable? If not, which rule does it break?

public class Series {
    private final String title;
    private final int seasons;
    public Series(String t, int s) { title = t; seasons = s; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public int getSeasons() { return seasons; }
}

A. Yes, it is immutable B. No: it can be extended C. No: strings must be copied D. No: fields must be static

Answer

B. Series is not final and has a public constructor, so a subclass can add changing fields or override getTitle(). Code holding a Series could then receive a mutable object. Marking the class final, or making its constructors private, fixes it. Strings are immutable themselves, so they need no copy (C), and the fields must not be static (D).

docs.title: Part 6 recap: object-oriented basics
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

Everything from Part 6 on one page. Each block links back to its section if you want the details.

docs.title: Class families, this and super
docs.text:
A class extends exactly one class. Without extends, it extends Object, so every family ends there. A child inherits the public and protected members of its parent, plus the package members when both classes share a package. private members are never inherited.

class Content {
    private final String type;
    Content(String type) { this.type = type; }
    String describe() { return type; }
}

class Movie extends Content {
    private final String title;

    Movie(String title) {
        super("movie");
        this.title = title;
    }

    @Override
    String describe() {
        return super.describe() + " " + title;
    }
}

this reaches every member of the current object, its own and the inherited ones. super reaches only what came from the parent: here, super.describe() reuses the parent's version before adding the title. → Building Classes on Top of Other Classes, Building Child Classes with this and super

docs.title: Constructor rules
docs.text:
• No constructor written? The compiler adds a default one, with no parameters.
  • The first line of every constructor calls another constructor: this(...) in the same class or super(...) in the parent. If you write neither, the compiler inserts super().
  • If the parent has no no-argument constructor, every child constructor must call super(...) with arguments itself.
class Content {
    Content(String type) { }
}

class Series extends Content {
    Series() {
        super("series");   // required: Content has no Content()
    }
    Series(int seasons) {
        this();            // calls Series(), which calls super("series")
    }
}

→ Building Objects the Right Way with Constructors

docs.title: The order objects are built in
docs.text:
1. Parent static variables and static initializers, in the order they appear: once, when the class is first used.
  2. The same for the child class: once.
  3. For each new object: the parent's instance variables and instance initializers, then the parent's constructor.
  4. The same for the child; the child's constructor runs last.
public class BuildOrder {
    static class Content {
        static { System.out.println("Content static"); }
        { System.out.println("Content instance"); }
        Content() { System.out.println("Content()"); }
    }

    static class Episode extends Content {
        static { System.out.println("Episode static"); }
        { System.out.println("Episode instance"); }
        Episode() { System.out.println("Episode()"); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Episode();
    }
}

Content static
Episode static
Content instance
Content()
Episode instance
Episode()

Every final instance field must get a value exactly once before the constructor ends. → The Order Java Builds Your Objects In

docs.title: Overload, override, hide, redeclare
Abstract classes
docs.text:
An abstract class can't be created with new. Its abstract methods have no body and end with a semicolon, and they can't be final, private or static. The first concrete subclass must implement every abstract method it inherits.

abstract class Media {
    abstract void play();
    void stop() { }
}

class Documentary extends Media {
    @Override
    void play() { }
}

A Media variable can hold a Documentary; new Media() doesn't compile. → Blueprints You Can't Instantiate

docs.title: Immutable objects
docs.text:
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public final class Watchlist {
    private final List<String> titles;

    public Watchlist(List<String> titles) {
        this.titles = new ArrayList<>(titles);   // copy on the way in
    }
    public int count() { return titles.size(); }
    public String title(int i) { return titles.get(i); }   // no getter for the list
}

A final class (or private constructors), private final fields, no setters, a defensive copy in the constructor, and no direct access to mutable fields on the way out. → Objects That Never Change

docs.title: Contracts Your Classes Promise to Keep
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

A Java class can extend only one parent. So how can a movie be playable, downloadable and rateable at the same time? With interfaces: contracts that list what a class promises to do. Here you'll learn how to write an interface, how a class implements one or several of them, which modifiers the compiler adds for you, and the newer kinds of interface methods: default, static and private.

▶️ The video is on the ADC with Mounir YouTube channel.

docs.title: In this series

docs.title: Declaring, implementing and extending interfaces
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Contracts Your Classes Promise to Keep · 1/4

You know how a class inherits from one parent, and how an abstract class forces its children to write some methods. Interfaces take that idea further.

docs.title: One parent, many contracts
docs.text:
A class can extend only one class. It can implement as many interfaces as it needs. An interface describes what an object can do, not how:

  • Playable promises a play() method;
  • Downloadable promises a download() method;
  • a Movie class can sign both contracts at once.

Like an abstract class, an interface is an abstract type: you never create an instance of it directly. When people say "an instance of an interface", they mean an object of a class that implements it.

docs.title: Writing an interface
docs.text:
public interface Playable {
    int MAX_SCREENS = 4;
    Number rating(int age);
}
  • interface replaces class.
  • MAX_SCREENS is a constant.
  • rating is an abstract method: a name, parameters and a return type, but no body. A semicolon replaces the braces.

An interface with no methods at all, such as interface Empty { }, compiles too. Two things never compile:

var p = new Playable();      // ❌ an interface is abstract
final interface Rated { }    // ❌ nobody could ever implement it

docs.title: Implementing interfaces
docs.text:
interface Playable { Number rating(int age); }
interface Downloadable { void download(); }

public class Movie implements Playable, Downloadable {
    public Double rating(int age) {    // a Double is a Number
        return 4.5;
    }
    public void download() { System.out.println("Saved"); }
}
Rule In Movie List the interfaces after implements, separated by commas Playable, Downloadable Provide every abstract method rating() and download() Keep them public interface methods are public, so the class can't hide them A covariant return type is allowed Double replaces Number

docs.title: Interfaces that extend interfaces
docs.text:
An interface can extend several interfaces:

interface Streamable { void play(); }
interface Downloadable { void download(); }
interface Offline extends Streamable, Downloadable { }

abstract class Media implements Offline { }    // may leave the work to its children

class Episode extends Media {                  // must write both methods
    public void play() { System.out.println("Playing"); }
    public void download() { System.out.println("Saved"); }
}

An abstract class can wait. The first concrete class in the chain must implement every inherited abstract method, or it doesn't compile. Extending several interfaces is safe because interfaces have no constructors and take no part in building an object: they only add rules.

docs.title: extends or implements?
docs.text:
From To Keyword How many class class extends one class interface implements many interface interface extends many

A class never extends an interface, an interface never extends a class, and an interface never implements anything.

The next page shows the keywords the compiler adds to every interface, and what happens when two interfaces ask for the same method.

docs.title: Implicit modifiers and duplicate methods
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Contracts Your Classes Promise to Keep · 2/4

You can declare and implement interfaces. This page shows what the compiler writes for you, and how one method can satisfy two contracts.

docs.title: What the compiler writes for you
docs.text:
Interfaces have implicit modifiers: keywords the compiler adds even if you don't write them. These two declarations are identical:

interface Playable {
    int MAX_SCREENS = 4;
    void play();
}

abstract interface Playable {
    public static final int MAX_SCREENS = 4;
    public abstract void play();
}
Element Implicitly the interface abstract a field public static final: a constant, read with Playable.MAX_SCREENS a method without a body abstract a method that isn't private public

Writing these keywords yourself or leaving them out gives exactly the same result.

docs.title: When your modifier fights the compiler
docs.text:
A modifier that contradicts an implicit one doesn't compile:

interface Playable {
    private int LIMIT = 4;     // ❌ fields are implicitly public
    protected void play();     // ❌ abstract methods are implicitly public
}

The implementing class has the same constraint. The method is public in the interface, so an implementation without a modifier gets package access, which is weaker:

interface Playable { void play(); }

class Movie implements Playable {
    void play() { }            // ❌ weaker access than public
}

The fix is public void play() { }. Abstract classes behave differently: there, a method without abstract needs a body, and a method without a modifier simply has package access. Only interfaces fill in these keywords for you.

docs.title: The same method from two contracts
docs.text:
When two interfaces declare the same method, one implementation satisfies both:

interface Kids { int rating(); }
interface Adults { int rating(); }

class Movie implements Kids, Adults {
    public int rating() { return 12; }
}

The declarations are compatible: one method can override both. Covariant return types count as compatible too. But if the signatures match and the return types are unrelated, no class can ever implement both:

interface Kids { int rating(); }
interface Adults { String rating(); }

class Movie implements Kids, Adults { }   // ❌ no rating() can return int and String

docs.title: Six kinds of interface members
docs.text:
Interfaces started with constants and abstract methods. Today they hold six kinds of members:

Member Body Access Belongs to constant — public the interface abstract method no public the instance default method yes public the instance static method yes public (or private) the interface private method yes private the instance private static method yes private the interface

Instance members run on the object that implements the interface. Class members belong to the interface itself, like static members of a class. An interface member is never protected and never has package access.

The next page covers the four kinds of members that have a body.

docs.title: default, static and private methods
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Contracts Your Classes Promise to Keep · 3/4

You know the six kinds of interface members. Four of them have a body: default, static, private and private static methods.

docs.title: default methods
docs.text:
A default method is declared with default and has a body. Every implementing class inherits it, and may override it.

interface Playable {
    String title();
    default String quality() { return "HD"; }
}

class Movie implements Playable {
    public String title() { return "Dune"; }   // quality() is inherited: "HD"
}

Default methods exist for backward compatibility: you can add one to an interface used by hundreds of classes, and none of them breaks. A default method only lives in an interface, is implicitly public, and is never abstract, final or static.

docs.title: Two defaults, one class
docs.text:
If a class inherits the same default method from two interfaces, Java can't choose, and the class doesn't compile. Overriding the method removes the ambiguity, and Interface.super.method() calls one parent's version:

interface Mobile  { default String quality() { return "720p"; } }
interface SmartTv { default String quality() { return "4K"; } }

class Player implements Mobile, SmartTv {
    public String quality() {             // required override
        return SmartTv.super.quality();   // "4K"
    }
}

docs.title: static methods
docs.text:
A static method has a body, belongs to the interface itself, and is public unless marked private. It is never abstract or final, and it is not inherited:

interface Pricing {
    static double tax() { return 0.2; }
}

class Plan implements Pricing {
    double fixed(double p) { return p + p * Pricing.tax(); }   // tax() alone doesn't compile
}

Always call it with the interface name. That way, two interfaces can declare the same static method without any conflict.

docs.title: private methods
docs.text:
private and private static methods remove duplicated code inside the interface, and are invisible outside it:

interface Notifier {
    default void newEpisode() { send("New episode"); }
    static void promo() { log("Promo"); }

    private void send(String m) { log("Push: " + m); }
    private static void log(String m) { System.out.println(m); }
}

docs.title: Who can call whom
Lab: a movie that plays on every screen
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Contracts Your Classes Promise to Keep · 4/4

Goal: write a Playable interface that uses every kind of method, then make a Movie sign three contracts and settle a collision between two default methods.

Setup: create EveryScreen.java (no package). All types go in this file. The first type has no main, so compile with javac EveryScreen.java, then run with java EveryScreen.

docs.title: Step 1 — The Playable interface and a movie
docs.text:
interface Playable {
    String title();

    static String brand() { return "ADCFlix"; }

    private String tag(String t) {
        return "[" + brand() + "] Playing " + t;
    }

    default String play() { return tag(title()); }
}

class Movie implements Playable {
    public String title() { return "Dune"; }
}

public class EveryScreen {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Movie dune = new Movie();
        System.out.println(dune.play());
    }
}

[ADCFlix] Playing Dune

Movie only writes title(). play() comes from the interface, and the private helper tag() adds the brand returned by the static brand().

docs.title: Step 2 — A second contract
docs.text:
Below Playable, add:

interface Mobile {
    default String quality() { return "720p"; }
}

Then replace the class line and the print line:

class Movie implements Playable, Mobile {

        System.out.println(dune.play() + " in " + dune.quality());

[ADCFlix] Playing Dune in 720p

Movie inherits quality() from Mobile without writing a line.

docs.title: Step 3 — Two defaults collide
docs.text:
Below Mobile, add SmartTv, and let Movie sign it too:

interface SmartTv {
    default String quality() { return "4K"; }
}

class Movie implements Playable, Mobile, SmartTv {

The class no longer compiles: Movie inherits two quality() defaults with the same signature. Override it in Movie, and pick the SmartTv version:

    public String quality() { return SmartTv.super.quality(); }

[ADCFlix] Playing Dune in 4K

docs.title: Step 4 — Call the static method
docs.text:
A static interface method is not inherited, so call it with the interface name. At the end of main:

        System.out.println("Brand: " + Playable.brand());

[ADCFlix] Playing Dune in 4K
Brand: ADCFlix

docs.title: Final code
docs.text:
interface Playable {
    String title();

    static String brand() { return "ADCFlix"; }

    private String tag(String t) {
        return "[" + brand() + "] Playing " + t;
    }

    default String play() { return tag(title()); }
}

interface Mobile {
    default String quality() { return "720p"; }
}

interface SmartTv {
    default String quality() { return "4K"; }
}

class Movie implements Playable, Mobile, SmartTv {
    public String title() { return "Dune"; }

    public String quality() { return SmartTv.super.quality(); }
}

public class EveryScreen {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Movie dune = new Movie();
        System.out.println(dune.play() + " in " + dune.quality());
        System.out.println("Brand: " + Playable.brand());
    }
}

docs.title: OCP exam prep: interfaces
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Contracts Your Classes Promise to Keep

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Create and use interfaces, identify functional interfaces, and utilize private, static, and default interface methods.

docs.title: Eight traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — No new, no final

An interface can't be instantiated with new, and it can't be marked final.

Trap 2 — Keywords mixed up

A class implements interfaces, an interface extends interfaces. A class never extends an interface, and an interface never implements anything.

Trap 3 — Weaker access

Interface methods are public: an implementing method without a modifier has package access and doesn't compile.

Trap 4 — Incompatible duplicates

Two inherited abstract methods with the same signature but unrelated return types can never be implemented by the same class.

Trap 5 — Two defaults collide

A class that inherits the same default method from two interfaces doesn't compile unless it overrides it.

Trap 6 — The super syntax

A specific parent default is called with Mobile.super.quality(), never Mobile.quality().

Trap 7 — static is not inherited

A static interface method must be called with the interface name, even inside the implementing class.

Trap 8 — static can't reach the instance

A static method can't call default, abstract or private non-static methods: there is no object to call them on.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Which lines do not compile?

1: interface Player {
2:     int VOLUME = 5;
3:     protected void pause();
4:     default void stop() { }
5:     static void reset();
6: }

A. Line 3 only B. Lines 3 and 5 C. Lines 2, 3 and 5 D. Lines 4 and 5

Answer

B. Line 3: interface methods are public or private, never protected. Line 5: a static method needs a body. Line 2 is a constant (implicitly public static final), and line 4 is a default method whose body is empty, which is still a body.

2. What does new Player().quality() return?

interface Mobile { default int quality() { return 720; } }
interface SmartTv { default int quality() { return 2160; } }
class Player implements Mobile, SmartTv {
    public int quality() {
        return Mobile.super.quality() + 1; } }

A. 721 B. 2161 C. 2880 D. Does not compile

Answer

A. The override removes the ambiguity, so the code compiles (not D). Mobile.super.quality() calls the Mobile version, which returns 720, plus 1. The SmartTv version is never called (not B).

3. Which expressions can fill the blank? (Choose two.)

interface Catalog {
    static int size() { return 42; }
    default int count() { return size(); } }
class Netflix implements Catalog {
    int total() { return ______; } }

A. size() B. Catalog.size() C. count() D. Catalog.count()

Answer

B and C. A static interface method is called with the interface name (B) and is not inherited, so size() alone is unknown inside Netflix (A). count() is a default method inherited by Netflix, and total() runs on a Netflix object (C). count() belongs to an instance, so it can't be called with the interface name (D).

docs.title: A Fixed Menu of Choices with Enums
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

A streaming platform sells exactly three plans: basic, standard and premium. Store the plan as a String and a typo slips through until the program runs. Java has a type made for closed lists like this one: the enum. Here you'll learn how to declare an enum, walk through its values, turn text into an enum value, use enums in a switch, and give every value its own data and behavior.

▶️ The video is on the ADC with Mounir YouTube channel.

docs.title: Declaring and using enums
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · A Fixed Menu of Choices with Enums · 1/4

You know how interfaces describe what a type can do. An enum describes something else: a type with a fixed list of values.

docs.title: Why not a String or an int?
docs.text:
Store a subscription plan as a String and nothing stops "premum", with a missing letter: the compiler accepts it and the bug only shows up at runtime. Store it as an int and 7 compiles too, although no plan 7 exists.

An enum fixes both problems:

  • a Plan parameter only accepts one of the values you declared, so it is type-safe;
  • a typo is a compiler error, not a runtime surprise;
  • the list of values is fixed once and for all.

docs.title: Your first enum
docs.text:
public class FirstEnum {
    enum Plan { BASIC, STANDARD, PREMIUM }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var p = Plan.PREMIUM;
        System.out.println(p);
        System.out.println(p == Plan.PREMIUM);
        System.out.println(p.equals(Plan.PREMIUM));
    }
}

PREMIUM
true
true
  • enum replaces class, then the values come, separated by commas. For a simple enum (values only), the semicolon after the list is optional.
  • Values are constants, so they are written in upper case with underscores: PREMIUM, FAMILY_PLAN.
  • Printing a value prints its name.
  • Each value exists only once in the program, so == is safe. equals() gives the same result.

docs.title: A closed list
docs.text:
The compiler keeps the list closed:

enum FamilyPlan extends Plan { }    // ❌ an enum can't be extended
if (Plan.PREMIUM == 2) { }          // ❌ an enum value is not an int

An enum is a type, like a class, not a number. Compare values with == or equals(), and ask for the position explicitly when you need it: p.ordinal() == 2.

docs.title: values(), name() and ordinal()
docs.text:
Every enum comes with these methods for free:

public class AllPlans {
    enum Plan { BASIC, STANDARD, PREMIUM }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (var plan : Plan.values()) {
            System.out.println(plan.name() + " " + plan.ordinal());
        }
    }
}

BASIC 0
STANDARD 1
PREMIUM 2
Method Returns values() an array of all the values, in declaration order name() the value's name as a String ordinal() the position, starting at 0

The ordinal never changes while the program runs, but code that works with names reads much better than code that works with numbers.

docs.title: From text to an enum: valueOf()
docs.text:
valueOf() takes a String and returns the matching value, which is handy when a user types a plan name:

public class FromText {
    enum Plan { BASIC, STANDARD, PREMIUM }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(Plan.valueOf("PREMIUM"));
        Plan.valueOf("premium");
    }
}

PREMIUM
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: No enum constant FromText.Plan.premium

The text must match the name exactly, case included. A wrong name compiles fine and fails at runtime with an IllegalArgumentException, because the compiler can't know what a String holds. And valueOf() never creates a value: it returns one that already exists.

The next page puts enums in a switch and gives each value its own data.

docs.title: Enums in switch, fields and constructors
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · A Fixed Menu of Choices with Enums · 2/4

You can declare an enum and walk through its values. Now let's branch on them, then give each value its own data.

docs.title: Switching on an enum
docs.text:
public class PlanSwitch {
    enum Plan { BASIC, STANDARD, PREMIUM }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Plan plan = Plan.PREMIUM;
        switch (plan) {
            case BASIC:
                System.out.println("With ads");
                break;
            case PREMIUM:
                System.out.println("4K, no ads");
                break;
            default:
                System.out.println("No ads");
        }
    }
}

4K, no ads

The case labels are the bare value names: case PREMIUM, never case Plan.PREMIUM. The compiler already knows the type of the switch variable, and in Java 17 the qualified name doesn't compile in a case label. default still catches every value without a case of its own.

docs.title: Switch expressions
docs.text:
The same rule holds in a switch expression, and an enum adds a bonus:

public class PlanQuality {
    enum Plan { BASIC, STANDARD, PREMIUM }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Plan plan = Plan.STANDARD;
        var q = switch (plan) {
            case BASIC, STANDARD -> "HD";
            case PREMIUM -> "4K";
        };
        System.out.println(q);
    }
}

HD
  • One case can list several values, separated by commas.
  • There is no default, and it still compiles: the cases cover every value of the enum, and the compiler checks it.
  • case Plan.BASIC -> and case 0 -> don't compile: no qualified name, and an enum is never an int.

docs.title: Enums that carry data
docs.text:
An enum can have fields, a constructor and methods:

public class Screens {
    enum Plan {
        BASIC(1), STANDARD(2), PREMIUM(4);

        private final int screens;

        Plan(int screens) {
            this.screens = screens;
        }
        public int getScreens() {
            return screens;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(Plan.PREMIUM.getScreens());
    }
}

4
  • BASIC(1) is a constructor call, without new.
  • As soon as the enum contains anything besides its values, the semicolon after the list is required.
  • An enum constructor is always private, even without the keyword. public or protected doesn't compile: only the enum creates its values.
  • Make the fields private final. Each value is shared by the whole program, so its data should never change.

docs.title: Built once, shared forever
docs.text:
public class BuiltOnce {
    enum Studio {
        ADCFLIX;
        Studio() { System.out.print("built,"); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.print("begin,");
        var a = Studio.ADCFLIX;
        var b = Studio.ADCFLIX;
        System.out.println("end");
    }
}

begin,built,end

The first time the enum is used, Java creates all its values, so the constructor runs once per value. The second access prints nothing: Java hands back the value it already built.

The next page gives each value its own behavior.

docs.title: A different body for each value
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · A Fixed Menu of Choices with Enums · 3/4

Each value can carry its own data. It can also carry its own behavior.

docs.title: One abstract method, one body per value
docs.text:
public class Labels {
    enum Quality {
        BASIC {
            public String label() { return "720p"; }
        },
        STANDARD {
            public String label() { return "1080p"; }
        },
        PREMIUM {
            public String label() { return "4K"; }
        };
        public abstract String label();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (var q : Quality.values()) {
            System.out.println(q + " " + q.label());
        }
    }
}

BASIC 720p
STANDARD 1080p
PREMIUM 4K
  • The enum declares an abstract method, so every value must give it a body, in braces right after the value's name.
  • It looks like an abstract class with tiny subclasses, and that's close to how it works.
  • Forget the body for one value and the enum doesn't compile.
  • The semicolon after the last value's closing brace (};) ends the list, before the rest of the enum.

docs.title: Override only the special case
docs.text:
When most values share the same behavior, give the method a normal body in the enum and override it only where needed. An enum can also implement an interface, exactly like a class:

public class Prices {
    interface Priced { double price(); }

    enum Tier implements Priced {
        BASIC, STANDARD,
        PREMIUM { public double price() { return 19.99; } };
        public double price() { return 9.99; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(Tier.BASIC.price() + " " + Tier.PREMIUM.price());
    }
}

9.99 19.99
Element Role price() in the enum shared body for BASIC and STANDARD PREMIUM { … } the one value with its own body implements Priced the enum must provide price(), like any class

docs.title: The values always come first
docs.text:
Whatever the enum contains, the list of values is always its first element, before any field, constructor or method. Simple or complex, an enum reads from the top: the menu first, then what each choice knows and does.

The lab puts these pieces together in one small program.

docs.title: Lab: a subscription plan picker
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · A Fixed Menu of Choices with Enums · 4/4

Goal: build a Plan enum for a streaming platform, print the whole catalog, turn a typed plan name into a Plan, and find its perk with a switch expression.

Setup: create PlanPicker.java (no package). The first type, Plan, has no main, so compile with javac PlanPicker.java, then run with java PlanPicker.

docs.title: Step 1 — A simple enum and a loop
docs.text:
enum Plan {
    BASIC, STANDARD, PREMIUM
}

public class PlanPicker {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (var plan : Plan.values()) {
            System.out.println(plan.name() + " " + plan.ordinal());
        }
    }
}

BASIC 0
STANDARD 1
PREMIUM 2

Values come back in declaration order, and the ordinal starts at 0.

docs.title: Step 2 — Data for every plan
docs.text:
Replace the list of values, then add two fields, a constructor and a describe() method below it:

    BASIC(1, "720p"), STANDARD(2, "1080p"), PREMIUM(4, "4K");

    private final int screens;
    private final String quality;

    Plan(int screens, String quality) {
        this.screens = screens;
        this.quality = quality;
    }

    String describe() {
        return name() + ": " + quality + ", screens: " + screens;
    }

In main, replace the print line inside the loop:

            System.out.println(plan.describe());

BASIC: 720p, screens: 1
STANDARD: 1080p, screens: 2
PREMIUM: 4K, screens: 4

The list now ends with a semicolon, required because the enum has other members. The fields are private final, and the constructor needs no modifier: it is private anyway.

docs.title: Step 3 — The user's choice and its perk
docs.text:
In main, below the loop:

        Plan chosen = Plan.valueOf("PREMIUM");
        String perk = switch (chosen) {
            case BASIC -> "With ads";
            case STANDARD -> "No ads";
            case PREMIUM -> "No ads, downloads";
        };
        System.out.println(chosen + " perk: " + perk);

BASIC: 720p, screens: 1
STANDARD: 1080p, screens: 2
PREMIUM: 4K, screens: 4
PREMIUM perk: No ads, downloads

valueOf() turns the text into the existing PREMIUM value; with "premium" it would throw an IllegalArgumentException. The switch has no default because its three cases cover every value.

docs.title: Final code
docs.text:
enum Plan {
    BASIC(1, "720p"), STANDARD(2, "1080p"), PREMIUM(4, "4K");

    private final int screens;
    private final String quality;

    Plan(int screens, String quality) {
        this.screens = screens;
        this.quality = quality;
    }

    String describe() {
        return name() + ": " + quality + ", screens: " + screens;
    }
}

public class PlanPicker {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (var plan : Plan.values()) {
            System.out.println(plan.describe());
        }
        Plan chosen = Plan.valueOf("PREMIUM");
        String perk = switch (chosen) {
            case BASIC -> "With ads";
            case STANDARD -> "No ads";
            case PREMIUM -> "No ads, downloads";
        };
        System.out.println(chosen + " perk: " + perk);
    }
}

docs.title: OCP exam prep: enums
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · A Fixed Menu of Choices with Enums

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Create and use enumerations with fields, methods and constructors.

docs.title: Eight traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — Closed and typed

An enum can't be extended, and an enum value can't be compared with an int: both are compiler errors.

Trap 2 — valueOf() is strict

valueOf() is case-sensitive. A String that doesn't match compiles fine, then throws an IllegalArgumentException at runtime.

Trap 3 — Bare case labels

In a switch on an enum, the label is the bare value name. case Plan.PREMIUM and case 2 don't compile in Java 17.

Trap 4 — Order matters

ordinal() starts at 0, and values() returns the values in declaration order.

Trap 5 — The semicolon

The semicolon after the values is required as soon as the enum has any other member.

Trap 6 — Private constructors

Enum constructors are implicitly private: public or protected doesn't compile.

Trap 7 — Built once

The constructor runs once per value, the first time the enum is used, not every time a value is read.

Trap 8 — Abstract methods

If the enum declares an abstract method, every value must implement it, or the enum doesn't compile.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. What does this code print?

enum Genre {
    DRAMA, COMEDY;
    Genre() { System.out.print("G"); } }
System.out.print("start ");
var g = Genre.valueOf("COMEDY");
System.out.print(" " + g.ordinal());

A. start G 1 B. start GG 1 C. GGstart 1 D. start GG 2

Answer

B. The first use of the enum, here valueOf(), builds every value, so the constructor prints G twice (not A), and nothing happens before that first use (not C). COMEDY is at position 1 because ordinals start at 0 (not D).

2. Which lines do not compile?

1: enum Plan {
2:     BASIC(1), PREMIUM(4)
3:     private final int screens;
4:     public Plan(int s) { screens = s; }
5:     int screens() { return screens; }
6: }

A. Line 2 only B. Line 4 only C. Lines 2 and 4 D. Lines 2, 3 and 4

Answer

C. Line 2: a field follows the values, so the list must end with a semicolon. Line 4: an enum constructor can't be public. Lines 3 and 5 are a legal private final field and a legal method with package access.

3. Which labels can fill the blank? (Choose two.)

enum Plan { BASIC, STANDARD, PREMIUM }
Plan p = Plan.STANDARD;
String s = switch (p) {
    ______ -> "HD";
    default -> "SD"; };

A. case STANDARD B. case Plan.STANDARD C. case 1 D. case STANDARD, PREMIUM

Answer

A and D. A case label is the bare value name (A), and one case can list several values (D). In Java 17, the enum name can't prefix the value in a case label (B), and an enum value is never an int (C).

docs.title: Deciding Who Can Extend Your Class
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

On a streaming platform, a piece of content is a movie, a series or a live event, and that's the whole list. With a normal class, anyone can extend Content with something you never planned for; with a final class, nobody can. Java 17 adds the middle ground: the sealed class, which names the classes allowed to extend it. Here you'll learn how to declare one, which modifier each subclass must choose, when the permits clause can be left out, and how to seal an interface.

▶️ The video is on the ADC with Mounir YouTube channel.

docs.title: Declaring a sealed class
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Deciding Who Can Extend Your Class · 1/4

Enums give you a closed list of values. A sealed class gives you a closed list of subclasses.

docs.title: Open, closed, or in between?
docs.text:
Until Java 17, a class had two settings:

Declaration Who can extend it? class Content anyone, anywhere final class Content nobody sealed class Content permits … only the classes you name

Very often the truth is in between: Content should have exactly three kinds of children, Movie, Series and LiveEvent. A sealed class names them, and the compiler rejects every other class that tries to extend it. The author keeps control of the hierarchy, and a reader sees every possible kind of Content in one line.

docs.title: Your first sealed class
docs.text:
public class FirstSealed {
    sealed static class Content permits Movie, Series { }

    static final class Movie extends Content { }

    static non-sealed class Series extends Content { }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Content c = new Movie();
        System.out.println(c.getClass().getSimpleName());
    }
}

Movie
  • sealed goes before class, like public, abstract or final.
  • permits follows the class name and lists the allowed subclasses, separated by commas.
  • Each permitted class still declares extends Content, as usual.
  • Each subclass also picks a modifier, here final and non-sealed: the next page explains them.

docs.title: Three new keywords
docs.text:
Keyword Goes on Meaning sealed a class or an interface only named types may extend or implement it permits a sealed type the list of allowed classes or interfaces non-sealed a subclass of a sealed type this branch is open again: anyone may extend it

They are contextual keywords: they only mean something in a type declaration, so an old variable called sealed still compiles: int sealed = 3;.

docs.title: Declarations the compiler rejects
docs.text:
public class sealed Content permits Movie { }   // ❌ sealed must come before class

sealed class Content permits Movie { }
final class Movie extends Content { }
final class Documentary extends Content { }     // ❌ not in the permits clause

The fix: put the modifier first and add Documentary to the list. A sealed class is often abstract too, but that is not required.

public abstract sealed class Content permits Movie, Documentary { }

docs.title: Same package, real subclasses
docs.text:
Two more rules:

  1. A sealed class and its direct subclasses must be in the same package (or, with modules, in the same named module).
  2. Every class in permits must really extend the sealed class.
sealed class Content permits Movie { }   // ❌ invalid permits clause
final class Movie { }                    //    Movie doesn't extend Content

Declaring a class with the right name is not enough: it has to be a real subclass. And a sealed class with no subclass at all doesn't compile either.

The next page looks at the modifier every subclass must choose.

docs.title: final, sealed or non-sealed subclasses
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Deciding Who Can Extend Your Class · 2/4

You can declare a sealed class and its guest list. Now each guest has a decision to make.

docs.title: Every child picks a modifier
docs.text:
A class that directly extends a sealed class must choose exactly one of three modifiers:

Modifier Meaning final the hierarchy stops here: nobody can extend this class sealed this class is closed too, with its own permits list non-sealed this branch is open again: any class can extend it

There is no default. Without one of these words, the subclass doesn't compile:

sealed class Content permits Movie { }
class Movie extends Content { }   // ❌ sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected

docs.title: final: the branch stops here
docs.text:
sealed class Content permits Movie { }
final class Movie extends Content { }
class DirectorsCut extends Movie { }   // ❌ cannot inherit from final Movie

final works exactly like the final you already know: Movie can be created and used, but nobody extends it. It is the simplest and safest choice when a subclass needs no children.

docs.title: sealed: a list inside a list
docs.text:
public class SealedChain {
    sealed static class Content permits Series { }
    sealed static class Series extends Content permits MiniSeries { }
    static final class MiniSeries extends Series { }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Content c = new MiniSeries();
        System.out.println(c instanceof Series);
    }
}

true
  • Series is sealed, so it follows the same rules as its parent: its own permits list, and each class on it picks a modifier again.
  • MiniSeries is an indirect subclass of Content. It is not named in Content, and that's fine.
  • The list is still fixed: a Content reference can only point to a Content, a Series or a MiniSeries.

docs.title: non-sealed: reopening one branch
docs.text:
public class OpenBranch {
    sealed static class Content permits LiveEvent { }
    static non-sealed class LiveEvent extends Content { }
    static class SportsEvent extends LiveEvent { }
    static class FinalMatch extends SportsEvent { }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Content c = new FinalMatch();
        System.out.println(c instanceof LiveEvent);
    }
}

true
  • LiveEvent is non-sealed: any class can extend it, named or not.
  • SportsEvent and FinalMatch need no modifier, because they don't extend a sealed class directly.
  • Content is still sealed: every FinalMatch is also a LiveEvent, and LiveEvent is on the list.

Opening a branch is never an accident: the author of Content sees every direct subclass at compile time and decides whether a non-sealed one is acceptable.

The next page shows when the permits clause can be left out, and how interfaces get sealed too.

docs.title: The permits clause and sealed interfaces
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Deciding Who Can Extend Your Class · 3/4

Every subclass now has its modifier. Two questions remain: is permits always needed, and can interfaces be sealed?

docs.title: When you can skip permits
docs.text:
It depends on where the subclasses live:

Where the direct subclasses are permits clause in other files required in the same file as the sealed class optional nested inside the sealed class optional 
// Content.java: same file, no permits needed
public sealed class Content { }
final class Movie extends Content { }
final class Series extends Content { }

Without permits, the compiler takes the subclasses it finds in the file. Each subclass still needs extends and one of the three modifiers: leaving out permits only saves you from repeating the names.

docs.title: Naming a nested subclass
docs.text:
If you do write permits for a nested subclass, the simple name doesn't work:

public sealed class Clip permits Trailer {   // ❌ cannot find symbol: Trailer
    final class Trailer extends Clip { }
}

In the class header, Trailer isn't in scope yet. Use the full name, or leave permits out:

public class NestedPermits {
    sealed static class Clip permits Clip.Trailer {
        static final class Trailer extends Clip { }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Clip c = new Clip.Trailer();
        System.out.println(c.getClass().getSimpleName());
    }
}

Trailer

When all the subclasses are nested, leaving permits out is the cleaner choice.

docs.title: Sealed interfaces
docs.text:
Interfaces can be sealed with the same rules: same package (or named module), and every permitted type must really implement or extend the interface. The permits list can name both classes that implement it and interfaces that extend it:

public class SealedInterface {
    sealed interface Playable permits Movie, Downloadable { }
    static final class Movie implements Playable { }
    non-sealed interface Downloadable extends Playable { }
    static class Episode implements Downloadable { }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Playable p = new Episode();
        System.out.println(p instanceof Downloadable);
    }
}

true

One difference to remember: an interface is always abstract, so it can never be final. An interface that extends a sealed interface is therefore sealed or non-sealed, never final:

final interface Downloadable extends Playable { }   // ❌ illegal combination of modifiers

The lab puts all of this together in one small program.

docs.title: Lab: a sealed content catalog
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Deciding Who Can Extend Your Class · 4/4

Goal: build a sealed Content hierarchy for a streaming platform, with one subclass for each modifier, print a catalog, ask Java for the list of permitted subclasses, then let a new kind of content in.

Setup: create ContentCatalog.java (no package). Its first class, Content, has no main, so compile with javac ContentCatalog.java, then run with java ContentCatalog. All the classes are in one file, so permits is optional here; we write it anyway to keep the list visible.

docs.title: Step 1 — The sealed class
docs.text:
Two imports at the top of the file, then Content:

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

sealed abstract class Content permits Movie, Series, LiveEvent {
    final String title;

    Content(String title) {
        this.title = title;
    }

    String describe() {
        return title + " (" + getClass().getSimpleName() + ")";
    }
}

describe() prints the title and the real class of the object.

docs.title: Step 2 — One subclass per modifier
docs.text:
final class Movie extends Content {
    Movie(String title) { super(title); }
}

sealed class Series extends Content permits MiniSeries {
    Series(String title) { super(title); }
}

final class MiniSeries extends Series {
    MiniSeries(String title) { super(title); }
}

non-sealed class LiveEvent extends Content {
    LiveEvent(String title) { super(title); }
}

class Concert extends LiveEvent {
    Concert(String title) { super(title); }
}

Movie is final, Series is sealed with its own list, and LiveEvent is non-sealed, so Concert extends it with no modifier at all.

docs.title: Step 3 — The catalog and the guest list
docs.text:
public class ContentCatalog {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Content> catalog = new ArrayList<>();
        catalog.add(new Movie("Night Shift"));
        catalog.add(new Series("Dark Harbor"));
        catalog.add(new MiniSeries("The Last Lighthouse"));
        catalog.add(new Concert("Summer Fest Live"));
        for (Content item : catalog) {
            System.out.println(item.describe());
        }
        for (Class<?> type : Content.class.getPermittedSubclasses()) {
            System.out.println("Permitted: " + type.getSimpleName());
        }
    }
}

Night Shift (Movie)
Dark Harbor (Series)
The Last Lighthouse (MiniSeries)
Summer Fest Live (Concert)
Permitted: Movie
Permitted: Series
Permitted: LiveEvent

MiniSeries and Concert are in the catalog although Content never names them: they come in through Series and LiveEvent. getPermittedSubclasses() returns exactly the permits list, without the indirect subclasses.

docs.title: Step 4 — A new kind of content
docs.text:
A Documentary that simply extends Content is refused: class is not allowed to extend sealed class: Content (as it is not listed in its 'permits' clause). Only the author of Content can let it in. Replace the first line of Content:

sealed abstract class Content permits Movie, Series, LiveEvent, Documentary {

Add the class below Concert, and one item below the concert in main:

final class Documentary extends Content {
    Documentary(String title) { super(title); }
}

        catalog.add(new Documentary("Deep Oceans"));

Night Shift (Movie)
Dark Harbor (Series)
The Last Lighthouse (MiniSeries)
Summer Fest Live (Concert)
Deep Oceans (Documentary)
Permitted: Movie
Permitted: Series
Permitted: LiveEvent
Permitted: Documentary

docs.title: Final code
docs.text:
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

sealed abstract class Content permits Movie, Series, LiveEvent, Documentary {
    final String title;

    Content(String title) {
        this.title = title;
    }

    String describe() {
        return title + " (" + getClass().getSimpleName() + ")";
    }
}

final class Movie extends Content {
    Movie(String title) {
        super(title);
    }
}

sealed class Series extends Content permits MiniSeries {
    Series(String title) {
        super(title);
    }
}

final class MiniSeries extends Series {
    MiniSeries(String title) {
        super(title);
    }
}

non-sealed class LiveEvent extends Content {
    LiveEvent(String title) {
        super(title);
    }
}

class Concert extends LiveEvent {
    Concert(String title) {
        super(title);
    }
}

final class Documentary extends Content {
    Documentary(String title) {
        super(title);
    }
}

public class ContentCatalog {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Content> catalog = new ArrayList<>();
        catalog.add(new Movie("Night Shift"));
        catalog.add(new Series("Dark Harbor"));
        catalog.add(new MiniSeries("The Last Lighthouse"));
        catalog.add(new Concert("Summer Fest Live"));
        catalog.add(new Documentary("Deep Oceans"));
        for (Content item : catalog) {
            System.out.println(item.describe());
        }
        for (Class<?> type : Content.class.getPermittedSubclasses()) {
            System.out.println("Permitted: " + type.getSimpleName());
        }
    }
}

docs.title: OCP exam prep: sealed classes
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Deciding Who Can Extend Your Class

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Create and use sealed classes and interfaces, with their permitted subclasses.

docs.title: Eight traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — sealed class, not class sealed

The sealed modifier always comes before the word class: public class sealed Content doesn't compile.

Trap 2 — Only the guest list

A class missing from permits can't extend the sealed class directly, whatever modifier it uses.

Trap 3 — Same package

A sealed class and its direct subclasses must be in the same package, or the same named module.

Trap 4 — The permits clause

Required when the subclasses are in other files; optional when they are in the same file or nested inside.

Trap 5 — One of three

Every direct subclass must be final, sealed or non-sealed. No modifier at all is a compiler error.

Trap 6 — Sealed needs children

A sealed class with no subclass anywhere doesn't compile, and a class named in permits must really extend it.

Trap 7 — Interfaces

An interface that extends a sealed interface is sealed or non-sealed, never final.

Trap 8 — Nested names

In permits, a nested subclass needs its full name: Clip.Trailer, not Trailer.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Which lines do not compile?

1: sealed class Show permits Drama, Comedy { }
2: final class Drama extends Show { }
3: class Comedy extends Show { }
4: non-sealed class Reality extends Show { }

A. Line 3 only B. Line 4 only C. Lines 3 and 4 D. Lines 1, 3 and 4

Answer

C. Line 3: Comedy is on the list but has no final, sealed or non-sealed modifier. Line 4: non-sealed is a valid modifier, but Reality isn't in the permits clause. Lines 1 and 2 are fine.

2. Which modifiers can fill the blank? (Choose two.)

sealed interface Streamable permits Clip, Live { }
______ interface Live extends Streamable { }
final class Clip implements Streamable { }
final class Replay implements Live { }

A. final B. sealed C. non-sealed D. abstract

Answer

B and C. sealed works because Live has a subclass, Replay, in the same file, so no permits is needed; non-sealed opens Live to any class. An interface can never be final (A). abstract adds nothing, since every interface is already abstract, and Live would still lack sealed or non-sealed (D).

3. What is the result of compiling Catalog.java?

1: public sealed class Catalog permits Entry {
2:     final class Entry extends Catalog { }
3: }

A. It compiles B. Line 1 does not compile C. Line 2 does not compile D. Lines 1 and 2 fail

Answer

B. In the header of Catalog, the simple name Entry is not in scope: write Catalog.Entry, or remove permits, since nested subclasses are found automatically. Line 2 is fine: final is one of the three allowed modifiers.
