docs.title: Immutable Data in One Line with Records
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

A streaming platform is full of small classes that only carry data: a movie with a title and a running time, an episode, a subscription plan. Written by hand, each one needs private fields, a constructor, getters, equals, hashCode and toString. A record gives you all of that in one line, and the result can never change after it is created. Here you'll learn how to declare a record, what the compiler writes for you, how to validate and clean the data with a compact constructor, and what a record body can and cannot contain.

▶️ The video is on the ADC with Mounir YouTube channel.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 From an encapsulated class to a record 3 min 2 Immutability and the long constructor 3 min 3 Compact and overloaded constructors 4 min 4 Lab: a validated movie record 4 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: Deciding Who Can Extend Your Class.

Code: Java17_Part_7_Interfaces_Abstract_Types on GitHub

docs.title: From an encapsulated class to a record
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Immutable Data in One Line with Records · 1/4

Sealed classes control who extends a type. Records solve a different problem: the pile of code you write just to carry data.

docs.title: Open fields are a risk
docs.text:
public class OpenFields {
    static class Movie {
        String title;
        int minutes;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Movie movie = new Movie();
        movie.title = "Night Shift";
        movie.minutes = -100;          // nothing stops this
        System.out.println(movie.title + " lasts " + movie.minutes + " minutes");
    }
}

Night Shift lasts -100 minutes

Any code in the same package can write a negative running time. The fix is encapsulation: make the fields private, give callers a method to read each value, and let the constructor refuse bad data. Go one step further, make the class and its fields final and add no setter, and the object can never change after new: it is immutable.

public final class SafeMovie {
    private final String title;
    private final int minutes;

    public SafeMovie(String title, int minutes) {
        if (minutes <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
        this.title = title;
        this.minutes = minutes;
    }

    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public int getMinutes() { return minutes; }
}

Safe, but long, and you still haven't written equals, hashCode or toString.

docs.title: The same idea in one line
docs.text:
public record Movie(String title, int minutes) { }
Part Meaning record replaces class (String title, int minutes) the components: each becomes a private final field { } the body, required even when empty

From that line the compiler generates the fields, a constructor taking the components in the declared order, one accessor per component, and equals, hashCode and toString based on every component.

docs.title: What you get for free
docs.text:
public class RecordBasics {
    record Movie(String title, int minutes) { }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var movie = new Movie("Night Shift", 118);
        System.out.println(movie.title());
        System.out.println(movie);

        var copy = new Movie("Night Shift", 118);
        System.out.println(movie.equals(copy));
        System.out.println(movie == copy);
        System.out.println(movie.hashCode() == copy.hashCode());
    }
}

Night Shift
Movie[title=Night Shift, minutes=118]
true
false
true
  • The accessor has the component's name: title(), not getTitle().
  • toString prints the record name and every component in square brackets.
  • equals compares values, so two records with the same data are equal, even though == sees two different objects.

The next page shows how to call a record correctly, and why it never changes.

docs.title: Immutability and the long constructor
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Immutable Data in One Line with Records · 2/4

A record writes its own constructor and accessors. This page shows how to use them, and what "immutable" means in practice.

docs.title: Calling the generated members
docs.text:
The generated constructor has exactly one parameter list: the components, in order.

public class CallingRecords {
    record Movie(String title, int minutes) { }
    record Intro() { }                       // zero components: legal

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Movie movie = new Movie("Night Shift", 118);
        // new Movie(118, "Night Shift");    // ❌ wrong order
        // new Movie("Night Shift");         // ❌ no such constructor
        // movie.getTitle();                 // ❌ no get prefix
        System.out.println(movie.title() + ", " + movie.minutes());
        System.out.println(new Intro());
    }
}

Night Shift, 118
Intro[]

There is no constructor with fewer arguments unless you write one yourself (page 3).

docs.title: Changing a record means building a new one
docs.text:
Every field of a record is final and there are no setters. To "change" a movie, you create another one from the old values:

public class DirectorsCut {
    interface Playable { String title(); }

    record Movie(String title, int minutes) implements Playable { }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Movie movie = new Movie("Night Shift", 118);
        Movie cut = new Movie(movie.title(), movie.minutes() + 12);
        Playable playable = cut;
        System.out.println(movie);
        System.out.println(cut);
        System.out.println(playable.title());
    }
}

Movie[title=Night Shift, minutes=118]
Movie[title=Night Shift, minutes=130]
Night Shift
  • The original movie is untouched.
  • A record is implicitly final: nothing can extend it, and it cannot extend a class either (record Trailer() extends Movie { } doesn't compile).
  • It can implement interfaces. Here the generated title() accessor already satisfies Playable.

docs.title: The long constructor
docs.text:
To reject bad data, you can write the constructor the compiler would generate, with the same parameters in the same order. When you declare it, the compiler doesn't add its own.

public class LongConstructor {
    record Movie(String title, int minutes) {
        Movie(String title, int minutes) {
            if (minutes <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("minutes: " + minutes);
            this.title = title;
            this.minutes = minutes;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(new Movie("Night Shift", 118));
    }
}

Movie[title=Night Shift, minutes=118]

Since every field is final, this constructor must assign every field. Leave out this.minutes = minutes; and the compiler reports variable minutes might not have been initialized. With twenty components, that's twenty boring assignments: exactly the boilerplate records were meant to remove.

The next page shows the shorter form Java offers instead.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_7_Interfaces_Abstract_Types on GitHub

← From an encapsulated class to a record · Back to the series · Next: Compact and overloaded constructors →

docs.title: Compact and overloaded constructors
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Immutable Data in One Line with Records · 3/4

The long constructor works but repeats every assignment. Records have a shorter form made for validation.

docs.title: The compact constructor
docs.text:
A compact constructor is the record name followed directly by a body: no parentheses, no parameter list.

public class CompactConstructor {
    record Movie(String title, int minutes) {
        Movie {
            if (minutes <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("minutes: " + minutes);
            title = title.strip();
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(new Movie("  Night Shift ", 118));
    }
}

Movie[title=Night Shift, minutes=118]

How it runs:

  1. The caller writes new Movie(" Night Shift ", 118) as usual.
  2. Your compact constructor runs. Inside it, title and minutes are the parameters: you can check them and reassign them.
  3. When your code ends, Java assigns each parameter to its field for you.

So title = title.strip(); cleans the input before it is stored. Writing this.title = … instead doesn't compile (cannot assign a value to final variable title): the fields belong to Java's step 3. And Movie() { }, with parentheses, is not a compact constructor at all but a different constructor.

docs.title: Overloaded constructors
docs.text:
You can add constructors with other parameter lists. Their first statement must call another constructor with this(...), always:

public class Overloads {
    record Movie(String title, int minutes) {
        Movie(String title) {
            this(title, 90);                  // must come first
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(new Movie("Paper Boats"));
    }
}

Movie[title=Paper Boats, minutes=90]
  • A statement before this(...), or no this(...) at all, doesn't compile.
  • Any transformation must happen inside the this(...) call: after it returns, every field is assigned and final.
  • Two constructors calling each other in a cycle don't compile.

docs.title: What a record body can contain
docs.text:
public class CustomRecord {
    record Movie(String title, int minutes) {
        static int MAX_MINUTES = 300;

        String label() {
            return title + " (" + minutes + " min)";
        }

        @Override
        public String title() {
            return title.toUpperCase();
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Movie movie = new Movie("Night Shift", 118);
        System.out.println(movie.label());
        System.out.println(movie.title());
        System.out.println(Movie.MAX_MINUTES);
    }
}

Night Shift (118 min)
NIGHT SHIFT
300
Allowed Not allowed static fields and methods instance fields (private int views;) instance methods, nested types instance initializer blocks ({ … }) overriding accessors, equals, hashCode, toString (kept public)

All instance data lives in the component list, and every field is set in a constructor. Keep records simple: they are meant to carry data.

The lab puts all of this together in one validated Movie record.

docs.title: Lab: a validated movie record
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Immutable Data in One Line with Records · 4/4

Goal: start from a one-line Movie record, use what the compiler generates, then add a compact constructor that rejects a bad running time and cleans the title, an overloaded constructor with a default, and a label() method.

Setup: create MovieCatalog.java (no package). Its first type, the Movie record, has no main, so compile with javac MovieCatalog.java, then run with java MovieCatalog.

docs.title: Step 1 — The record and a first run
docs.text:
record Movie(String title, int minutes) {
}

public class MovieCatalog {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Movie nightShift = new Movie("Night Shift", 118);
        System.out.println(nightShift);
        System.out.println(nightShift.title() + " lasts " + nightShift.minutes() + " minutes");
    }
}

Movie[title=Night Shift, minutes=118]
Night Shift lasts 118 minutes

The constructor, the accessors and toString were all generated.

docs.title: Step 2 — Equality and a new record
docs.text:
At the end of main:

        Movie copy = new Movie("Night Shift", 118);
        System.out.println(nightShift.equals(copy));
        Movie directorsCut = new Movie(nightShift.title(), nightShift.minutes() + 12);
        System.out.println(directorsCut);

Movie[title=Night Shift, minutes=118]
Night Shift lasts 118 minutes
true
Movie[title=Night Shift, minutes=130]

Two objects with the same values are equal, and the director's cut is a brand new record: the original is untouched.

docs.title: Step 3 — Validation, a default and a label
docs.text:
Fill the body of the record:

record Movie(String title, int minutes) {
    Movie {
        if (minutes <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Running time must be positive: " + minutes);
        title = title.strip();
    }

    Movie(String title) {
        this(title, 90);
    }

    String label() {
        return title + " (" + minutes + " min)";
    }
}

The compact constructor reassigns the title parameter, never this.title. The overloaded constructor calls this(...) on its first line.

docs.title: Step 4 — A short film
docs.text:
At the end of main:

        Movie shortFilm = new Movie("  Paper Boats  ");
        System.out.println(shortFilm.label());

New last line of the output:

Paper Boats (90 min)

The default gave ninety minutes, and the compact constructor stripped the spaces.

docs.title: Step 5 — A broken movie
docs.text:
At the end of main:

        Movie broken = new Movie("Broken Reel", -5);
        System.out.println(broken.label());

Movie[title=Night Shift, minutes=118]
Night Shift lasts 118 minutes
true
Movie[title=Night Shift, minutes=130]
Paper Boats (90 min)
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Running time must be positive: -5
    at Movie.<init>(MovieCatalog.java:3)
    at MovieCatalog.main(MovieCatalog.java:27)

The compact constructor refused the movie: it was never created, and its label was never printed. Every Movie that exists is valid and can never change.

docs.title: Final code
docs.text:
record Movie(String title, int minutes) {
    Movie {
        if (minutes <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Running time must be positive: " + minutes);
        title = title.strip();
    }

    Movie(String title) {
        this(title, 90);
    }

    String label() {
        return title + " (" + minutes + " min)";
    }
}

public class MovieCatalog {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Movie nightShift = new Movie("Night Shift", 118);
        System.out.println(nightShift);
        System.out.println(nightShift.title() + " lasts " + nightShift.minutes() + " minutes");
        Movie copy = new Movie("Night Shift", 118);
        System.out.println(nightShift.equals(copy));
        Movie directorsCut = new Movie(nightShift.title(), nightShift.minutes() + 12);
        System.out.println(directorsCut);
        Movie shortFilm = new Movie("  Paper Boats  ");
        System.out.println(shortFilm.label());
        Movie broken = new Movie("Broken Reel", -5);
        System.out.println(broken.label());
    }
}

docs.title: OCP exam prep: records
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Immutable Data in One Line with Records

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Create classes and records, and define and use instance and static fields and methods, constructors, and instance and static initializers; apply encapsulation and make objects immutable.

docs.title: Eight traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — Accessor names

The accessor is title(), never getTitle() or isTitle().

Trap 2 — One generated constructor

It takes the components in the declared order. There is no other constructor unless you write it.

Trap 3 — Implicitly final

A record can implement interfaces, but it never extends a class, and nothing extends a record.

Trap 4 — Empty record

record Intro() { } is legal: empty parentheses, then braces.

Trap 5 — Compact means no parentheses

Movie { } is a compact constructor. Movie() { } is a different, overloaded constructor.

Trap 6 — Parameters only

A compact constructor may reassign title, never this.title.

Trap 7 — this(...) first

An overloaded record constructor must call this(...) as its first statement, every time.

Trap 8 — Body limits

Static fields and methods: yes. Instance fields and instance initializer blocks: no.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
What does this code print?

record Show(String name) { }

var a = new Show("Dark");
var b = new Show("Dark");
System.out.print(a.equals(b) + " " + (a == b) + " ");
System.out.print(a);

A. true false Show[name=Dark] B. false false Show@1b6d3586 C. true true Show[name=Dark] D. It does not compile

Answer

A. The generated equals compares values: true. == compares references, and new created two objects: false. The generated toString prints Show[name=Dark].

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Which lines do not compile?

1: record Episode(String title, int minutes) {
2:     private static int count = 0;
3:     private int views;
4:     Episode {
5:         if (minutes < 0) minutes = 0;
6:         this.title = title.strip(); }
7: }

A. Line 3 only B. Line 6 only C. Lines 3 and 6 D. Lines 2, 3 and 6

Answer

C. Line 3: a record body cannot declare an instance field. Line 6: a compact constructor cannot assign the final field this.title. Line 2 (a static field) and line 5 (reassigning a parameter) are fine.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Which constructors can be inserted in the record? (Choose two.)

record Plan(String name, double price) {
    // INSERT CODE HERE
}

A. Plan() { } B. Plan(String n) { this(n, 9.99); } C. Plan() { this.price = 9.99; } D. Plan { price = Math.abs(price); }

Answer

B and D. B is an overloaded constructor whose first statement calls this(...). D is a compact constructor that reassigns a parameter. A and C are overloaded constructors that never call this(...), so they don't compile.

docs.title: Classes That Live Inside Other Classes
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

So far every class lived at the top level of its own file. Java also lets you write a class inside another class, and even inside a method. These nested classes come in four kinds: inner classes, static nested classes, local classes and anonymous classes. Here you'll learn where each one is declared, how to create it from anywhere, what it is allowed to read, and why local and anonymous classes only see variables that never change.

▶️ The video is on the ADC with Mounir YouTube channel.

docs.title: Inner classes
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Classes That Live Inside Other Classes · 1/4

Records keep data classes short. Nested classes keep helper classes close to the class that uses them.

docs.title: Four kinds of nested classes
docs.text:
A nested class is a class defined inside another class. Where you write it decides its kind:

Where Kind Belongs to Member level, next to fields and methods inner class an object of the outer class Member level, with static static nested class the outer class itself Inside a method local class that method call Inside an expression, with no name anonymous class that single statement

Nested classes keep small helpers private to their owner and put a class right where it is used. Overused, they make code harder to read and tie classes tightly together.

docs.title: An inner class shares its owner's data
docs.text:
public class StreamingPlatform {
    private String brand = "Flix";

    protected class Screen {
        public void show() {
            System.out.println("Welcome to " + brand);
        }
    }

    public void open() {
        new Screen().show();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new StreamingPlatform().open();
    }
}

Welcome to Flix
  • Screen reads brand as if it were its own field, even though brand is private: the inner class is part of StreamingPlatform.
  • Inside the instance method open(), new Screen() is enough: Java attaches the screen to the current object.
  • An inner class accepts any access level (public, protected, package, private), can extend a class, implement interfaces, be abstract or final, and, since Java 16, declare static members.

docs.title: Creating an inner object from static code
docs.text:
An inner object always belongs to an outer object. In a static method there is no current object, so new Screen() alone does not compile. Create the outer object first, then call new on it (a main for the class above):

public static void main(String[] args) {
    // new Screen();                       ❌ no StreamingPlatform object
    var platform = new StreamingPlatform();
    StreamingPlatform.Screen screen = platform.new Screen();
    screen.show();
    new StreamingPlatform().new Screen().show();   // same thing, on one line
}

Compiling the file produces two class files: StreamingPlatform.class and StreamingPlatform$Screen.class.

docs.title: The same name at every level
docs.text:
Inner classes can nest several levels deep, and each level can reuse a field name. Outer.this.field reaches the field of an outer level:

public class Series {
    int number = 1;

    class Season {
        int number = 2;

        class Episode {
            int number = 3;

            void print() {
                System.out.print(number + " ");             // closest: Episode
                System.out.print(this.number + " ");        // also Episode
                System.out.print(Season.this.number + " "); // one level up
                System.out.println(Series.this.number);     // two levels up
            }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Series.Season.Episode episode = new Series().new Season().new Episode();
        episode.print();
    }
}

3 3 2 1

To create an Episode you need a Season, and to create a Season you need a Series, hence the chain of .new. The full type name is Series.Season.Episode.

The next page removes the need for an outer object with static, then moves a class inside a method.

docs.title: Static nested and local classes
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Classes That Live Inside Other Classes · 2/4

An inner class always needs an outer object. Adding static removes that link; moving the class into a method limits it to that method.

docs.title: A nested class that needs no owner
docs.text:
public class StreamingPlatform {
    private String brand = "Flix";

    static class Plan {
        private double price = 9.99;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var plan = new Plan();
        System.out.println(plan.price);
    }
}

9.99
  • A static nested class belongs to the outer class, not to an object: new Plan() works directly in main.
  • The outer class can read the private members of Plan, because they are part of the same class.
  • The trade-off: Plan has no outer object, so it cannot read the instance field brand without a reference to a platform.
  • From outside, its name is StreamingPlatform.Plan. Like an inner class, it can be private or protected.

Think of it as an ordinary class that happens to live inside another one.

docs.title: A class that lives in a method
docs.text:
A local class is declared inside a method, like a local variable. It exists only there: objects can be created from it inside the method (and returned from it), nowhere else.

public class Catalog {
    private int bonus = 5;

    public void rate() {
        final int base = 80;
        class Scorer {
            int score() {
                return base + bonus;
            }
        }
        System.out.println(new Scorer().score());
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Catalog().rate();
    }
}

85
  • Scorer takes no access modifier at all (no public, no private), but it may be final or abstract.
  • Declared in an instance method, it reads the fields of the object, here bonus.
  • It reads the local variable base because base never changes.

docs.title: Only values that never change
docs.text:
A local class can read a local variable or parameter of its method only if it is final or effectively final: set once and never reassigned anywhere in the method.

public class Binge {
    void binge() {
        int episodes = 3;
        class Counter {
            int total() {
                return episodes * 2;   // ❌ does not compile
            }
        }
        episodes = 4;                  // this reassignment is the cause
    }
}

error: local variables referenced from an inner class must be final or effectively final

The reassignment comes after the class, yet it is enough to break the rule. Remove it, or declare final int episodes = 3;, and the code compiles.

Why this rule? The compiler turns a local class into its own class file and passes it a copy of the value. If the variable could still change, the copy would be wrong.

The next page goes one step further: a local class with no name at all.

docs.title: Anonymous classes
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Classes That Live Inside Other Classes · 3/4

A local class has a name and lives in a method. An anonymous class is a local class without a name, declared and created in a single statement.

docs.title: A class with no name
docs.text:
public class Checkout {
    abstract class Discount {
        abstract int amountOff();
    }

    public int price(int base) {
        Discount promo = new Discount() {
            int amountOff() { return 3; }
        };
        return base - promo.amountOff();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(new Checkout().price(10));
    }
}

7
  • The syntax is new, a type name, parentheses, then a class body in braces.
  • Discount is abstract, so it cannot be created. What is created is an unnamed class that extends Discount and provides amountOff().
  • The statement declares a variable, so it ends with a semicolon after the closing brace: };.

docs.title: The same syntax with an interface
docs.text:
public class Intro {
    interface Skippable {
        int seconds();
    }

    Skippable credits = new Skippable() {        // as a field
        public int seconds() { return 30; }
    };

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Skippable intro = new Skippable() {      // in a method
            public int seconds() { return 10; }
        };
        System.out.println(intro.seconds() + " " + new Intro().credits.seconds());
    }
}

10 30
  • new Skippable() { … } creates an unnamed class that implements the interface.
  • Interface methods are public, so the implementation must be public too. Writing int seconds() without public does not compile (weaker access).
  • An anonymous class can be declared outside a method, as the value of a field.
  • It has exactly one parent: it extends one class or implements one interface, never both (unless the class is Object). If you need more, write a named local class.

When the interface has a single abstract method, a lambda is often the shorter choice.

docs.title: The four kinds side by side
docs.text:
Inner Static nested Local Anonymous Access modifiers all all none none abstract / final yes yes yes no Extends / implements any any any exactly one type Reads outer instance members yes no if declared in an instance method if declared in an instance method Reads local variables — — final or effectively final final or effectively final

Since Java 16, all four kinds can declare static fields and methods.

docs.title: Lab: a media player with nested classes
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Classes That Live Inside Other Classes · 4/4

Goal: build one MediaPlayer that uses all four kinds of nested classes: an inner Screen reading the private title, a static nested Volume that needs no player, a local Timer inside play(), and an anonymous class implementing Subtitle.

Setup: create MediaPlayer.java (no package). Its first type, the Subtitle interface, has no main, so compile with javac MediaPlayer.java, then run with java MediaPlayer.

docs.title: Step 1 — The interface, the player and an inner Screen
docs.text:
interface Subtitle {
    String language();
}

public class MediaPlayer {
    private String title = "Night Shift";

    class Screen {
        void show() {
            System.out.println("Now playing: " + title);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MediaPlayer player = new MediaPlayer();
        MediaPlayer.Screen screen = player.new Screen();
        screen.show();
    }
}

Now playing: Night Shift

main is static, so the screen is created from a player with player.new Screen(). The screen reads the player's private title.

docs.title: Step 2 — A static nested Volume
docs.text:
Below the Screen class:

    static class Volume {
        int level = 7;
    }

At the end of main:

        MediaPlayer.Volume volume = new MediaPlayer.Volume();
        System.out.println("Volume: " + volume.level);

Now playing: Night Shift
Volume: 7

Volume is static: no player is needed to create it.

docs.title: Step 3 — A local Timer and an anonymous Subtitle
docs.text:
Below the Volume class, add a play method:

    void play(int minutes) {
        class Timer {
            String left() {
                return title + ": " + minutes + " min left";
            }
        }
        Subtitle sub = new Subtitle() {
            public String language() {
                return "English";
            }
        };
        System.out.println(new Timer().left());
        System.out.println("Subtitles: " + sub.language());
    }
  • Timer exists only inside play(). It reads the player's title (instance method) and the parameter minutes, which is effectively final.
  • The anonymous class implements Subtitle. Its method is public, and the declaration ends with };.

docs.title: Step 4 — Play a movie
docs.text:
At the end of main:

        player.play(118);

Now playing: Night Shift
Volume: 7
Night Shift: 118 min left
Subtitles: English

Four kinds of nested classes, each declared exactly where it is used.

docs.title: Final code
docs.text:
interface Subtitle {
    String language();
}

public class MediaPlayer {
    private String title = "Night Shift";

    class Screen {
        void show() {
            System.out.println("Now playing: " + title);
        }
    }

    static class Volume {
        int level = 7;
    }

    void play(int minutes) {
        class Timer {
            String left() {
                return title + ": " + minutes + " min left";
            }
        }
        Subtitle sub = new Subtitle() {
            public String language() {
                return "English";
            }
        };
        System.out.println(new Timer().left());
        System.out.println("Subtitles: " + sub.language());
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MediaPlayer player = new MediaPlayer();
        MediaPlayer.Screen screen = player.new Screen();
        screen.show();
        MediaPlayer.Volume volume = new MediaPlayer.Volume();
        System.out.println("Volume: " + volume.level);
        player.play(118);
    }
}

docs.title: OCP exam prep: nested classes
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Classes That Live Inside Other Classes

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Declare and instantiate Java objects including nested class objects; create and use interfaces.

docs.title: Eight traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — An inner class needs an owner

In static code, new Screen() does not compile: write platform.new Screen().

Trap 2 — Static nested classes

They cannot read the outer class's instance fields without a reference to an object.

Trap 3 — Outer.this.field

Season.this.number reads a shadowed field of an outer level; number and this.number mean the current class.

Trap 4 — Static members everywhere

Since Java 16, all four kinds can declare static members: a static field in an inner class is not an error.

Trap 5 — No access modifier on local classes

private class Timer inside a method does not compile. final and abstract are allowed.

Trap 6 — Effectively final

Local and anonymous classes read local variables only if they are final or effectively final. A reassignment anywhere in the method, even after the class, breaks it.

Trap 7 — One parent

An anonymous class extends one class or implements one interface, never both. Its interface methods must stay public.

Trap 8 — The semicolon

Type t = new Type() { … }; ends with }; because it is a declaration.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
What does new Show().new Season().print("Episode") print?

class Show {
    String name = "Show";
    class Season { String name = "Season";
        void print(String name) {
            System.out.print(name + " " + this.name);
            System.out.print(" " + Show.this.name); } } }

A. Episode Season Show B. Episode Episode Show C. Season Season Show D. It does not compile

Answer

A. name alone is the closest variable, the parameter: Episode. this.name is the field of the current Season. Show.this.name reaches the outer object: Show.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Which lines do not compile?

1: public class Player {
2:     private int volume = 5;
3:     static class Remote { int read() { return volume; } }
4:     class Screen { static int count = 0; }
5:     public static void main(String[] args) {
6:         var r = new Remote();
7:         var s = new Screen(); } }

A. Line 3 only B. Line 7 only C. Lines 3 and 7 D. Lines 3, 4 and 7

Answer

C. Line 3: a static nested class cannot read the instance field volume. Line 7: Screen is an inner class and main is static, so there is no Player to attach it to (new Player().new Screen() would work). Line 4 is fine since Java 16, and line 6 needs no outer object.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
The code does not compile. Which changes make it compile? (Choose two.)

interface Rating { int stars(); }
void rate(int base) {
    int bonus = 1;
    Rating r = new Rating() {
        public int stars() { return base + bonus; } };
    bonus++; }

A. None: it compiles as written B. Remove bonus++ C. Remove public D. Return base + 1 instead

Answer

B and D. The anonymous class reads bonus, which is incremented afterwards, so it is not effectively final. B removes the change; D stops reading bonus (base never changes). C would break the rule that interface methods are implemented as public.

docs.title: One Object, Many Faces with Polymorphism
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

In Java, a single object can be seen through several types at once: its own class, any of its superclasses, or any interface it implements. This is polymorphism, and it is the reason one method can work with many kinds of objects. Here you'll learn what a reference lets you see, how to cast up and down, which casts the compiler refuses and which ones fail at runtime, how instanceof keeps a cast safe, and why an overridden method follows the object while a static method does not.

▶️ The video is on the ADC with Mounir YouTube channel.

docs.title: Object type vs reference type
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · One Object, Many Faces with Polymorphism · 1/4

Nested classes decided where a class lives. Polymorphism decides how an object is seen.

docs.title: Three ways to hold the same object
docs.text:
When you create an object, you can store it in a variable of three kinds of types:

Variable type Example Cast needed? The object's own class Movie m = new Movie(); no Any superclass, including Object Content c = m; · Object o = m; no Any interface the object implements Downloadable d = m; no

Going from Movie to Content or Downloadable never needs a cast, because a Movie is always a Content and always a Downloadable. That is what makes code flexible: a method with a Content parameter accepts movies, episodes and documentaries alike, and code that only depends on an interface such as List works with every class that implements it.

docs.title: One object, three references
docs.text:
class Content {
    String title() { return "Dune"; }
}

interface Downloadable {
    boolean offline();
}

class Movie extends Content implements Downloadable {
    int minutes = 155;
    public boolean offline() { return true; }
}

public class References {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Movie movie = new Movie();
        System.out.println(movie.minutes);

        Downloadable d = movie;
        System.out.println(d.offline());

        Content c = movie;
        System.out.println(c.title());
    }
}

155
true
Dune

Only one new runs, so only one Movie exists in memory. The three variables are three different ways of looking at it.

docs.title: What the reference lets you see
docs.text:
Changing the type of the variable never changes the object. It changes what your code is allowed to call:

Downloadable d = new Movie();
System.out.println(d.minutes);      // ❌ does not compile: not in Downloadable

Content c = new Movie();
System.out.println(c.offline());    // ❌ does not compile: not in Content

Object o = new Movie();             // still a whole Movie in memory

The minutes field is right there in the object, yet a Downloadable reference only knows the methods of Downloadable. In the same way, a Content reference knows nothing about offline().

Two rules sum it up:

  1. The type of the object decides what exists in memory.
  2. The type of the reference decides what your code can use.

Storing the movie in an Object variable loses access to every Movie member, but the members are still there, waiting for a reference of the right type.

The next page shows how to get that access back with a cast, and when a cast fails.

docs.title: Casting objects and instanceof
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · One Object, Many Faces with Polymorphism · 2/4

The reference type decides what you can call. A cast changes the reference type.

docs.title: Up is free, down needs a cast
docs.text:
Movie movie = new Movie();
Content c = movie;              // up: implicit cast
Movie back = (Movie) c;         // down: explicit cast
System.out.println(back.minutes);

// Movie m = c;                 ❌ does not compile: missing cast
  • Going up, from a subtype to a supertype, is always safe: Java does it for you.
  • Going down, from a supertype to a subtype, needs the type in parentheses. The compiler only knows the reference is a Content, even when the object really is a Movie.

docs.title: Compile error or runtime crash
docs.text:
A cast can fail in two very different ways:

class Subscription { }

Movie movie = new Movie();
Subscription s = (Subscription) movie;   // ❌ does not compile: unrelated classes

Content c = new Content();
Movie m = (Movie) c;                     // compiles, then ClassCastException
Cast Compiler Runtime Between two unrelated classes refuses it — Down to a subclass, wrong object accepts it ClassCastException Down to a subclass, right object accepts it works

For every cast, ask two questions: what is the object really, and will the compiler allow this cast?

docs.title: Casting to an interface
docs.text:
Interfaces follow a looser rule. A class that does not implement an interface may still have a subclass that does, so the compiler cannot rule the cast out:

interface Rentable { }
class Trailer { }
final class Teaser { }

Trailer t = new Trailer();
Rentable r = (Rentable) t;                 // compiles, then ClassCastException

// Rentable x = (Rentable) new Teaser();   ❌ does not compile

When the class is final, no subclass can ever exist, so a Teaser can never be Rentable and the compiler refuses the cast.

docs.title: Checking before you cast
docs.text:
instanceof tests the real object before the cast, and its pattern variable is already typed:

public class SafeCast {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Content c = new Content();
        if (c instanceof Movie m) {
            System.out.println(m.minutes);
        } else {
            System.out.println("not a movie");
        }
    }
}

not a movie

(Content and Movie are the classes of the previous page.) If the test succeeds, m is a Movie inside the block, with no cast to write; otherwise the block is skipped and nothing crashes. Like a cast, instanceof does not compile between unrelated classes: movie instanceof Subscription is an error.

docs.title: Overriding vs hiding
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · One Object, Many Faces with Polymorphism · 3/4

The reference type decides what you can call. The object decides which version runs, but only for instance methods.

docs.title: The object decides which method runs
docs.text:
class Content {
    String label() { return "content"; }
    void describe() { System.out.println(this.label()); }
}

class Movie extends Content {
    String label() { return "movie"; }
}

public class Overriding {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Movie().describe();
    }
}

movie

describe() is written inside Content, yet the call to label() runs the version of the real object, a Movie. An overridden method is replaced everywhere, even in the calls written in the parent class, whatever the type of the reference. Mark a method final to stop subclasses from overriding it.

docs.title: Reaching the parent's version with super
docs.text:
The parent version is not lost. super.label() calls it, but only from the child:

class Movie extends Content {
    String label() { return "movie"; }
    void describe() { System.out.println(super.label()); }
}

With this Movie, new Movie().describe() prints content. Writing super.label() inside Content would not compile: there, super means Object, which has no label() method.

docs.title: Static methods are hidden, not overridden
docs.text:
class Content {
    static String badge() { return "C"; }
    void show() { System.out.println(badge()); }
}

class Movie extends Content {
    static String badge() { return "M"; }
}

public class Hiding {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Movie().show();
    }
}

C

A static method belongs to its class, not to the object. The call written inside Content runs Content's version. If badge() were an instance method, the same program would print M.

docs.title: The reference picks hidden members
docs.text:
Fields are never overridden either. With hidden members, the type of the reference decides:

class Content {
    int rank = 1;
    static String tag() { return "C"; }
}

class Movie extends Content {
    int rank = 2;
    static String tag() { return "M"; }
}

public class HiddenMembers {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Movie movie = new Movie();
        Content c = movie;
        System.out.println(movie.rank + " " + c.rank);
        System.out.println(Movie.tag() + " " + Content.tag());
    }
}

2 1
M C
Member Which version is used? Overridden instance method the real object's Hidden static method the class named, or the reference type Hidden field the reference type

A Movie object really holds two rank fields, one per class. This is legal but confusing: in real code, give new fields and static methods their own names.

docs.title: Lab: a playlist that plays any content
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · One Object, Many Faces with Polymorphism · 4/4

Goal: build a playlist that holds movies, episodes and plain content in one Content[] array, let overriding pick the right kind(), then use instanceof patterns to reach what a Content reference cannot see.

Setup: create Playlist.java (no package). Its first type, the Playable interface, has no main, so compile with javac Playlist.java, then run with java Playlist.

docs.title: Step 1 — The interface and the classes
docs.text:
interface Playable {
    String play();
}

class Content {
    String title;
    Content(String title) { this.title = title; }
    String kind() { return "content"; }
    String describe() { return kind() + ": " + title; }
}

class Movie extends Content implements Playable {
    int minutes;
    Movie(String title, int minutes) { super(title); this.minutes = minutes; }
    String kind() { return "movie"; }
    public String play() { return "Playing " + title; }
}

class Episode extends Content implements Playable {
    Episode(String title) { super(title); }
    String kind() { return "episode"; }
    public String play() { return "Streaming " + title; }
}

describe() calls kind() from inside Content. Movie and Episode override kind(), and implement play() as public because it comes from an interface.

docs.title: Step 2 — One array, one loop
docs.text:
public class Playlist {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Content[] items = { new Movie("Inception", 148), new Episode("Pilot"), new Content("Trailer") };
        for (Content item : items) {
            System.out.println(item.describe());
        }
    }
}

movie: Inception
episode: Pilot
content: Trailer

No cast is needed to put a Movie or an Episode in a Content[]. Each item is a Content reference, yet describe() printed movie and episode: the overridden kind() follows the real object.

docs.title: Step 3 — Play what is playable
docs.text:
item.play() does not compile: Content has no play() method. Inside the loop, below the println:

            if (item instanceof Playable p) {
                System.out.println("  " + p.play());
            }

movie: Inception
  Playing Inception
episode: Pilot
  Streaming Pilot
content: Trailer

The plain Trailer is not Playable, so its block is skipped, with no exception.

docs.title: Step 4 — The minutes of a movie
docs.text:
Below the first if:

            if (item instanceof Movie m) {
                System.out.println("  " + m.minutes + " min");
            }

movie: Inception
  Playing Inception
  148 min
episode: Pilot
  Streaming Pilot
content: Trailer

The field exists in the Movie object; the pattern variable m reaches it without a written cast.

docs.title: Final code
docs.text:
The four types of step 1, then:

public class Playlist {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Content[] items = { new Movie("Inception", 148), new Episode("Pilot"), new Content("Trailer") };
        for (Content item : items) {
            System.out.println(item.describe());
            if (item instanceof Playable p) {
                System.out.println("  " + p.play());
            }
            if (item instanceof Movie m) {
                System.out.println("  " + m.minutes + " min");
            }
        }
    }
}

The reference decided what the code could call, the real object decided which method ran, and instanceof kept every cast safe.

docs.title: OCP exam prep: polymorphism
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · One Object, Many Faces with Polymorphism

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Implement polymorphism and differentiate object type versus reference type; perform type casting, identify object types using the instanceof operator and pattern matching.

docs.title: Eight traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — The reference decides

A member the reference type does not declare does not compile, even if the object has it.

Trap 2 — Going down

Supertype to subtype always needs an explicit cast: Movie m = c; does not compile when c is a Content.

Trap 3 — Unrelated classes

A cast or an instanceof between two classes where neither extends the other is a compile error.

Trap 4 — Interfaces

A cast to an interface compiles unless the class is final. A wrong object throws a ClassCastException at runtime.

Trap 5 — Overridden methods

The real object's version runs, even when the call is written in the parent class.

Trap 6 — Hidden members

Static methods and fields are hidden, not overridden: the reference type, or the class where the call is written, decides.

Trap 7 — super

super.x() means the parent of the class it is written in; in a top class, that is Object.

Trap 8 — Find the object first

For any cast question, find the real object, then check what the compiler allows.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
What does this code print?

class Content { String name = "C";
    String kind() { return "C"; } }
class Movie extends Content { String name = "M";
    String kind() { return "M"; } }
Content c = new Movie();
System.out.print(c.kind() + c.name);

A. MM B. MC C. CC D. CM

Answer

B. kind() is overridden, so the Movie object decides: M. The field name is hidden, so the Content reference decides: C.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Lines 3–6 are in main. Which lines do not compile?

1: interface Rentable {}  final class Trailer {}
2: class Content {}  class Movie extends Content {}
3: Content c = new Movie();
4: Movie m = c;
5: Rentable r = (Rentable) c;
6: Trailer t = (Trailer) c;

A. Line 4 only B. Lines 4 and 6 C. Lines 5 and 6 D. Lines 4, 5 and 6

Answer

B. Line 4 needs an explicit cast. Line 5 compiles because Content is not final: a subclass could implement Rentable (it would throw at runtime here). Line 6: Trailer and Content are unrelated classes.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Which statements are true? (Choose two.)

interface Rentable {}
class Content {}
class Movie extends Content {}
Content a = new Movie();
Content b = new Content();

A. (Movie) a runs fine B. (Movie) b compiles, then throws C. (Rentable) a does not compile D. b instanceof String compiles

Answer

A and B. a holds a Movie. b holds a plain Content, so the cast compiles but throws a ClassCastException. C compiles (Content is not final). D: Content and String are unrelated, so it does not compile.

docs.title: Part 8 practice questions: functional programming
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Part 8 · Functional Programming

Optional page

Eleven exam-style questions covering all of Part 8. Try each one before opening its answer. To review a topic, go back to the Part 8 recap.

1. Which lambda fills the blank so the code compiles?

interface ContentFilter { boolean accept(Movie movie); }
ContentFilter newReleases = ____________________;

A. m -> { m.isNew() } B. (Movie m) -> return m.isNew(); C. Movie m -> m.isNew() D. (var m) -> { return m.isNew(); }

Answer

D. var in parentheses, a block with return and ;. A has braces without return or ;, B uses return without braces, C declares a type without parentheses.

2. Which of these are functional interfaces?

interface Rateable     { int rate(); String toString(); }
interface Playable     { void play(); default void pause() {} }
interface Downloadable { boolean equals(Downloadable d); void download(); }
interface Streamable extends Playable { void stream(); }

A. Rateable and Playable only B. Playable only C. Playable and Streamable only D. All four

Answer

A. toString() matches Object, so Rateable has one abstract method; Playable's default doesn't count. equals(Downloadable) isn't Object's signature → two. Streamable inherits play() and adds stream() → two.

3. Which interfaces complete blanks 1, 2 and 3?

____1____<User>    greet  = u -> System.out.println("Hi " + u.name());
____2____<Movie>   isHd   = m -> m.quality() == Quality.HD;
____3____<Episode> nextEp = () -> catalog.firstEpisode();

A. Consumer, Predicate, Supplier B. Function, Predicate, Supplier C. Consumer, Function, Supplier D. Supplier, Predicate, Consumer

Answer

A. A User in, nothing out → Consumer. A Movie in, a boolean out → Predicate. Nothing in, an Episode out → Supplier.

4. Which lambda is equivalent to String::startsWith here?

BiPredicate<String, String> match = String::startsWith;
System.out.println(match.test("Stranger Things", "Str"));   // true

A. (t, p) -> t.startsWith(p) B. (t, p) -> p.startsWith(t) C. t -> t.startsWith(p) D. (t, p) -> String.startsWith(t, p)

Answer

A. The first parameter is the object the method runs on, the second is the argument. B swaps them, C has one parameter, D calls a static method that doesn't exist.

5. How many of these lines compile?

1: Supplier<ArrayList<Movie>> watchlist = ArrayList::new;
2: Function<String, Integer> titleLength = String::length;
3: UnaryOperator<String> shout = String::toUpperCase;
4: BiFunction<String, String> joinTitles = String::concat;

A. One B. Two C. Three D. Four

Answer

C. Lines 1, 2 and 3. Line 4 fails: BiFunction needs three type parameters, two inputs and a result.

6. What does this print?

Function<Integer, Integer> addBonus = minutes -> minutes + 10;
Function<Integer, Integer> doubleIt = minutes -> minutes * 2;
var combined = doubleIt.compose(addBonus);
System.out.println(combined.apply(5));

A. 20 B. 30 C. 25 D. The code does not compile

Answer

B. compose runs its argument first: 5 + 10 = 15, then 15 × 2 = 30. andThen would give 20.

7. Given record Movie(String title, int year, String rating), what is printed?

Predicate<Movie> isNew  = m -> m.year() >= 2024;
Predicate<Movie> isKids = m -> m.rating().equals("G");
var forAdults = isNew.and(isKids.negate());
System.out.println(forAdults.test(new Movie("Toy Box", 2025, "G")));

A. true B. false C. The code does not compile D. An exception is thrown

Answer

B. isNew is true; isKids is true, so its negation is false. true AND false → false.

8. Which types can fill the blank? (Choose all that apply.)

double price = 15.99;
______________ toCents = p -> (int) (p * 100);
System.out.println(toCents.applyAsInt(price));   // 1599

A. DoubleToIntFunction B. DoubleFunction<Integer> C. ToIntFunction<Double> D. IntFunction<Double>

Answer

A and C. Both have applyAsInt(): A takes a double, C a Double (the price is autoboxed). B and D use apply(), and D expects an int.

9. Which parameter list makes this line compile?

BiPredicate<User, Subscription> canWatch = ____________________;

A. (var u, Subscription s) -> true B. (final var u, var s) -> true C. (var u, s) -> true D. (User u, s) -> true

Answer

B. var for both, and final is allowed with var. A, C and D mix styles.

10. Which lines cause a compiler error?

1: public void announce(List<User> users) {
2:     String message = "New season available!";
3:     int sent = 0;
4:     users.forEach(u -> u.send(message));
5:     users.forEach(u -> sent++);
6:     message = "Watch it now!";
7: }

A. Line 4 only B. Line 5 only C. Lines 4 and 5 D. Line 6 only

Answer

C. Line 6 reassigns message, so line 4 can't use it. Line 5 modifies sent inside a lambda. Line 6 itself is legal: errors are reported where the lambda uses the variable.

11. How many lines contain an error?

1: public void rate(Movie movie) {
2:     int score = 5;
3:     Predicate<Movie> worthIt = movie -> {
4:         int score = 8;
5:         return movie.stars() >= score; }
6: }

A. Zero B. One C. Two D. Three

Answer

D. Line 3 reuses movie, already a parameter. Line 4 redeclares score. Line 5 is missing the ; after the } that closes the lambda statement.

docs.title: Passing Behavior Around with Lambdas
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

Sometimes the only thing that changes in your code is one small rule. A lambda lets you hand that rule to a method in a single line, without writing a whole class. Here you'll see where lambdas come from, how they run, and every rule of their syntax.

docs.title: In this series

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: classes, interfaces and records.

Code: Java17_Part_8_Functional_Programming on GitHub

docs.title: From a filter class to a lambda
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · Passing Behavior Around with Lambdas · 1/3

docs.title: Thinking in functions
docs.text:
Object style Functional style build objects, change their state describe the result you want write the loop step by step pass small rules, let other code loop focus on how focus on what

Java stays object-oriented: functional programming is an extra tool on top. Its key piece is the lambda: a block of code with parameters and a body, but no name, that you can pass to a method.

docs.title: The scenario: filtering a catalog
docs.text:
public record Movie(String title, boolean isNew, boolean isKidFriendly) { }

public interface MovieFilter {
    boolean test(Movie movie);
}

MovieFilter asks one question about a movie and answers with a boolean. A method can print every movie that passes any filter:

static void print(List<Movie> catalog, MovieFilter filter) {
    for (Movie movie : catalog)
        if (filter.test(movie))
            System.out.print(movie.title() + " ");
    System.out.println();
}

print() is nicely generic: it doesn't know which rule it applies.

docs.title: The old way: one class per rule
docs.text:
public class KidFriendlyFilter implements MovieFilter {
    public boolean test(Movie m) {
        return m.isKidFriendly();
    }
}

print(catalog, new KidFriendlyFilter());

A new file and a new class for a single expression. Every new rule means another class.

docs.title: The new way: one line per rule
docs.text:
print(catalog, m -> m.isNew());              // new releases
print(catalog, m -> m.isKidFriendly());      // kid-friendly titles
print(catalog, m -> !m.isKidFriendly());     // everything not for kids

m -> m.isNew() reads as given a movie m, keep it if it's new. print() didn't change: it still expects a MovieFilter, and Java turns the lambda into one.

docs.title: Code now, run later
docs.text:
1. You write the lambda. print(catalog, m -> m.isNew()); checks no movie yet: it hands code to print().
  2. Java matches it to the interface. print() expects a MovieFilter, whose only abstract method is boolean test(Movie movie). So m is a Movie and the body must produce a boolean.
  3. print() runs it later, once per movie, when it calls filter.test(movie).

A lambda always needs a context that tells Java what it is: here, the MovieFilter parameter. That context is called the target type.

Lambdas can be written in several forms, from long to very short. The next page goes through every rule.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_8_Functional_Programming on GitHub

Next: lambda syntax →

docs.title: Lambda syntax, from long to short
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Passing Behavior Around with Lambdas · 2/3

A lambda is code you pass to a method, matched to the method's interface. Here's how to write one correctly.

docs.title: Anatomy
docs.text:
m -> m.isNew()                        // shortest form
(Movie m) -> { return m.isNew(); }    // longest form, same behavior
Part Role Parameters (left) m, or with its type: (Movie m) Arrow -> separates parameters and body; exactly one per lambda Body (right) one expression whose value is returned, or a block { … } of statements

docs.title: Trimming it down
docs.text:
(Movie m) -> { return m.isNew(); }    // full form
(Movie m) -> m.isNew()                // no braces, no return, no ;
m -> m.isNew()                        // no type, no parentheses
m -> { return m.isNew(); }            // mix and match: valid
(m) -> m.isNew()                      // parentheses kept: valid

Two rules:

  • Parentheses can be dropped only for exactly one parameter without a type. With a type, or with zero or several parameters, they're required.
  • Braces are all or nothing. Without braces: no return, no ;. With braces: you write return (if a value is expected) and end every statement with ;.

m -> {} is valid too: an empty block, for a method that returns nothing.

docs.title: Shapes that compile
docs.text:
() -> true                                     // 0 parameters: () required
t -> t.startsWith("Star")                      // 1 parameter
(String t) -> t.startsWith("Star")             // 1, typed: () required
(t, g) -> { return t.startsWith("Dark"); }     // 2 parameters
(String t, String g) -> t.startsWith("Dark")   // 2, typed

The last two never use g: a lambda doesn't have to use every parameter.

docs.title: Spot the broken lambda
docs.text: ❌ Doesn't compile ✅ Fixed Problem t, g -> t.startsWith("Dark") (t, g) -> t.startsWith("Dark") two parameters need () t -> { t.startsWith("Dark"); } t -> { return t.startsWith("Dark"); } braces need return t -> { return t.startsWith("Dark") } t -> t.startsWith("Dark") missing ; inside braces String t -> t.endsWith("Mirror") (String t) -> t.endsWith("Mirror") a typed parameter needs ()

docs.title: var can't hold a lambda
docs.text:
var rule = (Movie m) -> m.isNew();        // ❌ doesn't compile
MovieFilter rule = m -> m.isNew();        // ✅ the type gives the context
print(catalog, rule);                     // store it now, use it later

var infers its type from the value; a lambda infers its type from where it goes. With var, each waits for the other. Declare the variable with a real interface type, and the lambda becomes a value you can store, pass and reuse.

docs.title: Lab: building the rows of the home screen
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Passing Behavior Around with Lambdas · 3/3

Goal: power every row of a streaming home screen with one method, where each row's rule is a one-line lambda.

Setup: in an empty folder, create Movie.java, MovieFilter.java and HomeScreen.java. No package.

docs.title: Step 1 — The data and the rule
docs.text:
public record Movie(String title, boolean isNew, boolean isKidFriendly, int minutes) { }

@FunctionalInterface
public interface MovieFilter {
    boolean test(Movie movie);
}

One abstract method, Movie in, boolean out: any lambda of that shape can stand in for it. @FunctionalInterface asks the compiler to guarantee there's exactly one abstract method.

docs.title: Step 2 — One method for every row
docs.text:
import java.util.List;

public class HomeScreen {

    static void showRow(String name, List<Movie> catalog, MovieFilter rule) {
        System.out.println("=== " + name + " ===");
        for (Movie m : catalog) {
            if (rule.test(m)) {
                System.out.println("  > " + m.title() + " (" + m.minutes() + " min)");
            }
        }
        System.out.println();
    }
}

showRow() doesn't know what the rule is. It just asks it about each movie.

docs.title: Step 3 — A catalog and three rows
docs.text:
public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Movie> catalog = List.of(
            new Movie("Midnight Signal", true, false, 118),
            new Movie("The Lantern Fox", true, true, 95),
            new Movie("Empire of Sand", false, false, 172),
            new Movie("Ocean Pals", false, true, 88),
            new Movie("The Long Winter", true, false, 158)
        );

        showRow("New This Week", catalog, m -> m.isNew());
        showRow("Family Night", catalog, m -> m.isKidFriendly());
        showRow("Epic Watches", catalog, m -> m.minutes() > 150);
    }

No type is written for m: the MovieFilter parameter tells the compiler it's a Movie, so your editor even autocompletes m..

docs.title: Step 4 — A new row in one line
docs.text:
The product team wants short movies, under 100 minutes:

        showRow("Quick Bites", catalog, m -> m.minutes() < 100);

No new class, no change to showRow() or Movie.

docs.title: Step 5 — Run
docs.text:
$ javac *.java
$ java HomeScreen
=== New This Week ===
  > Midnight Signal (118 min)
  > The Lantern Fox (95 min)
  > The Long Winter (158 min)

=== Family Night ===

docs.title: OCP exam prep: lambda syntax
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Passing Behavior Around with Lambdas

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Use Java object and primitive streams, including lambda expressions implementing functional interfaces.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — Count the parentheses

m, s -> … and Movie m -> … don't compile. Parentheses may be dropped only for exactly one untyped parameter. (m) -> … is legal.

Trap 2 — Braces bring return and ;

m -> { m.isNew() } fails twice: no return, no ;. With braces you need both; without braces, neither.

Trap 3 — No var for lambdas

var f = (Movie m) -> m.isNew(); doesn't compile, even with a typed parameter. A lambda needs a target type.

Trap 4 — Strange but legal

() -> true, m -> {} and lambdas that ignore a parameter all compile. Don't reject an answer just because it looks unusual.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Which lambda can replace the comment so that the code compiles?

public interface MovieFilter { boolean test(Movie movie); }
print(catalog, /* INSERT LAMBDA HERE */);

A. Movie m -> m.isNew() B. m -> { return m.isNew() } C. (m) -> m.isKidFriendly() D. m -> { m.isNew(); }

Answer

C. Parentheses around one untyped parameter are optional, not forbidden. A needs parentheses for the type, B misses the ;, and D never returns the boolean.

2. Which lambdas can be assigned to rule? (Choose all that apply.)

interface EpisodeCheck { boolean check(String title, int minutes); }
EpisodeCheck rule = /* INSERT LAMBDA HERE */;

A. (t, m) -> m > 40 B. t, m -> m > 40 C. (t, m) -> { return t.isEmpty(); } D. (String t, int m) -> { m > 40; }

Answer

A and C. C ignores m, which is fine. B forgets the parentheses around two parameters. D has braces without return, and m > 40; isn't even a valid statement.

3. Which line does NOT compile?

1: MovieFilter a = m -> m.isNew();
2: MovieFilter b = (Movie m) -> m.isKidFriendly();
3: var c = (Movie m) -> m.isNew();
4: MovieFilter d = m -> { return !m.isNew(); };

A. Line 1 B. Line 2 C. Line 3 D. Line 4

Answer

C. With var, the lambda has no target type, even with a typed parameter. The other lines give it MovieFilter.

docs.title: The One-Method Contract Behind Every Lambda
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

A lambda has no name and no type of its own. It gets its meaning from a special kind of interface: a functional interface. Here you'll learn the one-method rule behind every lambda and a four-step check to tell, in seconds, whether an interface qualifies.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 Functional interfaces: the single abstract method rule 3 min 2 @FunctionalInterface, Object methods and the 4-step check 3 min 3 Lab: pluggable browse rules 4 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: Passing Behavior Around with Lambdas.

Code: Java17_Part_8_Functional_Programming on GitHub

docs.title: Functional interfaces: the single abstract method rule
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · The One-Method Contract Behind Every Lambda · 1/3

docs.title: Why a lambda needs a contract
docs.text:
m -> m.rating() > 8

This lambda has a parameter and a body, but no name and no type. On its own, Java can't tell what it's for. Its meaning comes from the type that receives it:

interface RatingRule {
    boolean check(Movie m);
}

RatingRule rule = m -> m.rating() > 8;

RatingRule has one method left to implement, check(). Java uses the lambda as its body: m is a Movie, and the result must be a boolean. This only works if there is exactly one blank to fill.

docs.title: The SAM rule
docs.text:
An interface with exactly one abstract method is a functional interface. This is the Single Abstract Method rule, or SAM.

public interface RatingRule {
    boolean check(Movie m);              // the only abstract method
}

// option 1: a full class
public class TopRated implements RatingRule {
    public boolean check(Movie m) { return m.rating() >= 8.0; }
}

// option 2: a lambda, same job, one line
RatingRule rule = m -> m.rating() >= 8.0;

A class can still implement a functional interface; a lambda is just the shortest way to do it.

docs.title: Inherited methods count
docs.text:
An interface inherits its parent's abstract methods. Count them too:

public interface Playable { void play(Episode e); }

public interface Bingeable extends Playable { }      // ✅ inherits play(): 1 abstract

public interface Rewindable extends Playable {       // ❌ play() + rewind(): 2 abstract
    void rewind(int seconds);
}

Rewindable is a valid interface, but not a functional one: a lambda can't implement two methods.

docs.title: Methods with a body don't count
docs.text:
Since Java 8 and 9, interfaces can contain methods with code. None of them count:

public interface Recommender {
    List<Movie> suggest(User u);                 // abstract: counts

    default int limit() { return 10; }           // has a body
    static Recommender none() { return u -> List.of(); }
    private void log(String msg) { }             // has a body
}
Method kind Counts toward the rule? abstract (no body) ✅ yes default no: it has a body static no private / private static no

Recommender is functional: suggest() is its only abstract method. But an interface with only default, static or private methods has zero abstract methods, and zero isn't one: it's not functional.

Next: an annotation that checks the rule for you, and a loophole involving Object.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_8_Functional_Programming on GitHub

Next: @FunctionalInterface and Object methods →

docs.title: @FunctionalInterface, Object methods and the 4-step check
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · The One-Method Contract Behind Every Lambda · 2/3

A functional interface has exactly one abstract method, counting inherited ones and ignoring those with a body. Two more details complete the rule.

docs.title: @FunctionalInterface guards the contract
docs.text:
@FunctionalInterface
public interface PlayerControl {
    void pause();
    void resume();            // ❌ compiler error: two abstract methods
}

@FunctionalInterface
public interface PlayerControl {
    void pause();
    default void resume() { } // ✅ only one abstract method
}
  • The annotation asks the compiler to check the rule, and fail if it's broken.
  • It doesn't create anything: an interface with one abstract method is functional with or without it.
  • It documents your intent: nobody can add a second abstract method later and silently break every lambda using it.

docs.title: The Object loophole
docs.text:
Every class extends Object, so every implementing class already has toString(), equals(Object) and hashCode(). An interface that redeclares them doesn't make anyone implement anything new:

public interface ContentFilter {
    String toString();
    boolean equals(Object o);
    int hashCode();

    boolean accept(Content c);   // the only method that counts
}

ContentFilter kids = c -> c.ageRating() <= 7;   // ✅ still functional

docs.title: Look-alikes that do count
docs.text:
The signature must match Object's exactly:

public interface SeriesMatcher {
    boolean equals(Series s);    // ❌ not Object's equals: a new abstract method
    boolean match(Series s);
}

equals(Series) isn't equals(Object), so SeriesMatcher has two abstract methods. Two more cases:

  • An interface that only redeclares toString() has zero abstract methods that count: not functional.
  • int toString(); doesn't compile at all: it clashes with Object's String toString().

docs.title: The 4-step check
docs.text:
1. List every abstract method, inherited ones included.
  2. Cross out methods with a body: default, static, private.
  3. Cross out exact public Object methods: String toString(), boolean equals(Object), int hashCode().
  4. Exactly one left? It's functional, and a lambda can implement it.

The annotation never decides; the count does. @FunctionalInterface only makes the compiler run this check for you.

The lab builds a functional interface with a helper default method, and plugs different rules into one browse method.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_8_Functional_Programming on GitHub

← Functional interfaces · Next: the lab →

docs.title: Lab: pluggable browse rules
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · The One-Method Contract Behind Every Lambda · 3/3

Goal: write one browse() method and give it any rule as a lambda, including a rule built by a default method.

Setup: in an empty folder, create ContentType.java, Content.java, ContentRule.java, StreamingPlatform.java and Main.java. No package.

docs.title: Step 1 — The content
docs.text:
public enum ContentType {
    MOVIE, SERIES, DOCUMENTARY
}

public record Content(String title, ContentType type, double rating) { }

The record gives us title(), type() and rating().

docs.title: Step 2 — The rule
docs.text:
@FunctionalInterface
public interface ContentRule {
    boolean matches(Content c);
    default ContentRule not() { return c -> !matches(c); }
}

matches() is the single abstract method. not() has a body, so it doesn't count: it returns a new rule that flips the answer.

Try adding boolean isPremium(Content c); under matches(): the compiler rejects @FunctionalInterface right away. Remove the line.

docs.title: Step 3 — One browse method
docs.text:
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class StreamingPlatform {
    private final List<Content> catalog = new ArrayList<>();

    public void add(Content c) {
        catalog.add(c);
    }

    public List<Content> browse(ContentRule rule) {
        List<Content> result = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Content c : catalog) {
            if (rule.matches(c)) {
                result.add(c);
            }
        }
        return result;
    }
}

browse() doesn't know what it filters for: the decision is plugged in from outside.

docs.title: Step 4 — Three rules
docs.text:
import java.util.List;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StreamingPlatform platform = new StreamingPlatform();
        platform.add(new Content("Inception", ContentType.MOVIE, 8.8));
        platform.add(new Content("Stranger Things", ContentType.SERIES, 8.7));
        platform.add(new Content("Red Notice", ContentType.MOVIE, 6.4));
        platform.add(new Content("Our Planet", ContentType.DOCUMENTARY, 9.3));
        platform.add(new Content("Emily in Paris", ContentType.SERIES, 6.9));

        show("Movies only", platform.browse(c -> c.type() == ContentType.MOVIE));
        show("Top rated (8.0+)", platform.browse(c -> c.rating() >= 8.0));

        ContentRule moviesOnly = c -> c.type() == ContentType.MOVIE;
        show("Hiding movies", platform.browse(moviesOnly.not()));
    }

    private static void show(String label, List<Content> list) {
        System.out.println("=== " + label + " ===");
        for (Content c : list) {
            System.out.println("  " + c.title() + " (" + c.type() + ", " + c.rating() + ")");
        }
        System.out.println();
    }
}

The third rule isn't written by hand: it asks the existing rule for its opposite.

docs.title: Step 5 — Run
docs.text:
$ javac *.java
$ java Main
=== Movies only ===
  Inception (MOVIE, 8.8)
  Red Notice (MOVIE, 6.4)

=== Top rated (8.0+) ===
  Inception (MOVIE, 8.8)
  Stranger Things (SERIES, 8.7)
  Our Planet (DOCUMENTARY, 9.3)

=== Hiding movies ===
  Stranger Things (SERIES, 8.7)
  Our Planet (DOCUMENTARY, 9.3)
  Emily in Paris (SERIES, 6.9)

Three different results; browse() didn't change by a single character.

docs.title: OCP exam prep: functional interfaces
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · The One-Method Contract Behind Every Lambda

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Use lambda expressions implementing functional interfaces.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — Count inherited abstract methods

An empty interface extending a functional one is functional. Add one abstract method in the child and it isn't anymore.

Trap 2 — default, static and private never count

They all have bodies. An interface with only these has zero abstract methods: not functional.

Trap 3 — The annotation is optional

@FunctionalInterface doesn't make an interface functional; it only triggers a compiler error when the rule is broken.

Trap 4 — Object signatures must match exactly

toString(), equals(Object) and hashCode() are free. equals(Movie) counts. int toString(); doesn't compile.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Which are functional interfaces? (Choose all that apply.)

interface Watchable { void watch(Movie m); }
interface Downloadable extends Watchable { }
interface Shareable extends Watchable { void share(User u); }
interface Ratable { default int stars() { return 5; } }

A. Watchable B. Downloadable C. Shareable D. Ratable

Answer

A and B. Downloadable inherits watch(): one abstract method. Shareable has two. Ratable has zero: a default method never counts.

2. What happens when you compile this code?

1: @FunctionalInterface
2: interface SubscriptionCheck {
3:     boolean isActive(Subscription s);
4:     static SubscriptionCheck always() { return s -> true; }
5:     default boolean isExpired(Subscription s) { return !isActive(s); }
6: }

A. It compiles B. Error on line 1 C. Error on line 4 D. Error on line 5

Answer

A. Only isActive() is abstract. The static and default methods have bodies, so the annotation's check passes.

3. How many methods of EpisodeSorter count toward the single abstract method rule?

interface EpisodeSorter {
    int compare(Episode a, Episode b);
    boolean equals(Object other);
    String toString();
    boolean equals(EpisodeSorter other);
}

A. 1 B. 2 C. 3 D. 4

Answer

B. compare() and equals(EpisodeSorter). equals(Object) and toString() match Object's public methods exactly and are free. So EpisodeSorter is not functional.
