docs.title: Passing Methods Around by Name
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

Many lambdas only pass their work on to a method that already exists. A method reference (::) points Java straight at that method instead. Here you'll learn the four shapes of method references, how to read each one, and when a lambda has to stay.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 The :: shortcut, static and object methods 3 min 2 Methods on the parameter, and constructors 3 min 3 Lab: filling and filtering the catalog 4 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: The One-Method Contract Behind Every Lambda.

Code: Java17_Part_8_Functional_Programming on GitHub

docs.title: The :: shortcut, static and object methods
docs.text: ☕ Java 17 · Passing Methods Around by Name · 1/3

docs.title: When a lambda only passes the baton
docs.text:
interface TitleAnnouncer {
    void announce(String title);
}

TitleAnnouncer a = title -> System.out.println(title);   // lambda
TitleAnnouncer b = System.out::println;                  // method reference

b.announce("Stranger Things");

The lambda receives title and hands it, untouched, to println. The method reference System.out::println says it directly: when announce() is called, call println with the same argument.

Like a lambda, it runs nothing when declared: println runs only when announce() is called.

docs.title: One shortcut, four shapes
docs.text:
# Shape Reference Equivalent lambda 1 static method Math::round x -> Math.round(x) 2 method on an object title::startsWith s -> title.startsWith(s) 3 method on the parameter String::isEmpty t -> t.isEmpty() 4 constructor Episode::new n -> new Episode(n)

A method reference behaves exactly like its lambda. It has no type of its own: like a lambda, it always fills a functional interface, whose parameters and return type tell Java which method to call.

docs.title: Shape 1 — A static method
docs.text:
interface PriceRounder {
    long round(double price);
}

PriceRounder ref = Math::round;            // same as p -> Math.round(p)
System.out.println(ref.round(15.49));      // 15
  • Syntax: ClassName::method, with no parentheses and no arguments.
  • The interface's parameter becomes the method's parameter.
  • Math.round exists for double and float; the interface takes a double, so Java picks that one. No match, or two equally good matches, is a compile error.

docs.title: Shape 2 — A method on an object you have
docs.text:
interface TitleMatcher { boolean beginsWith(String prefix); }
interface TitleCheck { boolean check(); }

var title = "Stranger Things";

TitleMatcher ref = title::startsWith;      // prefix -> title.startsWith(prefix)
System.out.println(ref.beginsWith("Str")); // true

TitleCheck empty = title::isEmpty;         // () -> title.isEmpty()
System.out.println(empty.check());         // false

The left side is a real object, here the variable title. The method always runs on that object; the interface's parameters become its arguments, even zero of them.

docs.title: When a lambda can't become a reference
docs.text:
TitleCheck c1 = title::startsWith("Str");    // ❌ no arguments after ::
TitleCheck c2 = title::startsWith;           // ❌ check() has nothing to pass as a prefix
TitleCheck c3 = () -> title.startsWith("Str"); // ✅ keep the lambda

A method reference is only a name: it can't carry fixed values or extra logic. It's a one-way street: every method reference can be rewritten as a lambda, but not every lambda as a method reference.

Shapes 3 and 4 are the trickier ones: the next page reads them step by step.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_8_Functional_Programming on GitHub

Next: the parameter and constructor shapes →

docs.title: Methods on the parameter, and constructors
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Passing Methods Around by Name · 2/3

Shapes 1 and 2 call a static method or a method on an object you already have. The last two shapes work differently.

docs.title: Shape 3 — The parameter becomes the object
docs.text:
interface TitleTester {
    boolean test(String title);
}

TitleTester blank = String::isEmpty;       // t -> t.isEmpty()
blank.test("");                            // true

isEmpty isn't static: you call it on a specific String. String::isEmpty means call isEmpty on whatever String arrives. A class name on the left doesn't mean the method is static.

With several parameters:

interface PrefixCheck {
    boolean check(String title, String prefix);
}

PrefixCheck pc = String::startsWith;       // (t, p) -> t.startsWith(p)
pc.check("Narcos", "Nar");                 // true
  • The first parameter is the object the method runs on.
  • The other parameters are passed, in order, as arguments.

docs.title: Shape 4 — A constructor
docs.text:
record Episode(String name) { }

interface EpisodeMaker {
    Episode make(String name);
}

EpisodeMaker maker = Episode::new;         // name -> new Episode(name)
Episode pilot = maker.make("Pilot");       // Episode[name=Pilot]

::new points at a constructor. There are no parentheses: Java matches the interface's parameters to a constructor, here the one taking a String. Each call to make() creates a new object.

docs.title: The four shapes side by side
docs.text:
Math::round           // p -> Math.round(p)               1 · static method
title::startsWith     // s -> title.startsWith(s)         2 · method on an object
String::isEmpty       // t -> t.isEmpty()                 3 · method on the parameter
String::startsWith    // (t, p) -> t.startsWith(p)        3 · method on the parameter
Episode::new          // n -> new Episode(n)              4 · constructor

How to read a reference:

Left side Method Shape a class static 1: the parameters become the arguments a variable any instance method 2: it always runs on that object a class instance method 3: the first parameter becomes the object a class new 4: a constructor

When unsure, rewrite the reference as a lambda in your head: the parameter order becomes obvious, and so does whether the counts line up.

The lab uses three shapes at once to fill, filter and print a movie catalog.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_8_Functional_Programming on GitHub

← The :: shortcut · Next: the lab →

docs.title: Lab: filling and filtering the catalog
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · Passing Methods Around by Name · 3/3

Goal: use three method reference shapes in one small program, and see the one case where a lambda has to stay.

Setup: create CatalogDemo.java. All types are nested inside it. Run it with java CatalogDemo.java.

docs.title: Step 1 — The types
docs.text:
import java.util.ArrayList;

public class CatalogDemo {

    record Movie(String title, boolean kidsFriendly) { }

    interface MovieFactory {
        Movie make(String t, boolean k);
    }

    interface MovieFilter {
        boolean keep(Movie m);
    }
}

The record gives a two-value constructor and a kidsFriendly() accessor. MovieFactory takes a String and a boolean and returns a Movie: exactly the constructor's shape.

docs.title: Step 2 — Fill the catalog with a constructor reference
docs.text:
Inside CatalogDemo:

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var catalog = new ArrayList<Movie>();

        MovieFactory factory = Movie::new;           // shape 4
        catalog.add(factory.make("Coco", true));
        catalog.add(factory.make("Narcos", false));

        System.out.println("Full catalog");
        catalog.forEach(System.out::println);         // shape 2
    }

Movie::new matches make(String, boolean) to the record's constructor. System.out::println calls println on one particular object, System.out, for each movie.

Full catalog
Movie[title=Coco, kidsFriendly=true]
Movie[title=Narcos, kidsFriendly=false]

docs.title: Step 3 — Filter with an accessor reference
docs.text:
At the end of main:

        MovieFilter family = Movie::kidsFriendly;     // shape 3
        catalog.removeIf(m -> !family.keep(m));

kidsFriendly() takes no argument, yet keep() takes a Movie: the Movie passed to keep() becomes the object kidsFriendly() runs on.

removeIf removes the elements for which its condition is true. We want to remove the movies that are not kid-friendly, so the answer must be negated with !. A method reference can't add !: this one stays a lambda.

docs.title: Step 4 — Print the result
docs.text:
System.out.println("Family catalog:");
        catalog.forEach(System.out::println);         // shape 2

$ java CatalogDemo.java
Full catalog
Movie[title=Coco, kidsFriendly=true]
Movie[title=Narcos, kidsFriendly=false]
Family catalog:
Movie[title=Coco, kidsFriendly=true]

Narcos is gone. A constructor reference built the movies, an accessor reference decided what's family-friendly, a lambda with ! removed the rest, and println printed what survived.

docs.title: OCP exam prep: method references
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · Passing Methods Around by Name

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — Parentheses after :: never compile

String::length() or title::startsWith("A") are always wrong: a method reference is a name only.

Trap 2 — A class name doesn't mean static

String::isEmpty is an instance method used on the parameter: the interface's first parameter becomes the object.

Trap 3 — Check parameter count and order

Translate to a lambda: String::startsWith for (a, b) means a.startsWith(b). If the counts don't line up, it doesn't compile.

Trap 4 — Fake syntax looks plausible

System::out::println and System.out.println aren't method references. The valid form is System.out::println.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Which line can replace the lambda with the same behavior?

interface TitleFormatter { String format(String title); }
TitleFormatter f = title -> title.toUpperCase();

A. String::toUpperCase B. String::toUpperCase() C. title::toUpperCase D. String.toUpperCase

Answer

A. The method runs on the parameter: shape 3. B has parentheses, C uses title, which only exists inside the lambda, and D isn't a method reference.

2. What is the result?

1: interface RatingCheck { boolean check(String title, String prefix); }
2: var show = "Dark";
3: RatingCheck r1 = String::startsWith;
4: RatingCheck r2 = show::startsWith;
5: System.out.println(r1.check("Dark", "D"));

A. Prints true B. Prints false C. Compiler error on line 3 D. Compiler error on line 4

Answer

D. Line 3 means (t, p) -> t.startsWith(p): fine. Line 4 runs on show, so both parameters would go to startsWith, which has no (String, String) version. Nothing prints.

3. Which statements are true? (Choose two.)

record Series(String name) { }
interface SeriesMaker { Series make(String name); }
SeriesMaker maker = Series::new;

A. Any method reference can become a lambda B. Any lambda can become a method reference C. Series::new is a constructor reference D. System.out::println() compiles

Answer

A and C. A lambda with fixed values or extra logic has no reference form, so B is false. D has parentheses after ::.

docs.title: The Ready-Made Lambda Toolkit
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

You don't need to write your own functional interfaces for everyday jobs: java.util.function ships dozens of them. Here you'll learn the core ones, how to pick the right one, how to combine them, and the primitive versions that avoid boxing.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 Supplier, Consumer, Predicate, Function 4 min 2 Combining filters and chaining functions 3 min 3 Primitive versions: no boxing needed 3 min 4 Lab: filtering and labeling the catalog 3 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: Passing Methods Around by Name.

Code: Java17_Part_8_Functional_Programming on GitHub

docs.title: Supplier, Consumer, Predicate, Function
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · The Ready-Made Lambda Toolkit · 1/4

Instead of one-off interfaces like MovieCheck or TitleMaker, Java offers generic ones in java.util.function. Every Java developer recognizes them at a glance.

docs.title: Supplier — no input, one output
docs.text:
public interface Supplier<T> { T get(); }

Supplier<LocalDate> today = LocalDate::now;
Supplier<List<Movie>> lists = ArrayList::new;

System.out.println(today.get());     // e.g. 2026-10-05
List<Movie> watchlist = lists.get(); // a new, empty list

A natural factory: each get() produces a value. Print today instead of today.get() and you get a generated name with $$Lambda: the lambda object, not its result.

docs.title: Consumer — input, nothing returned
docs.text:
public interface Consumer<T> { void accept(T t); }
public interface BiConsumer<T, U> { void accept(T t, U u); }

Consumer<String> show = System.out::println;
show.accept("Stranger Things");

var ratings = new HashMap<String, Double>();
BiConsumer<String, Double> rate = ratings::put;
rate.accept("Dark", 8.7);            // {Dark=8.7}

Bi means one more parameter: two inputs instead of one.

docs.title: Predicate — a yes-or-no question
docs.text:
public interface Predicate<T> { boolean test(T t); }
public interface BiPredicate<T, U> { boolean test(T t, U u); }

Predicate<String> blank = String::isBlank;
blank.test("  ");                                   // true

BiPredicate<String, String> starts = String::startsWith;
starts.test("Narcos", "Nar");                       // true

test() returns a primitive boolean, not a Boolean object.

docs.title: Function — turn one thing into another
docs.text:
public interface Function<T, R> { R apply(T t); }
public interface BiFunction<T, U, R> { R apply(T t, U u); }

Function<String, Integer> length = String::length;
length.apply("Wednesday");                          // 9

BiFunction<String, String, String> join = String::concat;
join.apply("Squid ", "Game");                       // Squid Game

The last type parameter is always the return type.

docs.title: Operators — same type in and out
docs.text:
UnaryOperator<String> shout = String::toUpperCase;  // a Function<String, String>
BinaryOperator<String> merge = String::concat;      // a BiFunction<String, String, String>

shout.apply("dark");                                // DARK
merge.apply("The ", "Crown");                       // The Crown

When every type is the same, the operator says it with one type parameter instead of two or three. The method is still apply().

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text:
Interface Method Returns Supplier<T> get() T Consumer<T> / BiConsumer<T,U> accept(T) / accept(T,U) void Predicate<T> / BiPredicate<T,U> test(T) / test(T,U) boolean Function<T,R> / BiFunction<T,U,R> apply(T) / apply(T,U) R UnaryOperator<T> / BinaryOperator<T> apply(T) / apply(T,T) T

To pick one: no input → Supplier; nothing returned → Consumer; a boolean → Predicate; same type in and out → Operator; otherwise → Function. Two inputs → the Bi version (or BinaryOperator).

💻 Code: Java17_Part_8_Functional_Programming on GitHub

Next: combining them →

docs.title: Combining filters and chaining functions
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · The Ready-Made Lambda Toolkit · 2/4

The built-in interfaces have a single abstract method, but also default methods that build new lambdas from existing ones.

docs.title: Combining predicates
docs.text:
Writing every combination by hand duplicates logic:

Predicate<Movie> kidsComedy  = m -> m.isKids() && m.genre() == COMEDY;
Predicate<Movie> adultComedy = m -> !m.isKids() && m.genre() == COMEDY;

Build small rules once, then combine them:

Predicate<Movie> kids = Movie::isKids;
Predicate<Movie> comedy = m -> m.genre() == COMEDY;

var kidsComedy  = kids.and(comedy);            // both true
var adultComedy = kids.negate().and(comedy);   // not kids, and comedy
var either      = kids.or(comedy);             // at least one true
Method Result p.and(q) true when both are true p.or(q) true when at least one is true p.negate() the opposite of p

Each returns a brand-new Predicate. If the definition of a comedy changes, you edit comedy once and every combination follows.

docs.title: Chaining consumers
docs.text:
Consumer<String> log  = t -> System.out.print("Log: " + t);
Consumer<String> push = t -> System.out.print(" | Push: " + t);

log.andThen(push).accept("Ozark");   // Log: Ozark | Push: Ozark

andThen() runs both consumers in order, giving both the same input. Nothing is passed from one to the other.

docs.title: andThen() versus compose()
docs.text:
Functions pass their result along, and the order matters:

Function<Integer, Integer> addAds    = min -> min + 5;
Function<Integer, Integer> toSeconds = min -> min * 60;

addAds.andThen(toSeconds).apply(45);   // (45 + 5) * 60 = 3000
addAds.compose(toSeconds).apply(45);   // (45 * 60) + 5 = 2705
Call Runs first Then f.andThen(g) f g receives f's result f.compose(g) g f receives g's result

Read andThen left to right; read compose right to left. Same pieces, different order, different answer: compute both on paper when in doubt.

Every interface so far works with objects. For int, long, double and boolean, Java has lighter versions.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_8_Functional_Programming on GitHub

← Core interfaces · Next: primitive versions →

docs.title: Primitive versions: no boxing needed
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · The Ready-Made Lambda Toolkit · 3/4

Predicate<Integer> turns every int into an Integer object. The primitive versions work directly on the value: lighter and faster.

docs.title: Int, Long, Double and Boolean versions
docs.text:
BooleanSupplier isLive = () -> true;
isLive.getAsBoolean();                       // true

IntSupplier episodes = () -> 8;
IntPredicate isLong = min -> min > 120;
IntUnaryOperator addAds = min -> min + 5;
DoubleBinaryOperator avg = (a, b) -> (a + b) / 2;
IntFunction<String> label = n -> "Episode " + n;

episodes.getAsInt();                         // 8
avg.applyAsDouble(8.0, 9.0);                 // 8.5
  • The prefix (Int, Long, Double) replaces the generic type: IntPredicate tests an int.
  • IntFunction<R> keeps only the return type generic.
  • When a primitive comes back, the method is renamed: getAsInt(), getAsBoolean(), applyAsDouble(), applyAsInt().

BooleanSupplier is the only interface for boolean: there is no BooleanPredicate or BooleanFunction. There are no char, float or String suppliers either.

docs.title: Converting between primitives and objects
docs.text:
ToIntFunction<Movie> minutes = Movie::durationMinutes;
DoubleToIntFunction stars = r -> (int) Math.round(r);
ObjIntConsumer<Episode> jump = (e, sec) -> e.seek(sec);

int length = minutes.applyAsInt(dune);       // 155
int rating = stars.applyAsInt(8.6);          // 9
jump.accept(pilot, 90);                      // seek to 1:30
Family In → out Examples ToXxxFunction<T> object → primitive ToIntFunction, ToDoubleFunction, plus Bi versions XxxToYyyFunction primitive → other primitive DoubleToIntFunction, IntToLongFunction ObjXxxConsumer<T> object + primitive → nothing ObjIntConsumer, ObjDoubleConsumer

You don't need to memorize every name: learn the patterns, and the name tells you the types.

Time to combine a Predicate, a Function and a Consumer in a real feature.

← Combining · Next: the lab →

docs.title: Lab: filtering and labeling the catalog
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · The Ready-Made Lambda Toolkit · 4/4

Goal: split a feature into a filter (Predicate), a formatter (Function) and an output (Consumer), each changeable on its own.

Setup: create CatalogLabelingDemo.java. Run it with java CatalogLabelingDemo.java.

docs.title: Step 1 — The data
docs.text:
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Consumer;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.function.Predicate;

public class CatalogLabelingDemo {

    record Movie(String title, int min, double rating, boolean kids) { }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Movie> catalog = List.of(
            new Movie("Dune", 155, 8.0, false),
            new Movie("Coco", 105, 8.4, true),
            new Movie("Enola Holmes", 123, 6.6, true),
            new Movie("Sing", 108, 7.1, true)
        );
    }
}

docs.title: Step 2 — Four building blocks
docs.text:
Inside main:

        Predicate<Movie> kids = Movie::kids;
        Predicate<Movie> top = m -> m.rating() >= 7;
        Function<Movie, String> label = m -> m.title() + " (" + m.min() + " min)";
        Consumer<String> show = System.out::println;
  • kids is a method reference: kids() returns a boolean.
  • top needs a comparison, so it's a lambda.
  • label turns a Movie into a String.
  • show decides where the text goes.

None of them knows about the others.

docs.title: Step 3 — Wire them together
docs.text:
for (Movie m : catalog)
            if (kids.and(top).test(m))
                show.accept(label.apply(m));

For each movie: if it passes kids and top, format it and send it out. Each interface uses its own method: test, apply, accept.

Predict first: Dune isn't for kids, Enola Holmes is rated 6.6. Then run:

$ java CatalogLabelingDemo.java
Coco (105 min)
Sing (108 min)

docs.title: Step 4 — Change only the output
docs.text:
Replace the Consumer with one that simulates a TV app:

        Consumer<String> show = s -> System.out.println("[TV] " + s);

[TV] Coco (105 min)
[TV] Sing (108 min)

Same filter, same format, a different destination, and one line changed. The Predicate decides what gets through, the Function how it looks, the Consumer where it goes.

docs.title: OCP exam prep: built-in functional interfaces
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · The Ready-Made Lambda Toolkit

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Use functional interfaces from java.util.function, including primitive specializations.

docs.title: Seven traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — Know the method names cold

get(), accept(), test(), apply(). Primitive versions rename them: getAsInt(), applyAsDouble()…

Trap 2 — Count the generic parameters

Function<List<String>> doesn't compile: Function needs <T, R>. BiFunction needs three; the operators take one.

Trap 3 — Operators force one type

UnaryOperator<Long> u = x -> 3.14; doesn't compile: the result must be a Long.

Trap 4 — Bi adds exactly one parameter

BiConsumer, BiPredicate, BiFunction exist. There is no BiSupplier, BinaryConsumer or BinaryFunction.

Trap 5 — Predicate versus Function

"Returns a boolean" (primitive) → Predicate<T>. "Returns a Boolean" (object) → Function<T, Boolean>.

Trap 6 — andThen() versus compose()

f.andThen(g) runs f then g; f.compose(g) runs g then f. Compute both before answering.

Trap 7 — Only one interface for boolean

BooleanSupplier is the only one. No BooleanPredicate, CharSupplier, FloatSupplier or StringSupplier.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Which interface fills the blank?

var catalog = new HashMap<String, Integer>();
_________<String, Integer> addShow = catalog::put;
addShow.accept("Dark", 3);

A. Consumer B. BiConsumer C. BiFunction D. BinaryOperator

Answer

B. accept() with two inputs is BiConsumer. Consumer takes one type parameter, BiFunction needs three and uses apply(), and BinaryOperator takes one type and uses apply().

2. What does this print?

Function<Integer, Integer> addAds = m -> m + 10;
Function<Integer, Integer> half   = m -> m / 2;
Function<Integer, Integer> plan   = addAds.compose(half);
System.out.println(plan.apply(60) + " " + addAds.andThen(half).apply(60));

A. 35 40 B. 40 35 C. 70 35 D. 40 40

Answer

B. compose runs half first: 60 / 2 = 30, + 10 = 40. andThen runs addAds first: 60 + 10 = 70, / 2 = 35.

3. Which two lines compile? (User has a public no-argument constructor.)

1: Supplier<User> s = User::new;
2: Predicate<String> p = String::isEmpty;
3: UnaryOperator<Integer> u = x -> x * 1.5;
4: Function<Episode> f = e -> e.title();

A. 1 and 2 B. 2 and 3 C. 1 and 4 D. 3 and 4

Answer

A. Line 3 returns a double where an Integer is required. Line 4 gives Function only one type parameter.

docs.title: How Lambdas See the Variables Around Them
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

A variable can show up in three places around a lambda: in its parameter list (what it receives), inside its body (what it creates) and outside it (what it borrows). Each place has its own rules, and the compiler enforces every one.

docs.title: In this series
docs.text:
# Page Reading time 1 Declaring lambda parameters 3 min 2 Variables inside a lambda block 3 min 3 Borrowing variables: the effectively final rule 3 min 4 Lab: turning a long lambda into a method reference 3 min

🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 candidates: exam traps and practice questions (optional)

Prerequisites: The Ready-Made Lambda Toolkit.

Code: Java17_Part_8_Functional_Programming on GitHub

docs.title: Declaring lambda parameters
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · How Lambdas See the Variables Around Them · 1/4

Parameters are the values a lambda receives when it runs. You can declare them in three ways.

docs.title: Three styles
docs.text:
Predicate<Movie> a = m -> m.isAvailable();          // no type
Predicate<Movie> b = (var m) -> m.isAvailable();    // var
Predicate<Movie> c = (Movie m) -> m.isAvailable();  // real type

Predicate<Movie> d = var m -> m.isAvailable();      // ❌ does not compile

All three valid lines do the same thing. The difference is the parentheses:

  • No type: with exactly one parameter, the parentheses are optional.
  • var: Java infers the type, but the parentheses become mandatory.
  • Real type: the parentheses are mandatory, and the type must match what the interface expects.

Parentheses can disappear only for a single parameter with no type at all.

docs.title: Where the type comes from
docs.text:
With no type or var, Java reads the type from the context, the place where the lambda is used:

Predicate<User> adult = u -> u.age() >= 18;          // the variable: u is a User

void watch(Consumer<Episode> c, Episode e) { c.accept(e); }
watch((var ep) -> ep.play(), pilot);                 // the method: ep is an Episode

void sort(List<String> titles) {
    titles.sort((var a, var b) -> a.compareTo(b));   // the list: a and b are Strings
}

To find a parameter's type, ask: what is this lambda assigned to, or passed to?

docs.title: One style per lambda
docs.text:
All the parameters of one lambda use the same style:

❌ Mixed ✅ Consistent (var t, r) -> t.isEmpty() (t, r) -> t.isEmpty() (var t, String r) -> true (var t, var r) -> true (String t, var r, Integer s) -> 1 (String t, String r, Integer s) -> 1 (Integer s, e) -> "Pilot" (Integer s, Integer e) -> "Pilot"

To fix a mixed list, add var or a type to every parameter, or remove it from all of them. var and real types can't be combined either.

docs.title: final and annotations
docs.text:
Like method parameters, lambda parameters accept modifiers:

Consumer<Episode> c1 = (final var e) -> e.play();
Consumer<Episode> c2 = (@Deprecated Episode e) -> e.play();
titles.sort((final var a, @Deprecated var b) -> a.compareTo(b));

Consumer<Episode> c3 = (final e) -> e.play();        // ❌ does not compile

final stops the parameter from being reassigned in the body. A modifier needs something to attach to: var or a real type. You'll rarely need this in real code.

Parameters are what the lambda receives. Next: what it creates inside its own body.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_8_Functional_Programming on GitHub

Next: variables inside the block →

docs.title: Variables inside a lambda block
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · How Lambdas See the Variables Around Them · 2/4

With curly braces, a lambda body becomes a normal Java block: it can declare variables, use if statements and loops.

docs.title: A block with local variables
docs.text:
BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> totalEpisodes = (seasons, perSeason) -> {
    int bonus = 1;
    int count = seasons * perSeason;
    return count + bonus;
};

System.out.println(totalEpisodes.apply(3, 8));   // 25
  • bonus and count exist only while the lambda runs. Code outside the braces can't see them.
  • A block that produces a value needs return, and a ; after each statement.
  • The assignment itself still ends with };: forgetting that last semicolon is a classic mistake.

docs.title: Lambdas share the method's scope
docs.text:
A lambda doesn't get a fresh world for names: it lives inside the scope of the method around it. This version has three mistakes:

void binge(int season) {
    int count = 0;
    Predicate<Integer> p = season -> {   // ❌ season is already a parameter
        int count = 5;                   // ❌ count already exists
        return season > count; }         // ❌ no ; after the closing brace
}

The fix uses fresh names and closes the statement:

void binge(int season) {
    int count = 0;
    Predicate<Integer> p = ep -> {
        int limit = 5;
        return ep > limit; };
}
Rule Why No reusing a parameter name season is still in scope when the lambda is declared No redeclaring a local count is already declared in the method End the statement with }; the ; inside belongs to return, not to the assignment

The same rule applies to the lambda's own parameter: inside m -> { int m = 0; … }, m is already defined.

These clashes are rare in real code, but they appear as soon as lambdas grow long: one more reason to keep them short.

The last place is the trickiest: variables the lambda borrows from outside.

💻 Code: Java17_Part_8_Functional_Programming on GitHub

← Declaring parameters · Next: the effectively final rule →

docs.title: Borrowing variables: the effectively final rule
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · How Lambdas See the Variables Around Them · 3/4

A lambda can use variables from the class or method around it, but not all of them on the same terms.

Variable Can the lambda use it? Instance and static fields ✅ always, and it can even change them Method parameters ✅ only if final or effectively final Local variables ✅ only if final or effectively final

docs.title: Effectively final
docs.text:
A variable is effectively final when it's assigned once and never reassigned, before or after the lambda, even without the final keyword.

Quick test: add final in front of it in your head. If the code still compiles, it's effectively final.

docs.title: The rule in action
docs.text:
import java.util.function.Consumer;

public class Player {
    private String quality = "HD";

    public void start(String title) {
        String device = "TV";
        Consumer<String> show = u ->
            System.out.println(u + ": " + title + " on " + device + " in " + quality);  // ❌ device
        quality = "4K";   // ✅ a field
        device = "Phone"; // makes device not effectively final
        show.accept("Ana");
    }
}
  • quality is a field: changing it is fine. The lambda reads the current value when it runs.
  • title is never reassigned, so it's effectively final.
  • device is reassigned, so it loses its status. The compiler reports the error on the lambda line, not on the reassignment:
error: local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final

Remove device = "Phone"; and it compiles and prints Ana: Dune on TV in 4K for start("Dune"). Note the 4K: the field changed before the lambda ran.

Changing a captured local inside the lambda is illegal too: u -> device = "Phone" doesn't compile. A lambda can read a captured local, never modify it.

docs.title: Why the rule exists
docs.text:
A lambda can run later, long after the line that created it (deferred execution). Java copies the value of the local variable into the lambda, so that value must not change behind its back. Fields don't have this problem: the lambda reads them through the object each time.

docs.title: Lab: turning a long lambda into a method reference
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · How Lambdas See the Variables Around Them · 4/4

Goal: refactor a filter buried in a block lambda into a named method, then a method reference, and prove all versions behave the same.

Setup: create Movie.java and CatalogFilter.java in the same folder, with no package.

docs.title: Step 1 — The data
docs.text: public record Movie(String title, int minutes, double rating) { }

docs.title: Step 2 — The "before" version
docs.text:
Start CatalogFilter.java:

import java.util.function.Predicate;

public class CatalogFilter {

    // Before: logic buried in a lambda
    Predicate<Movie> hit = m -> {
        int minMinutes = 90;
        double minRating = 4.0;
        return m.minutes() >= minMinutes
            && m.rating() > minRating;
    };

Braces, two locals and a return: a warning sign. The reader must work through every line to learn what's checked, and no name says "feature hit".

Try adding int m = 0; under minRating: the compiler answers variable m is already defined, because the body shares the scope of its parameter. Delete that line.

docs.title: Step 3 — Name it, then reference it
docs.text:
// Step 1: give the logic a name
    boolean isFeatureHit(Movie m) {
        return m.minutes() >= 90 && m.rating() > 4.0;
    }

    // Step 2: a one-line lambda...
    Predicate<Movie> p1 = m -> isFeatureHit(m);

    // Step 3: ...or a method reference
    Predicate<Movie> p2 = this::isFeatureHit;
  • isFeatureHit states the intent, is reusable and testable, and its m lives in its own method scope.
  • p1 only forwards its parameter, so it can become this::isFeatureHit: it fits Predicate<Movie> (takes a Movie, returns a boolean).

docs.title: Step 4 — Prove they agree
docs.text:
public static void main(String[] args) {
        CatalogFilter filter = new CatalogFilter();   // this::isFeatureHit needs a real object

        Movie[] catalog = {
            new Movie("Inception", 148, 4.8),
            new Movie("Night Drive", 95, 4.1),
            new Movie("Coffee Break Shorts", 22, 4.5),
            new Movie("The Endless Saga", 160, 3.2),
            new Movie("Ninety Minutes Flat", 90, 4.0)
        };

        for (Movie movie : catalog) {
            System.out.println(movie.title()
                + " -> before: " + filter.hit.test(movie)
                + " | lambda: " + filter.p1.test(movie)
                + " | method ref: " + filter.p2.test(movie));
        }
    }
}

Predict first: Ninety Minutes Flat passes on minutes (>=) but fails on rating (> 4.0, not >=).

$ javac Movie.java CatalogFilter.java && java CatalogFilter
Inception -> before: true | lambda: true | method ref: true
Night Drive -> before: true | lambda: true | method ref: true
Coffee Break Shorts -> before: false | lambda: false | method ref: false
The Endless Saga -> before: false | lambda: false | method ref: false
Ninety Minutes Flat -> before: false | lambda: false | method ref: false

Every row agrees. Same behavior, very different readability: this::isFeatureHit tells the whole story in one line. Refactoring changes how clearly code says something, never what it does.

docs.title: OCP exam prep: lambda variables
docs.text:
☕ Java 17 · 🎓 OCP 1Z0-829 · How Lambdas See the Variables Around Them

Optional page

This page is for readers preparing the Oracle Certified Professional Java SE 17 Developer exam (1Z0-829). The concepts are all you need otherwise.

Exam objective: Create and use lambda expressions, including local variables and effectively final variables.

docs.title: Four traps to watch for
docs.text:
Trap 1 — var and types need parentheses

var m -> … and Movie m -> … never compile. Parentheses are optional only for one parameter with no type and no modifier.

Trap 2 — Count the styles in the list

Check every parameter: no type, var, or real type. Any mix, like (var a, b) or (String a, var b), is a compile error.

Trap 3 — Name clashes and semicolons

A lambda parameter or block local can't reuse a name already in scope. In block lambdas, look for the ; after the closing brace.

Trap 4 — Reassigned anywhere = not allowed

A local or parameter changed before or after the lambda can't be used in it. The error points at the lambda, not at the reassignment: read the whole method.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text:
1. Which lambda can fill the blank?

BiPredicate<String, Integer> longTitle = ____________;

A. (var t, n) -> t.length() > n B. (String t, var n) -> t.length() > n C. (var t, var n) -> t.length() > n D. var t, var n -> t.length() > n

Answer

C. Same style for both, in parentheses. A mixes var with no type, B mixes a real type with var, D drops the mandatory parentheses.

2. How many lines cause a compilation error?

1: public void rate(Movie movie) {
2:     double avg = 4.2;
3:     Predicate<Movie> hit = movie -> {
4:         double avg = 4.5;
5:         return movie.rating() > avg; };
6: }

A. None B. One, line 4 C. Two, lines 3 and 4 D. Three, lines 3, 4 and 5

Answer

C. Line 3 reuses movie, already a method parameter. Line 4 redeclares avg. Line 5 is fine: it ends with };.

3. What is the result of calling start() with a valid User?

1: public void start(User user) {
2:     int profiles = user.profiles();
3:     Supplier<String> info = () -> user.name() + profiles;
4:     profiles++;
5:     System.out.println(info.get());
6: }

A. It prints the name and the original count B. It prints the name and the count + 1 C. Compiler error on line 3 D. Compiler error on line 4

Answer

C. Line 4 reassigns profiles, so it's no longer effectively final, and the compiler reports it where the lambda uses it: line 3. user never changes, so it's fine.

← Back to the series · All 1Z0-829 pages

docs.title: Part 8 recap: functional programming
docs.text:
☕ Java 17

Everything from Part 8 on one page. Each block links back to its section if you want the details.

docs.title: Lambda syntax
docs.text:
A lambda is a method with no name, passed around like a value.

Predicate<Movie> a = m -> m.hd();                     // shortest form
Predicate<Movie> b = (Movie m) -> m.hd();             // explicit type
Predicate<Movie> c = (var m) -> m.hd();               // var
Predicate<Movie> d = m -> { return m.hd(); };         // block body
BiPredicate<Movie, User> e = (m, u) -> u.canWatch(m); // two parameters
Supplier<Movie> f = () -> new Movie("Pilot", 2024);   // no parameter
  • Parentheses can be dropped only for exactly one parameter with no type.
  • No braces: one expression, no return, no ;. Braces: a real block, with return when a value is expected and ; after every statement.
  • One style for all parameters: none, all typed, or all var.

→ Passing Behavior Around with Lambdas

docs.title: Functional interfaces
docs.text:
A functional interface has exactly one abstract method, the one the lambda implements.

@FunctionalInterface
interface ContentFilter {
    boolean keep(Movie m);                                  // the one that counts
    default ContentFilter not() { return m -> !keep(m); }  // has a body: free
    static ContentFilter all() { return m -> true; }       // has a body: free
    String toString();                                      // from Object: free
}

default, static and private methods have a body, so they don't count. Abstract methods with the exact signature of an Object method (toString(), equals(Object), hashCode()) don't count either. @FunctionalInterface is optional: it only asks the compiler to check the rule. → The One-Method Contract Behind Every Lambda

docs.title: Method references
docs.text:
Kind Example Same as Static method Math::round x -> Math.round(x) Method on a known object history::contains t -> history.contains(t) Method on the parameter Movie::title m -> m.title() Constructor Watchlist::new () -> new Watchlist()

Use :: only when the lambda just forwards its parameters to one method: m -> m.rating() > 4 stays a lambda. → Passing Methods Around by Name

docs.title: Built-in interfaces
Variables and lambdas
docs.text: A lambda can use a local variable or parameter only if it's final or effectively final: never reassigned, anywhere in the method. The error shows on the lambda line. Fields are always fine, and can even be changed. Lambda parameters and block variables can't reuse a name already in scope. → How Lambdas See the Variables Around Them

docs.title: Everything together
docs.text:
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.*;

public class RecentDramas {
    enum Genre { DRAMA, COMEDY }
    record Movie(String title, int year, Genre genre) { }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Movie> catalog = List.of(
            new Movie("Midnight Harbor", 2022, Genre.DRAMA),
            new Movie("Laugh Track", 2021, Genre.COMEDY),
            new Movie("Old Wounds", 2018, Genre.DRAMA),
            new Movie("Silent Shore", 2023, Genre.DRAMA));

        Predicate<Movie> recent = m -> m.year() >= 2020;
        Predicate<Movie> drama = m -> m.genre() == Genre.DRAMA;
        Function<Movie, String> label = Movie::title;
        Consumer<String> show = System.out::println;

        for (Movie m : catalog)
            if (recent.and(drama).test(m))
                show.accept(label.apply(m));
    }
}

Midnight Harbor
Silent Shore

Each business rule is its own Predicate, method references replace forwarding lambdas, and nothing runs until test(), apply() or accept() is called: deferred execution.
